Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand their labels based on local, class-specific confidence rather than global, informative uncertainty. To address this issue, we introduce informative pseudo-labeling for Graph Neural Networks with limited data, which focuses on generating pseudo-labels for the most uncertain and informative nodes within each class. We achieve this by introducing a global uncertainty measure based on multiple criteria, including the impact of removing a node from the graph, the within-class distance, and the class imbalance. We then conduct a comprehensive set of experiments on various graph datasets and compare our proposed method against existing semi-supervised Graph Neural Network approaches. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our informative pseudo-labeling approach, achieving a 6% average improvement in accuracy over current pseudo-labeling techniques, with an impressive 1% increase in within-class accuracy. The source code for our informative pseudo-labeling approach can be found on the GitHub page at https://github.com/ExIron/Informative-Pseudo-labeling. Our research has been recognized with an Outstanding Paper award at the ACML2021 conference.

With a dataset comprising 400 million student records across 12 countries and 3 continents from 11 institutions, this model capitalizes on the wealth of historical enrollment examination information. By incorporating theoretical insights on academic pathways, the approach incorporates relevant features such as program characteristics, student attributes, and time-based factors.

In-depth analyses of three universities illustrate the effectiveness of this approach in mapping student enrollment patterns and identifying unexpected trends, highlighting its utility in policy research and education. Further research will explore the use of this model in policy research and education settings. A tool allowing university administrators to explore the visual representation of pathway models has also been developed, offering a starting point for an open dialogue between models and stakeholders. 

It's worth noting that while this research explores the potential applications of this approach, its primary goal remains the investigation of the efficacy of latent variable models in representing complex, multi-periodic data. A future direction could be the incorporation of prior knowledge regarding the underlying structure of these models in the form of constraints. By doing so, they can enhance the models' interpretability and provide universally applicable insights. A related but distinct challenge lies in the representation of pathway probability distributions over time within the context of the structural time-series model. 

Moreover, there are many variations of the basic latent variable model, each addressing a distinct aspect. For instance, semi-supervised models integrate both labeled and unlabeled data, semi-nonparametric models incorporate feedback from users, and linear and nonlinear models differentiate themselves based on their underlying matrix factorization structures or the presence of noise. A comprehensive understanding of these variations and their relevance to the problem at hand can significantly improve the models' performance in representing academic pathways. 

It's also demonstrated that the success of the described approach primarily lies in the accurate extraction of relevant features, which serve as a common foundation for all models. By employing both quantitative and qualitative methods of analysis, they can understand the underlying causes of enrollment patterns and eliminate noise. Moreover, they can leverage theory-driven and theory-inspired approaches to incorporate prior knowledge regarding program and student characteristics.

Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is addressed through a game-theoretic framework. When some vehicles in the platoon communicate with each other, while others do not, this study examines the strategies that stable and proactive vehicles adopt to avoid collisions and maintain a safe distance between one another within the context of a differential game. By extending the concepts of stability and existence to accommodate this scenario, it has been demonstrated through an example that the trajectories of both stable and proactive vehicles can converge towards a common point. Moreover, this study explores various control approaches that can be used to move the trajectories of the non-cooperative vehicles towards a more cooperative state, and it illustrates through an actual experiment that our proposed methodology can effectively guide the behavior of the non-cooperative vehicles towards a more cooperative state. The benefits of forming vehicle platoons in terms of reduced fuel consumption and lowered emissions are confirmed via simulation data. Furthermore, it has been observed that the formation of vehicle platoons can persist even after the communication link between some vehicles is lost. The stability of the vehicle platoon is also analyzed under various adverse conditions such as the presence of additive and multiplicative disturbances. A number of control approaches have been proposed to address this issue, and it has been demonstrated through an actual experiment that our proposed methodologies can effectively maintain the stability of the vehicle platoon within the context of a differential game. One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). When dealing with large machine learning models such as logistic regression, minimizing data and model parallelism can lead to extremely high communication costs. This research explores ways to parallelize SGD to minimize communication by maintaining synchronization at a finer granularity. We developed a communication-avoiding (CA) SGD approach for logistic regression, incorporating two different communication schedules. Experimental results on a 32-node cluster reveal that CA-SGD can reduce average communication by a 2.6-fold factor, also yielding a 0.04% performance increase compared to the conventional parallel SGD method. Furthermore, CA-SGD has the added benefit of allowing for a significant increase in step size, resulting in 2.5 times faster convergence. This capability makes CA-SGD not only suitable for logistics regression but also other scalable machine learning algorithms. This approach may be applied to any optimization algorithm although the current logic is inflexible and cannot be easily modified without altering the underlying code. A more flexible and extensible modification of CA-SGD is then presented, revealing opportunities for further improvement by integrating computational and communication operations. This concept is developed into an open-source C++ library called SpGSMm. We then examine various optimization methods, incorporating two communication schedules for each, and evaluate their performance across different step size policies. Ultimately, SpGSMm reveals that a majority (51.8%) of its methods demonstrate superior performance to vanilla SGD on the entire dataset, while 35.9% of its methods fail to improve upon it. This work serves as the foundation upon which SpGSMm was built and explains its inner workings. Moreover, SpGSMm has been utilized in training model average (TMA) for the 2021 DGX-Ray Automatic Model Selection (AMS) competition as specified by the competition, leading to second and third placements out of 64 entries. The local rules used in SpGSMm were pivotal to its success. This is particularly evident when comparing the performance of local rule 'proactive' on the AMS test dataset, with a model quality loss of 0.0006 when utilizing model average training, whereas all other local rules yield a loss greater than 0.1 when combined with model averaging. Consequently, the SpGSMm library was employed not only in influential model selection but also in a crucial application. It is worth noting that parts of this thesis were initially presented at the 2021, 2022, and 2023 conferences

The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet and social media significantly impacts public perception and user behavior, with generative models now making it quicker and cheaper to produce fake content. To safeguard users against misinformation in the near future, distinguishing deep learning model-generated content will be essential. For this purpose, researchers have compiled a dataset consisting of human and artificially generated headlines and discovered that humans have difficulty identifying the fabricated headlines in a substantial majority of cases. On the other hand, the most effective automatic method employed in this context, specifically transformers, demonstrated impressive accuracy, successfully filtering out around 85.7% of the content produced by language models. Notably, when applied to content produced by pre-trained language models in a limited capacity, it successfully filtered out more than 90% of the content. The findings suggest considerable potential for enhancing the capabilities of transformers in the near future. The dataset and the source code can be accessed at https://github.com/kaihax/GENERATED-TITLES. The paper has been published in the proceedings of WWW '23. 

Key words: Natural Language Processing, Generated Content, Transformers, HTTP Headers Analysis, Classification.

Future large-scale radio interferometers aim to detect 21\,cm signals across vast distances. To optimize cost, upcoming facilities should be built with hundreds of antennas, utilizing a uniform layout to minimize infrastructure expenses. However, traditional online data processing methods used in the field lead to computational costs that become economically unfeasible for a large number of antennas. To overcome this challenge, we investigate offline data processing methods, comparing their performance. We find that with the advancement of consumer-grade hardware, processing data offline can become the more appealing option. We further introduce a novel data processing method, dubbed the Calibrated Gridded Data Matrix (CGDM), and demonstrate that it requires proportionally less computing power to produce comparable results across a large array with hundreds of antennas. The CGDM's scalability enables it to process data from a large array with conventional hardware, while maintaining high precision. By using the CGDM with the simulation data from the SKA1-SUR, SKA2, FAST, and GRIF projects, we demonstrate its effectiveness in producing accurate results. The CGDM's computational complexity remains at $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$, making it a suitable choice for offline data processing in large-scale radio interferometers built on a regular grid with hundreds of antennas. By adopting the CGDM, it becomes feasible to significantly increase the size of large-scale radio interferometers built on a regular grid with conventional hardware, such as those found in China and Europe. Furthermore, this new method allows for the integration of a large-scale array with various facilities, enabling the evaluation of its performance with realistic simulations. By Interconnecting these facilities, it becomes possible to achieve high-performance, large-scale single-pixel imaging over an enormous area using the test beam method. To showcase the feasibility of this idea, we demonstrate a test beam mode using simulated data from the FAST telescope, and with online processing, we achieve high-quality, large-scale imaging results. By extrapolating this approach, we believe it will be possible to obtain high-quality, large-scale imaging results over an enormous area with the upcoming large-scale interferometers. For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for in-depth portfolio analysis but it places an excessive focus on understanding market uncertainty, failing to prioritize other essential factors like a fund's geographical and sectorial distributions.  In order to address these issues, we have developed a novel method that combines a Gradient Penalty with a Latent Representation, allowing for a more detailed examination of potential risks and rewards at multiple levels.  By training an autoencoder to capture underlying market patterns, and using the Variational Autoencoder-based Conditional GAN to generate diversified and allocable portfolios that meet specific investment targets, as proven by results on both simulated and real-world datasets.  Characterized by reduced trace, a more stable performance with less volatility is achieved along with enhanced diversification benefits that meet the specified targets.  It is observed that this class of models outperforms Markowitz portfolios in terms of both overall returns and sectorial stability.  The research also highlights the significant role that geographical distribution plays in investment.  Portfolio performance is evaluated across various metrics including mean, volatility, skewness, and drawdown to confirm the validity of our model.  Additionally, a Feature Importance analysis is used to determine the impact of specific market indices on portfolio behavior.  The research was tested using real-world dataset including assets from the S\&P 500, DAX, CAC 40, and FTSE 100 markets.  The models and data are available for download on https://github.com/Gr4phical/AcGAN-Markowitz.  Further research can focus on expanding our approach to broader markets, incorporating additional factors like environmental, social, and governance metrics, and exploring its applicability to multi-asset markets.  Furthermore, our approach may be suitably modified for application in level II Quantitative Easing analysis. A groundbreaking method utilizing Bayesian neural networks enhances the accuracy of classifying gamma-ray sources. The study focuses on identifying Fermi-LAT blazar candidates, comprising BL Lacertae objects and Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars. By incorporating Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MLE) layer in the neural network, the model's output predicts the 95% confidence interval for each classification result. The introduction of this novel algorithm yields improved classification efficiency for neibouring source classes. The study achieves overall classification accuracy of approximately 92.7% for three categories: BL Lacertae objects, Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars, and Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars without a measured redshift. Furthermore, a new system is proposed for expressing uncertainty in classification and the model's performance is evaluated against other recent algorithms in the field. The study's code will be made accessible through the known platform to facilitate future research. The research also explores the relationship between neural network uncertainty and the physical characteristics of the sources. The study's results include a new catalog featuring 341 blazar candidates, offering valuable insights into the method's performance. The analysis reveals that high uncertainty in the classification of BL Lacertae objects is associated with smaller statistical sample, lower luminosity, and a broader luminosity function, while positive classification with high uncertainty indicates large statistical sample, higher optical luminosity, and a broader luminosity function. The study highlights the necessity of considering the uncertainty in the classification for the assessment of physical blazar characteristics. fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this content remains inaccessible to many users, 
despite available solutions that aim to reduce this form of exclusion. Our research 
involved surveying 258 social media users and interviewing 20 participants, with 7 of 
them having visual impairments, to understand their perceptions of online content 
and how support tools are utilized. Our analysis of the results reveals that 
platforms' efforts are inadequate, and that mainstream users often aren't aware 
of accessible practices. By exploring the views of end-users on accessible 
practices, barriers they face, and motivating factors, we also suggest further 
approaches to boost user engagement and raise awareness about accessibility. 
Ultimately, we recommend that platforms adopt more effective strategies to 
enhance the accessibility of user-generated content. Our key recommendations 
involve offering clearer explanations of features in each platform's respective 
help sections, and making accessible content more visible to all users, not just

create accessible content using voice alone, rather than requiring typing, which

In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations using tensors and demonstrate the equivalence of three formulations within this framework. We establish that any operation between two hypergraphs must also be applicable to the tensor-based representations of these graphs. This allows us to identify and analyze certain properties of hypergraphs operated upon in this manner and to provide examples of such properties. Specifically, we determine the spectral characteristics of hypergraphs formed through tensor-based tensor and glue operations. The results can be extended to more general settings involving multiple input hypergraphs. Furthermore, our research reveals a connection between certain tensor-based operations and the Cartesian product of graphs, as well as properties and spectral characteristics of hypergraphs formed through tensor joins. This research not only offers a unified framework for hypergraph operations but also enables the efficient computation and analysis of such operations. We illustrate the utility of our approach by applying it to real-world data, demonstrating its value in analyzing complex hypergraph structures. The proposed approach has been implemented in the open-source tool, LGM. A shared repository containing the data, used in our analysis, can be found at https://github.com/amirveyseh/Hypergraph-Based-Data-Analysis. In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time using repeated measurements, the measure of change often follows a nonlinear trajectory. Linear and logistic models are commonly inadequate to capture this change, necessitating models like mixed effects or spline-based models that can accommodate nonlinear patterns. Recent advancements in digital cognitive assessment tools have increased the likelihood of incorporating more precise, high-resolution outcomes in model frameworks. We advocate for the use of natural cubic splines (NCS) as a primary method to capture a treatment's time-dependent effects in linear models, incorporating single observations of change scores as outcomes. NCS can address several limitations associated with mixed models, such as noncompliance, provide robust inference without the need for residual diagnostics, and offer efficient computation through matrix operations. This approach also has appealing statistical properties, including unbiased estimation and stability and differentiability across time points. Utilizing data from the donepezil donepezil-donepezil vs placebo-donepezil vs placebo donepezil vs placebo trial, we demonstrate through simulation that the approach strongly resists both model- and non-model-related residual effects. Donepezil's estimated effect is found to be significant at p = 3.8 x 10(-5) with 95% confidence intervals ranging from 0.80 to 1.18. Finally, the methodology is expanded to analyze donepezil's time-dependent effects in recent trials. A novel computational strategy called Action-CSA is introduced, enabling the global exploration of reaction pathways via optimization of the Onsager-Machlup action using conformational space annealing. Action-CSA is capable of sampling multiple reaction pathways without initial guesses and successfully captures both the most dominant pathway and a variety of alternative routes. Pathway diversity is maintained through a crossover operation, facilitating the efficient sampling of pathway space. Action-CSA is evaluated by identifying reaction pathways for alanine dipeptide and hexane, demonstrating strong agreement between the approach and extensive molecular dynamics simulations regarding pathway ranks and transition times. Moreover, Action-CSA identifies a mini-protein folding pathway that matches existing molecular dynamics simulations and experimental findings. Notably, the strategy identifies a diverse set of reaction pathways within several hundred nanoseconds, significantly outperforming existing metadynamics and stratanalysis approaches. Action-CSA presents significant potential as a valuable tool in protein and chemical systems, enabling the efficient exploration of energy landscape and rate limiting factors with or without the use of auxiliary variables. It effectively identifies multiple reaction pathways without initial guesses and opens up opportunities for constructing a complete reaction network through the systematic exploration of pathway space. The approach can be extended to explore the space of pathways by adding latent variables to the action function. Finally, the long-standing debate on the rate-limiting factors of hexane can be resolved via Action-CSA, which successfully identifies a diverse set of criteria consistent with existing knowledge and experimental findings. However, the optimization strategy does not converge to a single solution. Instead, the diverse solutions indicate uncertainty in system optimization. It is notable that the approach presents significant potential in exploring energy landscapes in systems of interest. In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by non-orthogonal grant-free access with low signaling overhead. This research proposes a novel two-stage approach using a genetic algorithm (GA) to generate user-specific sequences for low-latency grant-free uplink access. First, the initial GA finds a subsampling strategy to transform a lattice with evenly spaced sequences into a more packed layout. Subsequently, the second-stage GA, utilizing sequence-subsampling pairs, identifies user-specific sequences for granted units, ensuring each unit has a unique sequence or precode to combat collisions. These unit sequences combine to form the final set of active sequences, addressing both sequence-and-subsampling collaboration for optimizing active sequence performance. This method offers automated sequence design without needing intricate hyperparameters, ensuring efficiency in computational resources. This method also uses underlaid lattice sequences to actively mitigate multi-user interference. Simulation results show that our proposed two-stage design can achieve better performance than conventional methods, such as random sequences or orthogonal sequences with projected sequences allocation (OSA), by reducing the detection probability of false alarms by 30% and 25.6% for different values of active users, while maintaining a similar false alarm rate as OSA. This method also shows enhanced computational efficiency in sequence design. This method has been tested and validated to work with a real-world 5G new radio (NR) uplink field, providing grant-free active sequence performance that outperforms existing methods. A few approaches to model the thermodynamic behavior of moist air rely on approximations that can lead to inconsistencies in accordance with the 1st and 2nd laws of thermodynamics. A new strategy has emerged that aims to eliminate these inconsistencies by leveraging thermodynamic potentials derived from their natural variables. In this paper, this strategy is applied to both exact thermodynamic descriptions and two commonly employed approximations. By utilizing a consistent framework, it becomes possible to determine the required extensive variables. A dynamic model benefiting from thermodynamic consistency has also been developed and tested in a simulation environment. Although the strategy offers a means to circumvent the resolution of complex thermodynamic problems, it is essential to note that the resulting simplifications may not be applicable in specific instances where the thermodynamic framework is expansive enough to account for variations in the characteristics of moisture. A discussion on the applicability of the strategy in atmospheric models in the presence of interactions with the ocean and as part of global climate models is also presented. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the strategy has the potential to expand the time-frame of such models. Furthermore, a new approach to the treatment of interactions between the atmosphere and oceans is proposed, one that relies on the derivation of a dependent extensive enthalpy for simplicity. A test simulation using this method reveals an improvement in accuracy in atmospheric models when applied in conjunction with the thermodynamically consistent framework for use in both fine-scale local models and global climate simulations. A discussion on the strategy's potential to contribute to the understanding of atmospheric dynamics, in particular to the resolution of systematic and subscale interactions, is also presented. This enables the analysis of dynamic effects with a focus on the generation of weather patterns and the potential for their maintenance. Ultimately, the strategy's potential contribution to the reduction of model uncertainty by means of systematic error analysis is presented. A discussion on the strategy's potential to be applied across a diverse array of complex multi-phase multi-component fluid models in the presence of a variety of complex phase interactions is presented. This includes an examination of its potential to be applied in models of the behavior of aging materials in construction (asbestos), the modeling of dynamic behavior in solutions containing polymers, the treatment of the flow of molten metals during the casting process and the simulation of dynamic systems containing suspensions that move through pipes. This in turn may ultimately enable the reduction of the resulting model uncertainty on the model's predictions for the dynamic behavior of such complex systems. Research on dialogue state tracking from transcribed speech, a crucial component of dialogue systems, has received little attention due to the dominance of text-based approaches. However, neural architectures for automatic speech recognition (ASR) continue to demonstrate superior performance over traditional methods. This work investigates the integration of neural ASR and dialogue state tracking, highlighting the need for a systematic approach to address the resulting ASR ambiguity. We develop a confidence measure for the ASR output using a confusion network of nearby words. This confidence measure is applied to the training of a neural dialogue state tracker. Empirical results reveal that the proposed confidence measure effectively mitigates ASR ambiguity and, when combined with a tracker, results in improved performance on the SDK 1.0.02 dataset compared to using accurate transcribed data. Moreover, the study shows that the ASR output confidence measure can be utilized in other neural dialogue state tracking architectures. The source code and data will be made accessible via GitHub. The work is initially presented at IJCAI 2020. An updated version of this article was published in 2021.

As social media increasingly influences public perceptions globally, researchers have focused on tackling the pervasive issue of hate speech online. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as heightened social divisions and violent crimes. Previous studies have employed automated hate speech detection methods, but they often fall short by overlooking broader social and cultural contexts. Furthermore, few attempts have been made to explore the explainability of such models, given the severe social and legal repercussions of inaccurate predictions. Our research introduces a sophisticated, deep learning-based framework that integrates multimodal inputs: (a) to accurately recognize hate speech by analyzing the underlying meaning of tweets and (b) to provide transparent interpretations of the models' decision-making processes. Our proposed framework surpasses baseline models and serves as a significant contribution in explaining the models' behavior. Our analysis reveals that the majority of errors in our framework occur on well-known, strongly classified hate speech data, while its failures often involve nuanced, context-dependent instances of hate speech and non-hate speech. This research aims to shed light on the importance of developing multimodal, automated hate speech detection models that are both accurate and interpretable. Our work also addresses limitations in current models and sheds light on the logic behind their behavior. Our analysis provides insights for enhancing the precision of such models, especially with regard to detecting hate speech in its more subtle forms. Our comprehensive evaluation is based on the recent 11k dataset, containing 11,000 annotated tweets on 4 categories of hate speech and non-hate speech. Our interpretation of the models' logic is presented through a form of backward propagation, starting with the model's output and moving backwards through the different input modalities. Our work explores the interpretability of the models by analyzing the role of different features (such as the presence of a user name, the text of the tweet and the profile picture) in the model's decision-making process through experiments and analysis. Our experiments and analysis reveal that the models are influenced more by the text of the tweet and the presence of a user name compared to the profile picture. Our research also highlights the influence of different words in the tweet and their importance in the model's decision-making process through various experiments and analysis. Our experiments and analysis assume that the features influencing the model's decision-making process are those that are present in the model's input (i.e. the text of the tweet). We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, building on earlier work which revealed that these networks exhibit either periodic or bifurcated states depending on the network's connection configuration. This work extends these findings to theta neurons with inhibitory connections and reveals that degree distributions significantly impact the behavior of these networks. By applying a reduced model and solving the associated equation, we identify and analytically calculate the stability boundaries for period-one and period-two orbits. Furthermore, through a combination of numerical integration and Monte Carlo simulation, we establish the degree distribution that triggers bifurcation and transitions from periodic to chaotic states in these theta neuron networks. Our analysis also shows that these theta neuron networks exhibit distinct trends in the bifurcation diagram compared to those of simple neurons, highlighting the significance of incorporating theta neurons. Ultimately, our work emphasizes the importance of considering the biophysical and topological properties of neuronal networks when designing and interpreting experimental results. The findings presented have implications for the development of artificial networks and understanding natural neural circuits. The analytical approach used in this work demonstrates that degree distributions can significantly impact the behavior of these theta neuron networks. Given the limited understanding of this effect, our analysis offers valuable insights. Consequently, this work contributes to the advancement of artificial and computational neurosciences by acknowledging the role of degree distributions in neuronal network dynamics. Furthermore, these findings could influence the modification of biological neural networks for the cultivation of self-emerging properties. The content of this thesis adds to the body of knowledge in this field and sheds light on a previously understudied aspect of neuronal network dynamics. The contribution of this content can be evaluated using metrics such as the Hirsch index or impact factors, which indicate the significance of this work to the neurosciences and theoretical neurosciences. The approach used in this study is empirical. The specific question addressed by this study is whether neural networks with theta neurons and inhibitory connections exhibit distinct trends in the bifurcation diagram and behavior as the degree distribution changes. This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel with interconnected user pairs, characterized by a collection of interconnected rectangles, with each rectangle defined by paired rates of mutual information. While this formula is computationally impractical in most cases due to its information-theoretic complexity, it provides valuable insights into the nature of channel capacity. By narrowing the scope to a specific class of interference relationships and leveraging graphical representations, we develop an algorithm that significantly simplifies capacity calculations, yielding results for previously unaddressable interference channels. Furthermore, we illustrate the algorithm's value with exemplary applications to previously unsolved interference channels. At the time of writing, this paper presents the first known capacity region formula for the 'chain' and 'cube' interference channels, with the latter also known as the 'cube problem'. Moreover, this paper's results not only enhance our understanding of these channels, but they are also adaptable to a wider range of interference relationships with shared resources, making the formulated capacity region an essential tool in network coding and cognitive radio research. Finally, this paper's reduction of information-theoretic complexity enables the calculation of capacity rates in terms of a collection of coupled rate-ratio distributions, thereby opening the door for future machine learning applications in this area. Such an approach not only sheds new light on the theoretical limitations of communication systems but also sheds light on the nature of complex information-processing tasks. Ultimately, this paper's formulation paves the way for future collaborations between the information-theoretic and machine learning communities on a range of interference channels and related systems. Numerical simulations provide additional insights into the nature of capacity. Our experimental findings, which include the generation of closed-form capacity formulas for the cube and chain channels, highlight the significant practical value of the formulated algorithm. By extending its application to the recently-introduced multi-antenna cube problem, this paper's formulation drives further breakthroughs in this area. At the time of writing, this problem remains an unsolved challenge in the field of communication systems, with the reduction of information-theoretic complexity representing a key factor in its capacity calculations. Moreover, this paper's formulation enables the calculation of sum rate capacities that are in line with existing lower bound limits, thereby shedding light on the nature of optimal transmission strategies in this area. Ultimately, this paper's collaborative approach to the reduction of information-theoretic complexity not only enhances our understanding of the multi-antenna cube problem but also opens the door for future research on this topic. To achieve this, we'll create a component that, similar to the direct flow, can isolate the central, nearly spherical component of nuclear collisions. By utilizing a flow framework that's analogous to a cylinder-to-ellipsoid transformation, we'll be able to extract information about the 3-dimensional shape of this central component. Furthermore, we'll be able to explore how this central component is influenced by parameters like beam energy, impact parameter, and participant baryon multiplicity. Additionally, we'll be able to analyze how the various dimensions of this collision are impacted by the properties of the nuclear equation of state. To test the reliability of this new flow technique, we'll apply it to simulations of $Au+Au$ collisions at 200 MeV per nucleon, using the transport model (Quasi-elastic version of UrQMD). We'll then compare the results to experimental data from the FOPI Collaboration. By utilizing this flow technique, we'll be able to derive valuable, participant-centric information about the properties of nuclear matter at various stages of the pre-equilibrium and equilibrium phases, as well as provide significant insights into the complex features of the systems that participate in the nuclear reactions at the Quark-Gluon Plasma and the onset of the critical endpoint phase transition. We'll also be able to provide valuable, detailed insights into the contribution of the radial flow that occurs during the hadronization process. We'll be able to investigate this critical aspect of the system with specific experiments at the STAR, the BESIII, and the NICA colliders. Research into coronavirus detection via clinical data has involved the application of diverse machine learning methods using data such as blood test results and vital signs. However, risks associated with these models, including patient data exposure, pose significant challenges. Furthermore, several studies suggest that these models may experience deterioration when confronted with data from patients who were not part of the training dataset, a phenomenon referred to as "shift learning". In this study, we explore the utilization of adversarial training to train machines to ignore irrelevant information, with an emphasis on protecting patient identity and symptom data through the deliberate introduction of misleading information. We specifically concentrate on distinguishing patients testing positive for COVID-19 from those testing negative using vital sign data. Our study, which entitles "Adversarial training of COVID-19 diagnosis model on obscured patient data," involves training a model to ignore all data components, with results showing improved robustness when confronted with data from patients who were not part of the training dataset. Our study also achieved comparable results to state-of-the-art models trained using patient symptoms, a recent study by Bhojak et al. who achieved an F1-score of 87.11%. Our model achieved an F1-score of 86.95%. These studies provide novel hope for the development of models capable of making COVID-19 diagnoses using vital sign data that are resistant to data manipulations and can be deployed safely and with data privacy considerations in mind. Although this study did not address the specific challenge of identifying patients at risk of severe COVID-19, our study did achieve comparable results to another recent study who achieved an F1-score of 85.51% in identifying severe cases using patient symptoms. A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an essential edge AI technology that builds upon graph convolutional networks. Despite its utility, incorporating GNN models into wireless communication systems poses challenges due to the need to balance computation and communication tradeoffs. To address this, researchers have developed decentralized learning methods using GNNs. This paper examines a specific wireless communication scenario where a base station desires to estimate the distribution of data packets across users via a GNN model. However, the base station does not have prior knowledge of the graph topology, requiring it to resort to statistical machine learning. Notably, the base station needs to estimate the graph's degree distribution, a crucial graph statistic. To resolve this, the paper proposes a degree-agnostic GNN approach, using the Diffusion Graph to approximate the graph and leverage the graph's degree distribution. The proposed approach is based on the matrix perturbation theory and the Laplacian eigenexpansion. Moreover, the paper investigates computing the GNN model in a wireless communication system, incorporating the effects of wireless noise and limited pilot transmission (LPTR) on the base station. Ultimately, the results demonstrate that the proposed approach can efficiently estimate the user data arrival process. Specifically, the performance under heavy-tailed degree distributions reveals that the proposed approach can closely track the empirical degree distribution with a suitable choice of the diffusion parameter. Moreover, the results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a lower mean squared error (MSE) compared to a degree-based GNN model. Interestingly, the proposed approach exhibits a higher degree of robustness to variations in the degree distribution, as evidenced by its performance under different heavy-tailed degree distributions. The proposed approach has a lower MSE for a given choice of the diffusion parameter. Moreover, the proposed approach outperforms the degree-based GNN model in terms of a lower MSE for a given choice of the diffusion parameter. Ultimately, the proposed approach reveals that the GNN model introduces an additional loss in the estimation process, whereas the degree distribution introduces an inherent loss in the estimation process. The tradeoff between these losses depends on the degree distribution, the GNN model, and the diffusion parameter. The proposed approach can be generalized to other wireless communication systems that rely on degree distribution. The proposed approach reveals that the GNN model performs better when the degree distribution has a given polynomial form. Moreover, the proposed approach performs better for a lower value of the parameter in the polynomial. The threat of homicide death tolls has raised concerns worldwide and demands attention from researchers and government officials, a trend observed over the past few decades. This paper investigates a case study in Goias, a Brazilian state, focusing on the relationship between the variables number of homicides and urbanization levels, which is a significant factor to consider in understanding the homicide problem. By applying statistical methods, we derive a correlation matrix for cities with more than 20,000 inhabitants within Goias from 2002 to 2014. Subsequently, we use the hierarchical Agglomerate method to analyze and segment this data. As a result, we identify three distinct clusters, revealing correlations among cities' homicide rates and levels of urbanization, highlighting the significance of urban center size in influencing homicide dynamics. These findings provide valuable insights for government officials and researchers, offering scope for further investigation into the causes of homicide, which vary by region, leading to a better comprehension of the phenomenon and more focused efforts in crime prevention. Moreover, our analysis sheds light on the dynamics of violence, underscoring the importance of urban planning and conditions in the occurrence of homicide. It also offers a relevant contribution to the study of social systems through the application of clustering techniques. Finally, our work presents innovative perspectives to investigate the homicide phenomenon. Moreover, we can predict the homicide rates for cities in Goias based on the characteristics of their residents and urban environments. This study serves as a relevant case to investigate other social problems and to develop strategies for improving the lives of population in urban areas of Goias. Furthermore, we can perform the same analysis for other states of Brazil, among other countries of Latin America. Moreover, we can study other social problems. Finally, we can use the analysis to improve the quality of life of the population in urban areas. The results were achieved by using the open-source software, using data provided by the Brazilian Secretary of Security. The achievement demonstrate that it's possible to improve the life of the population through public policies oriented by data. Our goal is to enhance accelerated stochastic gradient descent to optimize its performance in different problem settings and data conditions. To achieve this, we develop a customized stochastic gradient descent method that adjusts to changing noise levels and makes the most of its random sampling. By thoroughly examining the algorithm's properties, we establish that it will converge at an accelerated rate in an optimistic scenario and also provide a strategy to manage memory constraints. Furthermore, we support our findings with experimental results demonstrating the algorithm's efficacy on a range of test cases. As the core step of this algorithm is a form of stochastic gradient descent, we develop an efficient variant that reduces computational overhead. Experimentally, we verify that this algorithm excels over established optimization methods and achieve substantial performance improvements on the training of a CNN for CIFAR-10. This oscillator, having one or two degrees of freedom, lacks equilibrium. Such a system serves as a means to establish dynamic non-stationary memory. It has also been established that this type of system is analogous to well-documented nonlinear self-oscillating systems. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that both the process of forming and erasing dynamic non-stationary memory are independent of initial conditions, with erasure requiring a combination of heat sources. This type of system may be used in devising new and innovative memory technologies. The distinct features of this type of system are, first and foremost, simple physical processes and, secondly, high fidelity of oscillations. The process of dynamic non-stationary memory can be observed in both short and long term scenarios, with the latter requiring accounting for multiple relaxation times. This type of system is capable of withstanding large changes in temperature, as opposed to other types of systems. The process of dynamic non-stationary memory can be repeated multiple times, with the possibility of decoherence-free transitions between different periods of non-stationary memory. This type of transition occurs through the process of analytic continuation and is exemplified by the process of transition from first to second harmonic oscillations. It has also been demonstrated that this type of transition can be treated as regular Markovian transition and, as such, is independent of initial conditions. The process of dynamic non-stationary memory and transition from first to second harmonic oscillations can be used to explain the origin of regular discrete structures, observed in spectroscopy of molecules and nanoparticles. Developing robots with skilled hands that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is crucial for numerous applications. Creating a robotic grasp system necessitates an extensive and diverse dataset that can accurately predict successful grasps. In comparison to other object-related datasets, a comprehensive grasp dataset is notably underrepresented. To address this gap, a large-scale simulated dataset called DexGraspNet has been introduced, comprising over 620,000 grasp attempts for over 400 objects. In contrast to other datasets, a key feature of DexGraspNet is its ability to apply various grasp techniques, making it a versatile resource. Additionally, a large-scale benchmark was established to assess the efficacy of simulation-based grasp algorithms. Furthermore, the dataset will be accessible in two formats: (i) a Torch dataset for direct utilization with deep learning libraries and (ii) an open-source scene file for direct reproduction in popular virtual environments. The proposed approach is intended to accelerate simulated object grasping techniques, ultimately benefiting real-world robotic applications. The dataset can be accessed at: https://sites.google.com/view/dexgrasnet. The code is available at: https://github.com/Paranjaikamal/DexGraspNet. As the dataset is continuously updated, it can be accessed via the aforementioned GitHub link. A paper outlining the dataset's details has been published at the ICCV 2022 convention. Information on other related work can be found at: https://sites.google.com/view/drc-grasp-net. A web-based interface called GraspTV has been developed to determine the efficacy of various grasp algorithms. Please visit the interface at: https://grasptv.github.io. The TV value represents the efficacy of different algorithms, with higher values indicating more accurate grasp techniques. For example, at the time of writing, the TV value stood at 142 for AlexNet, 153 for VGG16, 163 for ResNet, 163 for FastRCNN, and 170 for Igrasp. We plan to maintain TV values, offering a dynamic benchmark for object grasping algorithms. We encourage the community to adopt TV values as a standard performance metric, analogous to training loss or the widely-used COCO metrics in object detection and segmentation. We are collaborating with other Grasping Researchers to develop a more robust evaluation tool. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a turbo spin echo sequence, with motion compensation achieved through a k-space deep tiler. The proposed method enables image reconstruction in both spatial dimensions and the respiration dimension by synchronizing data collection with the respiratory cycle and filling in missing data with a neural network. To evaluate its quality, a figure of merit is proposed that considers both the prescribed and actual spatial dimensions. The proposed method achieves an index of 0.87, indicating high image fidelity. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a smaller student model. Unlike general knowledge distillation techniques that may overlook the importance of information flow, InDistill leverages a pioneering task to pinpoint the key details the teacher model uses to accomplish its tasks and compress these into their corresponding subspace within the student model. This allows the student model to inherit the knowledge from the teacher model more efficiently while modeling the essential information flow. Comprehensively, model performance evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, MNIST, and ImageNet reveal that InDistill consistently outperforms existing model compression methods, especially when dealing with complex datasets like ImageNet, where it achieves around 78.2% accuracy when compressing ResNet-50 to be of 4MB model size. Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and their respective level set foliations are examined. The equivalence of these functions is shown to necessarily result in the topological equivalence of their foliations. Conversely, this phenomenon is not the sole topological equivalence scenario, as evidence is presented with a homology class of a specific rectangular shape exhibiting a distinct foliation that cannot be topologically equivalent to any foliation defined by a linear function. However, a condition for determining topological equivalence between two foliations defined by linear functions is established, and this condition is found to be sufficient as well. The equivalence criterion for these functions is based on the topological equivalence of their respective foliations and the identification of specific structures within these foliations, specifically separable leaves and the union of leaves capturing entire domain areas. The proof that each condition is sufficient for the topological equivalence of foliations involves the use of specific homeomorphism classes, as does the proof that each condition is necessary. The homeomorphism classes for the topological equivalence in this context involve the employment of two distinct methods: for the existence of a homology for the entire domain, and for the separation of individual leaves. The proof that each condition is necessary involves the use of specific homeomorphism classes as well as an additional requirement for separating individual leaves, and we demonstrate the necessity by examining two distinct submersion functions whose foliations are topologically equivalent and whose structures resemble the rectangular example previously described. The proof that each condition is sufficient as well as the demonstration of the necessity can be summarized through the following steps: for any submersion function, and its foliations defined by level sets, we can apply a series of subsequence operations that reflect past decompositions in order to find two specific types of leaf unions. Either both leaves capture entire domain areas or they are separable. We can apply a combination of homeomorphism classes in order to find a submersion function whose leaf set capture resembles the original, and in the process, either both leaves capture entire domain areas or specific leaf separable conditions are identified. The problem is resolved through the demonstration of the necessary and sufficient conditions based on either leaf capture or leaf separation, and in addition to this, a condition of leaf separation is found to be necessary for the topological equivalence of foliations defined by linear functions. A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its implementation on both central and graphical processing units and interfacing with the PySCF electronic structure code. We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can choose between participating directly in the auction or being represented by an intermediary. The aim is to develop robust auction designs that don't rely on the buyer-demand function and aren't influenced by the intermediaries' role in the auction. 

Previous studies have focused on robust auction designs that adapt to varying demand functions, but not to the impact of intermediaries. To address this, our paper considers two approaches - one based on the Frank-Wolfe method and another on Sellers' ex-post mechanism design.

For the first approach, we aim to find the maximum revenue that can be achieved by selling $k$ items in an auction with a given distribution of buyers and valuations, and an unspecified demand function. We establish that the distribution of buyers and valuations determines the maximum revenue for a given k and $\beta$, and that this revenue can be found using a convex optimization problem.

For the second approach, we aim to design a stable (or regular) mechanism that doesn't depend on the buyer-demand function and isn't influenced by the intermediaries' role in the auction. We examine the ex-post mechanism design and find that it is robust to the impact of intermediaries, and we show that this mechanism does not better than the pay-per-bid (PPB) mechanism, which is known to be the best mechanism in this scenario.

We establish that the ex-post mechanism design has a better revenue guarantee when compared to Sellers' mechanisms, and we show that this revenue guarantee is the best possible revenue guarantee that can be achieved by a mechanism in this scenario.

Finally, we compare the ex-post mechanism design and the PPB mechanism in terms of simplicity and we show that the PPB mechanism is simpler than the ex-post mechanism design. Additionally, we compare the ex-post mechanism design and Sellers' mechanisms in terms of simplicity and we show that the ex-post mechanism design has a better simplicity guarantee when compared to Sellers' mechanisms. Additionally, we compare the ex-post mechanism design and Sellers' mechanisms in terms of fairness and we show that the ex-post mechanism design has a better fairness guarantee when compared to Sellers' mechanisms.

Overall, our research finds that the PPB mechanism is the best mechanism in this scenario and it is simpler than the ex-post mechanism design to implement. We believe that this mechanism has a simple and efficient design that can be achieved by a mechanism in this scenario and it is worth further investigation to understand its generalization properties.

To facilitate efficient abstractive summarization, we focus on task-specific knowledge in this study. Traditionally, pre-trained language models are relied upon to draw on their inherent knowledge. Conversely, we introduce an innovative framework where specific prompts related to entities are provided as structured information during inference. To effectively incorporate these entity prompts, we design an optimization-based approach rather than manually specifying them. Our results indicate that this approach leads to substantial performance improvements of up to +3.6 ROUGE-1 or +6.2 ROUGE-L when compared against pre-trained models without entity prompts, achieved on various datasets including those for the SARI score evaluated on range of abstractive summarization datasets. Notably, this gain is comparable to state-of-the-art models with fine-tuning on specific stories. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach can effectively integrate entity prompts with pre-trained language models to generate more accurate and coherent summaries. This enables the creation of summaries with accurate entity-specific information, thus reducing the likelihood of inaccuracies and inconsistencies within the generated summaries. Moreover, we show that by combining this approach with data augmentation techniques, it's feasible to achieve notable improvements in the generated summaries even without providing the entity prompts. Ultimately, this study highlights the feasibility of designing structured entity prompts to optimize task-specific performance. In the context of glaciology, particularly when modelling contact problems involving grounded ice sheets, a semicoercive variational inequality for incompressible fluid flow arises. This paper focuses on a finite element approximation of this inequality in a two-dimensional setting. It is known that traditional Stokes equilibrium models are inadequate for accurately describing the stress states near grounding zones. Consequently, a variety of modified Stokes equilibrium models have been proposed in recent research to capture the influence of ice-sheet rheology on horizontal stress components. Although these models can generate more realistic horizontal stress estimates, they pose a challenge for numerical analysis due to their non-linear characteristics. This paper establishes the existence of a weak solution to the modified Stokes variational inequality for a diverse class of anisotropic, semi-coercive materials using theoretical methods derived from elastic perfect plasticity. Furthermore, it demonstrates the convergence of finite element approximations to this weak solution, with support for both regular and irregular meshes. To achieve this goal, a local approximation operator framework bystood significant analytical hurdles presented by the formulation's non-linearity. This research represents an advancement in this direction. Moreover, drawing from the underlying theories associated with elastic perfect plasticity enables the development of more comprehensive analysis for generalised models describing plastic behaviour across a wide range of materials exhibiting multiple yield surfaces. This study is expected to serve as a foundational reference for future analyses involving approximation and discretisation techniques applied to various modified Stokes models for grounded ice sheets and other applicable contact problems. Finally, numerical examples were performed to verify the results presented in this research. This study was partially financed by a grant from the EPSRC and fully financed by a grant from the ERC. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows relate to other factors in the disk of a starbursting galaxy. Our data from NOEMA revealed a dense gas disk with a high rotation speed, but also significant dust absorption. From NOEMA's observations, we measured the gas properties across the galaxy and found the gas ionization level to be higher than expected. Our analysis using KCWI showed the outflow is confined to a narrow region and is likely to be influenced by the rotation of the galaxy. We found the outflow is weak in the center but becomes strong in the edges and is closely linked to regions of intense star formation. However, we also found that the outflow is not solely driven by star formation, as it's also apparent in areas with no known star-forming regions. By examining the ionization level across different regions, we concluded the outflow is not solely responsible for the low ionization level in the disk. Instead, we found that the gas in the disk is largely photoionized by the intense star-forming regions. Our analysis using NOEMA's observations of CO(2-1) and CO(1-0) also found no correlation between outflow rate and other factors in the galaxy. Our results imply outflow rates in the galaxy could be influenced by gas column density, implying that the outflow in the galaxy may be regulated by the layer of gas. However, we found this is not the case in other galaxies with similar gas column densities. We suggest further studies to investigate. To facilitate this, we made available a dataset that includes NOEMA's observations of CO(2-1) and CO(1-0), as well as KCWI's observations of SII, SII*B2S1, and SIII. This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely used topological invariant with numerous applications across various disciplines. Previous research primarily addressed its use in studying phenomena in one less dimension than the input data, hence typically 1 less dimension than expected. This work presents a comprehensive approach to calculate the Euler characteristic for data in equal dimensions with more than three variables, making it suitable for high-dimensional scenarios. As a result, this research provides a solid foundation for topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces. To achieve this, it often reduces the dimensionality of the data, applying concepts from multivariate statistics. This reduction is not only a necessary step but also a crucial aspect of the Euler characteristic calculation method. Thus, this research examines the relationship between Euler characteristic calculation methods and the process of dimensionality reduction. By combining these perspectives, this study develops a deeper understanding of the subject. Moreover, it investigates the current challenges associated with analytical Euler characteristic calculations and explores the use of machine learning methods to address these limitations. Finally, this research demonstrates the practical applications of Euler characteristic analysis to real-world problems in two fields: computer vision and geoscience. By employing the proposed methods, it is possible to identify key features in image data set by applying a support vector machine classification. This is illustrated through a demonstration on a typical image dataset. Furthermore, the capabilities of the calculated Euler characteristic surfaces are evaluated using a dataset obtained from the GeoLife project, showcasing the effectiveness of the generated heat map in representing location-based activities. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of suitable features for advanced topological data analysis in high-dimensional spaces and its practical applications in computer vision and geoscience. As a result, this study provides a significant advancement in the calculation of Euler characteristic for data in four-dimensional spaces or higher, facilitating its use as a feature selection method in image classification and location-based activity detection in human mobility contexts. With the proposed methods, it is possible to perform quantitative analysis and generate visualizations of the investigated phenomena. The developed code is available on GitHub, enabling its use and further development. The project's repository can be accessed at https://github.com/marioarias/EulerCharacteristicSurfaces. The provided code includes the Euler characteristic calculation functions, dimensionality reduction, feature generation, and data visualization utilities. This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for pp -> ttj events, particularly focusing on the dileptonic decay channel, with an approximation based on the narrow width assumption. Our objective is to quantify the magnitude of off-shell and non-resonant influences on the forms of various differential distributions that will be crucial for top quark mass determination via template fitting techniques. Our results demonstrate that, at the 13 TeV production energy, the effects of non-resonant and off-shell contributions are significant in the differential distributions. Off-shell effects are particularly prominent in the top quark rapidity and b-quark tagging jet rapidity distributions, while non-resonant contributions dominate the Q2 and T-t (top quark transverse momentum) distributions. Interestingly, the computation reveals that the principal source of non-resonant contributions stems from background processes such as QCD, W+jets, and qQbar events, rather than the tt production with a jet fake insurance. By applying a fitting procedure with template distributions derived from both the accurate and approximate computations, we found that, at the 5 sigma confidence level, the two methods yield identical top quark mass values. Furthermore, the investigation also reveals that the top quark mass extraction can be performed with satisfactory precision even with the narrow width approximation, provided that specific differential distributions, collectively known as 'baselines', which dominate the template fit, are utilized. Our recommendation is that future experimental analyses utilize the 'baselines' extracted from the comprehensive computation to derive the most accurate top quark mass. Additionally, the study provides recommendations and suggestions to the experimental community to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of the top quark mass extraction. Our work could serve as a resource for the 13 TeV analyses of the ATLAS and CMS experimental programs at the effective collision energy of 13 TeV. We have developed and made publicly available the code for the pp -> ttj event computation, which can be used with the FastJet package to generate differential distributions. Our code is expected to be a valuable tool for the experimental communities in the future. We plan to extend our code and undertake a comparable investigation for the ttZ events. We strongly believe that our code and study could facilitate the extraction of various physical quantities of unstable particles. We intend to leverage our code and experience to derive predictions for several stable particles. Our work is also expected to influence the development of new computational tools. The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent presentations restricts their adoption in high-stakes applications. Effective countermeasures against these deceptive attempts are vital for the safe integration of facial recognition technology. Current approaches have shown limitations, often becoming overly specialized in training datasets and struggling to adapt to unseen attack methods and environments. In this research, transfer learning is applied from the vision transformer model to tackle the challenge of detecting unknown anti-spoofing attacks. Experimental results conducted on widely accessible datasets showcase the superiority of our proposed solution, outperforming state-of-the-art methods significantly in zero-shot scenarios within the HQ-WMCA and SiW-M datasets, while also achieving substantial improvements in cross-database evaluations. Furthermore, our approach surpasses competitive baselines in cross-database evaluations across a broad range of more than 20 public datasets. Moreover, incorporating a temporal self-attention mechanism enhances model generalizability by capturing the temporal dependencies of presentation types. Our proposed technique achieves impressive accuracy of 97.3% and 94.1% on the HQ-WMCA and SiW-M datasets respectively, paving the way for the widespread use of facial recognition in critical applications. The code for our approach has been made publicly available on GitHub at the specified link. Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from trial and error. Our research focuses on a wide-ranging investigation of the deep reinforcement learning framework, encompassing core principles, critical challenges, and cutting-edge applications. In light of the significant advancements achieved by AlphaGo, Google's self-playing game player, we explore how deep reinforcement learning can be applied to create autonomous vehicles that learn and adapt while navigating roads and interacting with complex environments. We delve into the learning algorithm's two primary components, policy network, and value network, as well as the functions of other critical support modules, including experience memory, reward mechanisms, and image stabilization systems. Additionally, we highlight the challenges posed by time constraints, variable reward distributions, fragmented experience data, and image complexities in autonomous driving environments, along with potential solutions designed to enhance sample efficiency, reduce training times, and minimize reliance on abundant data. Ultimately, we outline a future research direction for our deep reinforcement learning framework, aiming to enable autonomous vehicles to independently explore and map the surrounding environment. Evolutionary algorithms have seen an increase in efficiency by utilizing parallel processing, allowing multiple generations to evolve concurrently.  Despite this improvement, evaluation time variability among different agents can hinder the performance of parallel evolutionary algorithms.  As a result, some agents may have the opportunity to generate a greater number of solutions while others may have fewer chances.  This time-discrepaney can be mitigated through a Parent Selection strategy that ensures all agents participate in the evolution process with fair and unbiased results.  To enhance convergence and effectiveness, we introduced a frequency-based parent selection method as a component of this hybridized PMOEA.  As a result, the hybrid PMOEA was able to improve convergence and achieve better quality solutions than its counterparts, specifically in the Multi-objective Optimization of Ant Colony Optimization Algorithm (MOACO) research study.  Furthermore, the hybrid PMOEA outperformed MOACO in quality output across multiple run tests, showcasing its reliability.  To verify the efficacy of the proposed technique, a comprehensive experiment was conducted using 12 numerical test functions and the Real-world Application of the Microwave Filter Design (MFD) problem.  Specifically, the results demonstrated superior performance over MOACO in quality using the $V$-metric measurement.  To support the proposed method's validity, an ablation study was also performed to confirm its effectiveness.  This study was showcased at the $1^{st}$ Indian Conference on Intelligent Computing and Intelligent Information (ICICII) 2021.  The source code for this research can be accessed at the following repository location: https://github.com/ExAraH/PMOEA.git.  To facilitate additional research, the data generated during this study can be retrieved at the following repository location: https://github.com/ExAraH/PMOEA_data.  The proposed technique has been registered at the Standard Reference Discovery system with the following ID: exaraH-PMOEA-2021. Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software,
particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for thoroughly
examining software adherence to specifications through precondition/postcondition
declarations. The improvement of semantic parsing methods and increasing
computational capabilities enable the extraction of formal logical structures from
natural language inputs with rising precision and breadth, enabling the use of
logical forms as a software specification method. This research presents a method
based on Hoare logic to translate logical forms into software code and assess its
effectiveness in generating verifiable specifications for practical programs.
Additionally, we discuss limitations in specifying Hoare logic requirements for
software with language models lacking complete grammatical structure. We propose
hoisting techniques to address these limitations and imply methods for generating
logical forms with more flexibility in their structure. Finally, we outline the
potential extension of this investigation, exploring the use of logical forms for
formal verification beyond Hoare logic, leveraging more advanced semantic property
descriptions through predicate logic. This approach offers a novel method for
formal verification centered on natural language specifications, offering a unique
extension to established program analysis methods. An implementation of the
methodology and the developed verifications have been made available online.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance but lacks systems to handle failures and is not capable of withstanding malicious attacks. In order to address these shortcomings, we have enhanced Canopus with a new failure detection system and tested it to be resilient to various types of failures and multiple types of attacks. The evaluation of our Canopus modification revealed that it results in a slight increase in latency but allows the Canopus network to function efficiently even under Canopus' original parameters during certain types of failures. The need for additional hardware redundancy was also diminished in most scenarios. Furthermore, our proposed system was found to be more efficient than other approaches capable of withstanding failures and malicious attacks. The consequence of this is that Canopus is now capable of functioning in environments previously thought to be hostile towards it. In the future, we intend to expand our research into additional topics. The code for our system can be found at https://github.com/keystone-os/RCanopus. This inconsistency arose despite earlier research employing solely equilibrium experiments, not linear transport properties, indicating that one may be misled by data from the latter. A general discussion highlights how this misunderstanding occurs, after which it's demonstrated that the neutron spin echo findings can be reinterpreted to produce results that are in line with the prior equilibrium results. This study examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It reveals that the momentum is a constant, and the model exhibits de Broglie pilot-wave dynamics. Unlike earlier loop quantum cosmological models, this one does not require a quantum state to describe the system. Instead, the momentum serves as the wave function, defining the probability distribution of the scale factor. Calculations show that the momentum is quantized at multiples of the square root of the Planck constant multiplied by the Hubble constant, indicating that the scale factor is confined to discrete values. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that the momentum-based model is equivalent to the Hamiltonian-based model in terms of dynamics. However, unlike the Hamiltonian-based model, this momentum-based model exhibits symmetry. Finally, this study explores constraints from both Hamiltonian and momentum perspectives, revealing that the two approaches result in similar quantum conditions for the scale factor. At the quantum level, both Hamiltonian- and momentum-based models exhibit the same regularity properties. Nonetheless, this study warns against translating this result from the ADM framework to gravity, where the momentum represents a different physical quantity than it does in cosmology. Instead, this result constitutes an intriguing case study in quantum cosmology. Further research should seek to generalize this understanding to other models derived from the ADM Hamiltonian. Such an exploration may uncover novel phenomena within quantum cosmology. Moreover, this study sheds light on distinctions between quantum states and momenta in determining probability distributions within the Schrödinger approach, highlighting a potential link between these two formalisms. Future work should seek to expand on these findings to alleviate the ambiguity surrounding the choice of states in pilot-wave dynamics. Ultimately, this theoretical contribution fosters a deeper comprehension of the complex interplay between states, momenta, and symmetries in quantum mechanics, encouraging research into these fundamental concepts. Moreover, this study adds to the burgeoning field of quantum cosmology by exploring novel approaches such as those based on the ADM Hamiltonian. As quantum mechanics continues to inspire modifications to classical theories, researchers may uncover fresh perspectives on fundamental quantum phenomena. Furthermore, this work contributes to the emerging field of quantum gravity via its investigation of cosmological implications. While the study assumes that the universe comprises a single perturbation, it paves the way for models derived from more general gauge-invariant phase spaces. Such generalized phase spaces could result from the expansion of the ADM theory to include perturbations, thereby allowing for the derivation of primordial quantum gravitational constraints.
