Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods use a valuation function approximation to determine near-optimal approaches. However, in partially observable systems, these valuations are dependent on an extensive sequence of past events, making the computation and storage of these values highly impractical. Researchers have addressed this challenge through the application of various algorithms based on dynamic system models that utilize a hidden state to describe the system's condition. We propose an alternative approach by employing recurrent neural networks, which use a hidden state analogous to a Bayesian belief state to determine the valuation function. We present a general method known as ABRG that uses these valuations to develop gradient-based optimization techniques via backpropagation. This approach is comparable to existing partially observable Monte Carlo sampling methods but offers a theoretical guarantee of near-optimality as the number of model parameters increases. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach in both simple theoretical models and the complex game of Atari Pendulum. Our results demonstrate that our method leads to significantly improved performance in both scenarios. Importantly, we found that our approach leads to a significant reduction in the required sequence length to achieve a valuation accuracy of 1% when compared to existing partially observable Monte Carlo sampling methods. For instance, while Monte Carlo sampling method led to an accuracy of 1% at a sequence length of 20, our approach achieved similar accuracy at a sequence length of 1. We believe that our theoretical model provides valuable insights into the relationship between the underlying uncertainty model, the complexity of the hidden state, and the required sequence length to achieve a valuation accuracy of 1%. Furthermore, we found that our recurrent neural network-based approach leads to a substantial reduction in training time when compared to the Monte Carlo sampling method. For instance, our Monte Carlo sampling method achieved a 1% accuracy after 11 million training samples, whereas our recurrent network led to similar accuracy after training for 200,000 iterations with a batch size of 64. This significant difference in training time is primarily due to the fact that the Monte Carlo sampling method requires multiple iterations to achieve a 1% accuracy, whereas our recurrent network leads to similar accuracy after a single pass, which allows for further training without repeating the process. We evaluated the effectiveness of our approach in both scenarios and found that our theoretical model provides valuable insights into the relationship between the underlying system parameters, the complexity of the hidden state, and the required sequence length to achieve a valuation accuracy of 1%. In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on spatial and temporal features extracted from 2D or 3D convolutional networks.  However, we believe that understanding an action involves also considering its context - objects and individuals within a video scene - so we've developed a novel model integrating self-attention and graph convolutional networks to better model context like actor relationships and object interactions. This self-supervised method aims to reduce annotation dependency by using the graph to represent temporal relationships between scenes within a video. As a result, it's more effective in action detection without relying on bounding box annotations. This approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in action detection with open vocabulary on HMDB51 and UCF101, achieving up to a 3.5% improvement in top-1 accuracy for the top model on the UCF101 dataset. A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset to evaluate state-of-the-art image copy detection methods. With over 200 participants involved, the winning entries are subjected to both qualitative and quantitative analysis in this paper. Key findings indicate that the most challenging transformations for the participating algorithms are extreme cropping of images, incorporation into unrelated content, combined with pixel-level disturbances. Notably, the winning approaches employed training with robustly augmented examples, self-supervised learning, score normalization, and ensemble techniques. Furthermore, the research also identifies areas for the further improvement of the participating methods and suggests a potential solution to overcome the remaining limitations. Ultimately, the paper concludes that the participating algorithms demonstrate a remarkable capacity to effectively identify image duplicates, with the top approaches demonstrating over 99% accuracy in detecting exact duplicates and approximately 98% accuracy in detecting transformed duplicates. Thus, the winning methods can serve as strong candidates for industrial application in order to prevent image plagiarism. The research is supported by extensive experimental results, detailed analysis and in-depth description of the underlying techniques. The research researchers plan to make their code and training configurations publicly available in the near future. The benchmark dataset, together with the challenge, have been made accessible through the following repositories -- ipcc2021 and ipcc2021-data (with 77,268 original images and 215,091 transformed images, respectively). This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields by applying the lowest order constraint variational (LOCV) method, with the pairings of nucleons of the same and opposite signs (same-sign and opposite-sign pairings) being taken into consideration. We obtained significant outcomes, which include the energy per nucleon (E/N), its variation with intensity of the magnetic field (dE/N-B), and the saturation point of nuclear matter (muon chemical potential, mu). Our analysis indicates that same-sign pairings are stable under weak magnetic fields but collapse in strong magnetic fields, whereas opposite-sign pairings exhibit stability in intense magnetic fields but are unstable under weak magnetic fields. The study also reveals that same-sign pairings have a lower energy per nucleon compared to opposite-sign pairings at zero magnetic field. Moreover, we discovered that same-sign pairings can satisfy the nuclear matter saturation point (mu = 0) without violating the principle of Pauli exclusion at a significantly high intensity of magnetic field (B = 1016 G). This research may have significant implications for the study of compact stars, as it could influence our comprehension of the internal structure and properties of compact stars influenced by intense magnetic fields. The study could potentially offer new insights into the behavior of nucleons under strong magnetic fields and varying fermion densities inside compact stars. Such knowledge may help in addressing long-standing queries in theoretical astrophysics, such as the mechanism of superconductivity and superfluidity inside compact stars and the occurrence of quark-deconfinement inside neutron stars within the framework of the phase diagram of QCD. The study may also aid in the explanation of observed characteristics of giant magneto-rotopausable compact stars. The study is found to be useful for explaining magnetisation energy per nucleon (dE/N-B) as a function of magnetic field (B) for both same-sign and opposite-sign pairings. Furthermore, our study reveals significant differences in the behaviour of dE/N-B for same-sign and opposite-sign pairings with varying (dE/N-B)_{sat} values at a weak intensity of the magnetic field. This study also shows that same-sign pairings exhibit a specific pattern of saturation in the energy per nucleon as a function of intense magnetic fields, which may aid in understanding quark-deconfinement inside compact stars. The study may also be used to investigate the occurrence of cold dense star with intense magnetic field and the possible phase transitions within the framework of the phase diagram

Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated Relative Entropy Coding, a highly efficient compression technique, into the distributed training framework. By introducing a simple adjustment to REC, we derived a differential privacy compliant algorithm, which provides quantifiable guarantees. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach substantially decreases communication costs while maintaining high data privacy standards. Compared to traditional methods, DP-REC achieves a 50 times reduction in communication overhead at a minimal model size increase. Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information, making research in scientific papers easily accessible to scholars by compiling experimental outcomes and highlighting novel discoveries. Current table analysis techniques can fall short due to recognition errors stemming from the conversion of PDFs into document images, resulting in information loss. This study develops a solution to table extraction by leveraging Graph Neural Networks and incorporates tailored representation embeddings that improve differentiation between tables, table headers, and other document components. An experimental assessment was conducted on a combined dataset from PubLayNet and PubTables-1M to evaluate the proposed approach's efficacy. The findings demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses existing benchmarks, achieving significant improvements in model accuracy, specifically a 6.14% rise over the second-best alternative. The implemented technique has been made publicly available through the GitHub repository at https://github.com/leonardo-vilar/GraphNEZ. This repository serves as a the foundation for this study's methodology and experimental results, enabling replication of the experiments and access to the developed models and code. An online demo of the table extraction model can also be accessed at https://table-extraction-demo.leonardo-vilar.com/. This work has been approved by the LRE-IBM, code #LRE-2021-12-01-14. Our proposed approach's competitive performance is graphically illustrated by comparison with other state-of-the-art methods, with the model's 80.24% accuracy surpassing the second-best alternative, PubLayNet, by 6.14%. The model's 80.24% accurate table extraction also outperformed the third-best alternative, TableDetection, by 4.89%. We further analyzed and graphically presented the 10 most significant improvements over the second-best alternative, with the model's accuracy increasing by 10.57% (from 69.38% to 80.24%) and the number of samples considered. The enhanced accuracy is attributed to the model's superior performance on specific entries, such as table description, which the model accurately predicted 99.63% of the time, surpassing the second-best alternative, TableDetection, by 4.63%. This study's contributions are twofold: (1) an accurate Graph Neural Network-based model for table extraction from PDFs that outperforms the second-best alternative, TableDetection, by 4.89%; and (2) by incorporating tailored representation embeddings that improve differentiation between tables, table headers, and other document components. This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover peers' relevant characteristics and problem-solving abilities as the game unfolds. Building on this concept, our study provides a complete characterization of dynamic CH solutions for two-typed games where players are differentiated by their traits, not their cognitive abilities. Furthermore, we investigate how varying parameters affects the distinctiveness of characteristics and cognitive abilities. Interestingly, our findings indicate that mid-game character revelation often results in further insight, unlike early or late in-game revelations. Additionally, our analysis shows that the game's outcome is more susceptible to changes in parameter values when players' cognitive abilities and trait distributions diverge. Such outcomes can even mirror those of an extensive form game solved through LP. The theoretical framework established here can be extended to more complex games, including larger cognitive skill distributions, which is further explored in another related study.

Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, several methods for population estimation have been implemented. In our research, we evaluated the effectiveness of integrating multiple data sources - election registration, mobile tower data, and satellite imagery - to achieve accurate and independent population estimation in Mozambique. By utilizing a machine learning approach, we tailored our model to prioritize population estimation accuracy in urban and rural areas. The results demonstrate that the model can accurately estimate population density across various districts, utilizing a combination of independent variables. The model's estimations show a $4-13\%$ increase in accuracy over the 2017 census, specifically in urban areas. By adapting to the unique characteristics of each district, our model mitigates overfitting. The model's ability to operate independently of government data makes it suitable for applying in other low-to-mid income countries. The estimated population density maps are available at https://www.kaggle.com/view/414163153 for public use. Over the past ten years, significant advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. These developments led to the creation of novel systems such as cuckoo and xor filters. Moreover, adaptive solutions have recently been introduced, enabling the avoidance of potential errors on a case-by-case basis. This research aims to introduce a new type of dynamic filter that eliminates the risk of incorrect positive results. Such filters can be utilized in data retrieval systems as well as data compression methods. Experimental findings confirm that the proposed filter is more effective than existing alternatives. This research is available on arXiv under reference arXiv:2101.10021. Further details about the proposed filter can be found in dissertation arXiv:2101.10020. A publicly accessible implementation of the proposed filter can be found at https://github.com/farshadk/aqf. This implementation allows users to evaluate and compare the performance of the proposed filter in comparison to existing solutions. Notably, the proposed filter does not require significant modifications to existing code and can be easily applied as an additional layer of filtering in existing systems. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of implementing the proposed filter with minimal memory overhead. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed filter can handle up to C/$(r+1)$ elements without requiring additional storage, given $r$ elements per block. Furthermore, the proposed filter design enables the creation of compact representations. Experimental results indicate that the proposed filter can achieve a reduction of at least 15% in storage requirements compared to existing solutions, while allowing for a single pass design. This significant improvement in performance occurred as a result of eliminating the need for overlap handling between filter entries. Experimental findings revealed the importance of accurately handling set operations during construction. Accurate handling of set operations during construction led to a 23% reduction in storage requirements. Experimental results also confirmed the benefits of adapting the proposed filter to commonly occurring entry patterns in existing systems. To overcome the limitations associated with the smoothing effect in fluid dynamics, which emerges from treating fluids as continuous media, researchers have created advanced methods based on Lagrangian mechanics. Here, we present a novel approach to fluid dynamics using a hierarchical two-speed model Groundwork Unified Lagrangian method, which combines generalised Lagrangian Kinetics and Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics. This framework deconstructs fluid dynamics into basic flows and eliminates unnecessary details, similar to the concept of zooming in and out in computer graphics. Additionally, our model enables the simulation of diverse fluid states by altering its smoothing level according to specific requirements. To extend our model to multi-phase interactions, we developed a strategy for efficiently representing surfaces using a simplified geometric model. This approach facilitates the simulation of complex interactions between fluids and rigid bodies using a model representing the interface of fluids. We present detailed mathematical descriptions of our model as well as its application to fluid-structure interactions. We also provide performance data and demonstrate the model's potential with various examples of engineering applications. To support future researchers, we have released our model along with supporting code through an open platform. A detailed user manual is also provided as an supplementary document. Ultimately, our model offers a range of benefits including the ability to modify smoothing levels for accurate results, model the dynamics of porous rigid bodies, and simulate the impact of external forces on fluid behaviour. This framework holds potential for expansion to cover a broad range of engineering disciplines including solid mechanics. Nevertheless, it appears that extending this model to cover solid dynamics will necessitate the adoption of new formulations of kinematics and dynamics. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current algorithms. We develop and test a quantum version of the K-means method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a classical variant by analyzing both real-world and artificially created datasets. Results indicate that the quantum model is non-deterministic and is prone to specific issues as the dataset size increases. Nevertheless, the approach exhibits a promising speedup for datasets with a limited number of features, making it a promising starting point for further research and development. Overall, our investigation contributes to the advancement of quantum machine learning technologies and serves as a foundation for future advancements in this field. Additionally, the source code used in this research is available to facilitate ongoing progress towards quantum-enhanced machine learning. A new, experimental approach to the creation of a quantum clustering model may offer insights to researchers, while the associated code enables them to build upon and improve our results. A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's given pitch values far from its average pitch value.  In other words, it can control pitch, but with limitations.  We suggest a simple way to improve pitch control in FastPitch.  We add a new component to FastPitch that modifies pitch values based on a record of how pitch correlates with speech in a particular language called English.  We use a way to measure speech that's designed to minimize changes in speech quality when pitch is altered.  We test our modification by changing the pitch in audio files using FastPitch and saving both the modified audio and a record of the modification that's applied.  We compare the quality of the modified audio to the quality of the speech made with FastPitch's original design and find that our modification significant improves the quality of the modified audio for all the tests we did.  In fact, our modification results in better or equal quality for a given pitch value than FastPitch does for pitch values close to its average pitch value and much better or equal quality for pitch values far from its average pitch value.  We also found that our modification allows FastPitch to synthesize speech that's nearly indistinguishable from human speech for all the tests we did.  We even optimized our modification to work with FastPitch's companion text-to-speech system called MelDiablo and were able to get MelDiablo to produce high quality speech for a wide range of pitch values. This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object persistence principles. A crucial element of our approach is recognizing how to track objects across frames that involve multi-step reasoning. A significant problem with existing models is their inability to engage in persistent object-based reasoning. In response, we have developed Hopper - a cutting-edge transformer model - to tackle this challenge. Hopper's architecture allows it to build connections between objects within a single frame and also to anticipate these connections by considering the objects' relationships. Importantly, our proposed model can engage in multi-step object tracking. We have put together a new spatiotemporal reasoning dataset called HRV-CPS and conducted thorough evaluations of our Hopper model. The results show that Hopper has achieved exceptional performance of 83.1% on the HRV-CPS dataset - representing a 9.1% enhancement over the highest previously reported result. Moreover, our findings indicate that Hopper's performance heavily surpasses the existing state-of-the-art transformer-based model by 41.5%. We have made the HRV-CPS dataset accessible on https://github.com/serve-apex/HRV-CPS. A live demo of our Hopper model is available at https.//serve-apex.com/hopper. Furthermore, our experiment outcomes are available on https://github.com/serve-apex/hopper-experiments. Hopper wins the 2nd place in NeurIPS 2022 Spatiotemporal Reasoning Challenge with an accuracy of 81.5%. The code for our solution can be found at https://github.com/serve-apex/SR-Challenge. Our accompanying paper titled 'Hopper: Multi-hop Transformer for Spatiotemporal Reasoning' has received the runner-up award at NeurIPS 2022 Swav and the 2nd place in NeurIPS 2022 Spatiotemporal Reasoning Challenge with an accuracy of 81.5%. This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in relevance and importance, affecting the quality of the cluster. To overcome this limitation, our method modifies the traditional fuzzy k-means objective function using two distinct entropy terms. The first term optimizes cluster compactness by maximizing inter-cluster separation and minimizing within-cluster variance. The second term dynamically weights features according to their unique contributions, promoting better data partitioning. The effectiveness of our approach is evaluated through multiple datasets and comparisons with established state-of-the-art clustering methods. Our results indicate that this algorithm surpasses baseline clustering methods in accuracy, achieving an average improvement of 0.64%. Moreover, our method performs comparably in terms of computational complexity. The source code for this algorithm is publicly available at https://github.com/polymatlab/Variable-Feature-Fuzzy-k-Means. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite extensive research over two decades. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution to this long-standing problem by introducing an innovative algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE model parameters for a wide range of non-linear transformations. This new algorithm uniquely estimates expert parameters through an analysis of the correlation matrix formed by samples drawn from various experts, a concept surprisingly absent in existing MoE model literature. This method enjoys exceptional performance benefits, accurately learning both mixture coefficients and expert parameters in just one iteration, a feat unheard of in traditional algorithms. We further enhance our algorithm's ability to handle varying numbers of experts at different levels, a capability missing in existing work. This new algorithm demonstrates impressive ability to handle complex MoE models, accurately learning parameters for up to 256 experts across 8 different layers, a task traditional algorithms struggle to accomplish. We also present a new generic framework for neural networks and ensemble learning systems, a concept abandons the traditional use of grid-based architectures, instead embracing a new, more flexible approach. We demonstrate that our new algorithm has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of highly-complex neural networks, surpassing the performance of competing methods, with results that indicate a reduction of at least 10% in the required number of parameters. All of the code used in this paper is openly available at: https://github.com/mathieuh/mixture-of-experts-new-algorithms. This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry. The course covers the primary aspects of the theory, including the valuation theory in torsion-free double covers of graphs. We also explore the role of minima of chip-firing games on metric graphs in the context of the Siegel moduli scheme and learn how these appear as Jacobians of holomorphic line bundles on a genus g curve. We further investigate how the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs can be represented as tautological sheaf cohomologies on Jacobians, if one considers a genus g curve as a metric graph with the Plucker embedding. Lastly, we delve into the relationship between the minima of chip-firing games on the boundary of the Siegel half-plane and the compactified moduli space of line bundles on curves. The course also touches on tropical aspects of the theory and includes exercises with answers at the end. The associated lecture videos and further information can be accessed at the listed reference. The material assumes only basic knowledge of graph theory, algebraic geometry up to the level of Gorenstein's 'Arithmetic Geometry,' and the theory of toric geometry as presented in Vegosen's 'Tropical Cycle Counting on Compactified Moduli Spaces.' It represents an introduction to the content of Chapter 7 of the textbook by Keel and Mason. The material is suited for advanced undergraduate and graduate students. Discovering a global symmetry in nature has been a challenging task. Although scientists have found one instance - the axion - they still search for more. While a global symmetry remains intact at the quantum gravity level, its breaking produces necessary ratios of electroweak and gravitational energies. However, this ratio is constrained by cosmic birefringance observations. By analyzing the CHIME survey, we have set a constraint on the combination of quantum gravity and the Standard Model. Specifically, we have limited the ratio of Weakened Global Symmetry to under $10^{-18}$ in the case of $U(1)_{B-L}$ and gotten similar results for other global symmetries. This means that if nature's global symmetry isn't related to $U(1)_{B-L}$, then we can assume that any such symmetry isn't significantly broken. An exception to this is if a newly discovered symmetry has its breaking protected from gravity, which could explain why we see no symmetry if such an instance exists. We've also established a relationship between the strength of a global symmetry's breaking and the strength of its associated particles. An analogy to this is electric charges in QCD, with the strong force's characteristic threshold known as the Landau pole. By looking at various possible global symmetries and their associated thresholds, we see that some may exist at very high but still within reach energy levels, around a few trillion GeV. An instance could exist where a newly discovered particle's mass equals its symmetry breaking threshold in much the same way that the Higgs mass equals the electroweak energy ratio. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from a broader, more comprehensive training dataset. Despite this capability being an integral aspect of modern deep learning, limited research has been conducted to investigate the underlying underlying factors that govern the transferability of DNNs. Consequently, consensus models and heuristic methods have been developed to facilitate the selection of relevant pre-trained models and adjustment of network architectures for enhanced performance on down-stream tasks. Notably, research has suggested that data incompatibility and model incompatibility are key factors governing the transferability of DNNs. Furthermore, consensus models have been employed to estimate the transferability of data samples and guide open-set classification. Building on this foundation, our study aims to advance the understanding of DNN transferability by re-examining the concepts of data incompatibility and model incompatibility. Through in-depth analysis, our study demonstrates that the established concepts of data incompatibility and model incompatibility are in fact redundant and can be attributed to a single key factor. By discovering that some features of the base domain are incompatible with the pre-trained model, our study proposes the concept of feature incompatibility. Furthermore, our study proposes the use of correlation incompatibility to measure the degree of feature incompatibility. Notably, our study validates the generalizability of the proposed approach on multiple public datasets, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of the proposed concept of feature incompatibility. The proposed research is set to empower the development of innovative consensus models and provide new insights into the understanding of DNN transferability. Our analysis reveals that the conditions generating the Thakurta metric, previously investigated in a study by Böhm et al., involve a single black hole feeding on non-interacting isotropic dust throughout the entire universe. This leads to a realization that the processes driving black hole feedings proposed by Böhm et al. cannot occur in isolation. As a result, we conclude that the Thakurta metric does not accurately represent the system of a single black hole and cosmical matter. Consequently, we examine whether a more comprehensive model of a black hole drawing out a fixed amount of dust at constant rate could satisfy the conditions that gave rise to the Thakurta metric. Even with this modification, we find that it is impossible to satisfy these conditions. This conclusion implies that the bounds of non-primordial black holes derived from LIGO-Virgo data, remain valid. Significantly, this leads to strong bounds of $10^{-13} < f_{\rm crit}(M_{\rm BH}) < 10^{-5}$ in the range $M_{\rm BH} \approx 1 M_{\odot} - 100 M_{\odot}$, with the exact value of $f_{\rm crit}$ dependent on $M_{\rm BH}$. These bounds supersede existing primordial black hole limits and render the Thakurta metric unfeasible for describing either primordial or cosmic black holes. Although the idea of black holes feeding on dust is an intriguing one, our analysis suggests that it remains an unsolved problem. Furthermore, we outline the conditions under which a more plausible model of a black hole embedded in a dust cloud, described by Painlevé-III, could satisfy the conditions that gave rise to the Thakurte metric. However, we conclude that even this model is unfeasible due to conflicting bounds of primordial black holes and the spectrum of gravitational-wave events detected by the LIGO-Virgo collaboration. Consequently, it remains to be seen whether a more realistic model of a black hole embedded in a dust cloud, different from Painlevé-III, can be developed. By exploring this topic, we hope to stimulate the development of a more complete and realistic model in the future. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that the problem of a black hole embedded in a dust cloud remains an open problem to be solved. The complexity of gap formation by pebble accretion highlights the need for factors other than pebble zone evolution and drag forces to influence the process. Factors like the evolution of the protoplanet and wind affecting dust and pebbles are significant but we explore the impact of a more-probabilistic, stochastic approach in this study. Utilizing a numerical simulation with an enhanced code for dust evolution, we show that localized disturbances in the protostellar disk can shift the pebble zone, altering the pebble accumulation zone and potentially the formation location of planets. The formation location of planets in such scenarios can be directly linked to the location of the pebbles, leading to a high probability of planet formation near the disk's midplane. Furthermore, we propose a simplified statistical model for planet formation location, indicating that multiple formation locations are possible. The developed model could have far-reaching implications, providing potential solutions to problems like the lack of close-in super-Earths and ringed super-Earths in the area of pebble dominance. The formation of planets in the disk's turbulent midplane could explain the observed population of super-Earths via pebble accretion, while variations in this process might contribute to the formation of ringed super-Earths. The proposed statistical model for planet formation location could explain their current observed population without the need for a ring to develop in the accretion zone. The incorporation of further factors like the protostar's evolution, wind and turbulence effects could further shape planet populations and explain their current distribution.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate safely and efficiently in diverse environments before being released to the public, accurately assessing their performance in varying scenarios is crucial. Given the regulatory restrictions on medical software and the scarcity of comprehensive labeled medical datasets, our approach revolves around predicting a model's performance in an unfamiliar setting using its predicted responses alone, without requiring any modifications to its training process or assumptions about its original training environment. This "black-box" model assessment technique is based on conformal prediction and relies on the exchangeability of data from the model's training and the new setting. By applying this approach to two large datasets, we successfully estimated models' performance in similar fields, namely diagnosing a heart condition and identifying objects within an MRI image. Our results demonstrate that our technique provides reliable, and in some cases accurate, predictions of performance in practice. This accurate assessment of model performance under varying conditions facilitates the effective deployment of models that are reliable in their target environment. When performing cosmological inferences based on the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, standard analyses usually only consider a specific feature related to baryon acoustic oscillations. In this research, we investigate whether these standard analyses adequately capture the relevant cosmological information. To address this, we directly fitted synthetic Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, including cross-correlations with quasars, without compressing the data, and then compared the results with the conventional BAO analysis. Our findings suggest that the additional information does not significantly influence BAO fitting. However, when we focused on cosmological parameters beyond $\Omega_m$, incorporating the full data led to more precise constraints. This revealed that using mean synthetic spectra with quasar cross-correlations yielded the most robust results. In contrast, our analysis indicates that including UV background information with broad-band spectra, especially when fitting the mean, led to less accurate cosmological parameter fitting. This study also investigated whether leveraging auto-correlation data for fitting source distributions could mitigate this impact and provide more precise measurements. Although using auto-correlation is not a solution to the fitting bias, we demonstrated that with corrective methods, using auto-correlation could potentially be beneficial in separating mean and amplitude to enhance fitting. This research highlights various advanced techniques for improving cosmological fitting by directly utilizing the rich information present in Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions. It presents the initial steps towards a more comprehensive and straightforward analysis method of Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions. Moreover, our presentation demonstrates how to generate synthetic correlation functions that can facilitate more accurate model testing and error analysis in future cosmological fittings. A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, auxiliary gauge potential. This study proposes an alternative approach by developing a variational strategy for precisely creating initial ground states through adiabatic evolution of an appropriately constructed Hamiltonian without the need for a complex gauge vector. This goal is achieved by constructing a family of Hamiltonians applied to a general ansatz state, allowing researchers to control adiabatic evolution by adjusting a set of parameters that define the ansatz. We also demonstrate the robustness of this new approach by verifying its accuracy under realistic limits of evolution speed. This study proposes an innovative mass reconstruction technique for examining the lower mass spectrum resulting from top-quark pairs produced in association with a generic scalar boson. By utilizing a novel method of mass reconstruction, it has been demonstrated that a resolution of at least double can be achieved in the invariant mass of the top and bottom quark system. This improved resolution enables better mass range exploration in experiments at the LHC. Furthermore, we develop a statistical framework using a simplified top-quark model to efficiently identify optimal mass reconstruction events and discover a non-standard scalar boson. By utilizing a top-quark mass assumption of 172.44 GeV, our analysis shows that future 14 TeV LHC experiments can discover scalar bosons with couplings to top and electroweak bosons approximately an order of magnitude weaker than the standard model's top quark coupling. Additionally, under certain conditions of non-standard interplay between the scalar bosons of the two Higgs doublet model, we find that this discovery potential can be realized with significantly reduced experimental acceptance rates. Finally, we maintain that the principle of mass reconstruction with an order of magnitude lower computational complexity is a valuable consideration for advancing experimental research at future colliders. Therefore, we advocate exploring this concept further in theoretical, experimental, and application studies. An associated computational file detailing our novel mass reconstruction technique has been made publicly available for rapid incorporation into future searches into light Higgs phenomena at the LHC. This software is written in the ROOT programming language, a leading choice for HEP research, and we provide accompanying macros for interpreting search data with the ROOT 6 and HepData 3.4 tools. Furthermore, we provide a companion document outlining the development and testing of the mass reconstruction technique, demonstrating its reliability through multiple statistical assessments. These studies include the distribution of mass smearing across simulated invariant masses, using simulated data to evaluate and compare our novel technique with standard methods, and performing Monte Carlo simulations of top-quark pair production in association with a generic scalar boson to measure the experimental sensitivity of the proposed algorithm at the LHC. Using the ROOT programming language, we create computational files for simulating and analyzing this phenomenon at the LHC. Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two new unsupervised and scaled-down parsing models, running on existing language models, which can automatically learn or adapt to new languages and datasets with limited or no annotations. The first model relies on a top-down approach analyzing sentence structure by using a language model to detect main syntactic constructions and then estimating the probability of specific word arrangements within these frameworks. The second model takes a bottom-up approach starting with the analysis of individual words and then progressively refining sentence structure. Various experiments were conducted on multiple datasets to compare the performance of these models with or without incorporating token-level pre-training. Results indicate that the top-down model outperforms the other approaches and when combined with fine-tuning, achieves nearly parabolic improvement in dependency parsing accuracy with increasing token-level pre-training epochs. Moreover, the top-down model shows a significant gain of 5.7 and 9.6 in overall parsing accuracy when applied to unsupervised and few-shot parsing scenarios respectively. The models' implementation details can be found at this link: \url{https://github.com/linweidi83/Top-Down Parsing from Pre-trained Language Models.} \end{document}

Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In an effort to enhance classification and generation applications, we've developed a novel network that combines multiple neural tangent kernels - one for each layer - as opposed to earlier strategies focusing on a single kernel. Additionally, we've also explored ways to train these networks using supervision, rather than relying on pseudo-labels. Through comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, we've established that NTK networks yield superior performance and better understanding compared to existing methods. Notably, we've seen significant performance improvements in both pseudo-label and supervised training scenarios. Importantly, we've seen that the benefits of supervised methods over pseudo-labels continue to amplify as we move to multi-layer models. Given the relatively small dataset at disposal in critical areas, we strongly believe that exploring supervised methods of training neural tangent kernels is particularly crucial. Building on the Heisenberg algebra concept of minimal length, a new geometrical approach to the Bohr-Mottelson model for nuclei is explored. By combining deformed canonical commutation relations with the Pauli-Podolsky prescription, a quantized Hamiltonian operator for triaxial nuclei is derived. This operator is compared to one for axially symmetric, prolate nuclei, where an infinite square potential well in the collective shape variable is used. As a result, eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian are found to be connected to zeros of irrational order Bessel functions, explicitly dependent on the minimal length parameter. This research contributes a new quasi-dynamical symmetry point in nuclear structure, where theoretical results indicate minimal length effects on energy eigenvalues to be low for the hydrogen-like polyadenosine system. Additionally, emulations of numerical methods reveal that the novel collective shape is found to be triaxial around a specific ratio, closely aligned with the $fs$ transition and thus potentially influential for triaxial harmonic oscillators. This research is further extended to develop a new shape evolution mechanism through a perturbative approach, where a theoretical understanding is gained for the minimal length parameter's effect on energy eigenvalues. This reveals that minimal length parameter values of around twice the size of the collective shape variable's expectation value can produce energy increments of around 10%. Finally, within the newly discovered symmetry, a symmetry related to the minimal length parameter is identified, where properties of irreducible representations of the $U(1)$ group are explored. This research is extended to develop a new shape evolution mechanism involving the minimal length parameter, where a symmetry related to the pseudo-su(3) group is identified at the four-dimensional level. This is done by applying irreducibility conditions to the tensor operators' product, where closure and saturation conditions for the irreducible decomposition are found to be linked to the closure and saturation conditions for the quadratic invariants' irreducible decomposition. Furthermore, within the SU(3) group, where closure and saturation conditions for the irreducible decomposition have been realized through specific commutation relations, a new symmetry related to the minimal length parameter is identified at the six-dimensional level. This is done by applying irreducibility conditions to the tensor operators' product, where energy eigenvalues are found to be connected to the roots of the minimal length parameter-dependent generalized Dedekind eta function. Several other research notes are appended to provide further insight into the minimal length parameter's effects on various nuclear structure characteristics. This includes the study of an idealized nucleus

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research delves into the development of omnidirectional precoding solutions for multi-user systems and array sensors. Building upon the success of conventional Golay complementary matrices, GCMs, more efficient GCMs called PGCMs have been proposed. Unlike conventional GCMs, PGCMs enable the separation of multiple spatially overlapping signals at distinct angles of arrival within a single GCM period. This research contributes towards addressing the challenge of ensuring low sidelobes in OCP by designing a new PGCM with extremely low sidelobes using a novel construction method. Utilizing this PGCM, OCP can easily achieve significant gains in throughput enhancements. Furthermore, a method of constructing PGCMs using regular two-dimensional grids is also proposed, allowing for the utilization of established design methods and reductions in computational complexity. Utilizing this approach, various PGCMs have been created and made public for download at [website]. This includes 88 unique PGCMs with different sizes and performance characteristics. One key advantage of these PGCMs is the ability to achieve low sidelobes and high main lobe gain simultaneously. This research provides a comprehensive overview of PGCMs and their potential to enhance omnidirectional precoding performance. It is hoped this publication may serve as a valuable resource for researchers and engineers working with OCP. Additionally, a new generation of multilevel PGCMs called nPGCM is proposed. This innovative nPGCM enables the separation of up to n distinct signals within a single nGCM period. As such, it is expected to significantly enhance transmission efficiency in communication systems by designing nPGCMs with improved performance characteristics, including enhanced main lobe gain and low sidelobes. Furthermore, a method of constructing nPGCMs using regular two-dimensional grids is also proposed. This allows for the utilization of established design methods and reductions in computational complexity. One key advantage of this research is the ability to easily control the complexity of the nPGCMs, including the number of levels, n, the size of the nGCMs, and the amount of overlap between signals and arrays. This level of control is expected to enhance usability and efficiency in communication systems by designing nPGCMs with improved performance characteristics. This research provides a comprehensive overview of nPGCMs and their potential to significantly enhance precision gain. It is hoped this publication may serve as a valuable resource for researchers and engineers working with OCP.

Not least importantly, the approach surpasses numerous state-of-the-art methods in multiple metrics, including unsupervised change detection, land cover change mapping, and image classification. A comprehensive study examines the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an extensive, high-accuracy dataset. The concept was first introduced by Rosenfeld in 1977; this research demonstrates that scaling leads to a nearly linear correlation between residual entropy and reduced viscosity across a broad range of substances (argon, methane, CO2, and several others), including different model potentials. The initial "universal" correlation of Rosenfeld was limited, and this work reveals that scaling viscosities according to their density and molecular size substantially improves the correlation's accuracy. The resulting relationship holds for substances with significantly differing viscosities, densities, and molecular shapes. For example, it successfully correlates the viscosities of gas-phase substances with those of nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations. In a practical application, this correlation enables the estimation of viscosity with approximately 10% precision based solely on knowledge of the substance's temperature and density. Additionally, this research develops expressions for comparing similar fluids and lists corresponding parameters for numerous substances. Finally, this research assesses the current status and potential of using residual entropy to develop general, practical models for viscosity. Importantly, it identifies the key factor contributing to the failure of corresponding-state principles in simple molecular liquids: the presence of structural anomalies that start to influence potential properties at moderate densities (approximately two times the normal density of argon). It appears that current model potentials are not near their critical points even at extremely high pressures (more than 20 times the normal pressure of argon). Therefore, with ongoing advancements in simulation technology, it may become feasible to access rare fluid states that could play a significant role in geophysical and industrial processes. Furthermore, this research outlines a starting point for developing general, accurate models of viscosity and other fluid properties. Importantly, it highlights the necessity for model potentials to capture the substance's density-dependent structural variations to accurately capture its corresponding-state behavior. By addressing these limitations, it may be possible to establish simple, practical models for viscosity and other fluid properties. A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea brings concepts from areas like chaos theory and dynamical systems into the study of quantum foundations. Despite this potential, developing a clear hidden-variable model for it has been a challenge, making it hard to properly evaluate. In this piece, a hidden-variable model for the theory is developed and several aspects of the theory are analyzed with it. Our results indicate that many arguments supporting the theory fail when examined closely. The model itself displays superdeterministic and nonlocal properties with a quantum state, and it includes a hidden variable that contains redundant information. Using earlier analysis, our work further suggests that superdeterminism cannot adequately address the puzzle posed by the Bell correlations. The puzzle revolves around generating the quantum correlations without requiring any information about them. In conclusion, our research indicates that Invariant-set theory, like other superdeterministic theories, falls short of explaining the Bell correlations. The hidden-variable model for the theory may also offer new insights into the superdeterminism approach in general. It demonstrates how local hidden-variable models with no superdeterminism can produce nonlocal correlations, highlighting a distinction between superdeterminism and nonlocality. Therefore, superdeterminism does not seem capable of generating nonlocality even when assuming a high degree of predestination. In any case, this is not an evaluation of the plausibility of superdeterminism as an explanation for the world. Rather, it is an examination of the ability of superdeterminism to explain the quantum world as revealed by the Bell tests. Finally, our research indicates that superdeterminism and nonlocality are not as closely tied to each other as some might have thought based on prior analyses. The hidden-variable models for both approaches have turned out to be essentially the same, making it harder to distinguish between them. As a result, superdeterminism may be regarded either as an alternative to nonlocality or as a form of nonlocality itself, depending on one's preference for terminology. We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications. (ii) an economical use of model parameters to minimize memory usage. (iii) an efficient error rate trades off some accuracy for significantly lower computational and memory demands. The advantages of our CNN include superior interpretability (use of binary activation functions), reduced training and runtime latency, and running efficiently within real-time frameworks. The proposed model was proven effective in spotting keywords in ambient voice commands recorded in interior settings. With it, we were able to achieve an error rate of 4.7% on the Google Speech Commands Dataset while using only 476.5 KB of on-device storage and performing approximately 1.79 million multiplications per frame. This far surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions offering similar or better error rates but with significantly more computations and model parameters. The source code for our work can be found at https://github.com/acowgill/accident-snitch. The accident-snitch repository delivers our source code, where we expand upon the work discussed here. In particular, we report accident detection based on audio with 0.23% false positives and 8.23% false negatives. The model was tested on 3000 recordings (20 seconds each) from Google Speech Commands Dataset with words resembling those heard in emergency situations such as "help," "emergency," and "fire." The corresponding compute and memory footprint for this detection model is 924.8 KB and approximately 18 million multiplications per frame, respectively. As a result, we were able to generalize our ACCNN across multiple applications including accident detection. Interestingly, ACCNN achieved higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art TinyNN with comparable computational and memory footprint. Incorporating the ACCNN detector into our real-time framework yields accident detection in under 46 milliseconds. Such low latency is crucial in detecting emergencies. We further enhance latency and computational efficiency by employing model pruning. The resulting pruned-ACCNN achieved error rate of 0.23% with 76.1% multiplications removed from the original model. Our research reveals the effectiveness of this approach over existing methods, as it offers more consistent results and better performance on larger datasets. In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable computing services but also need to control and monitor diverse applications such as robotics vision, audio and video streaming, with stringent real-time performance requirements. Unfortunately, monolithic operating systems often fall short by failing to isolate different components and inadequately allocating system resources. Furthermore, they overlook the potential virtualization of hardware resources, missing an essential feature in modern computing systems. To address these issues, we introduce T-Visor, a hypervisor for embedded real-time systems that achieves improved resource sharing, enhanced safety and dependability, and better system performance by allowing for the virtualization of both hardware and application layers. By implementing T-Visor on the beaglebone board and conducting a case study, we evaluate its effects on real-world embedded applications and benchmark its performance. The results show that T-Visor enables efficient resource utilization, offers high safety guarantees and exceptional platform flexibility. To further facilitate the adoption of T-Visor in real-world scenarios, we provide guidance and best practices on its practical application. The source code of T-Visor's hypervisor and our case study's implementation are freely accessible on GitHub. These studies demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of using a hypervisor in embedded real-time systems. They also highlight various issues that arise during practical implementation and provide valuable lessons that can inform the development of future software hypervisors. Ultimately, this research explores the potential applications and usability of software hypervisors in real-world embedded real-time systems.

When two coupled populations of oscillators have synchronized and asynchronous elements respectively, a chimeric state can arise in such networks. We've analyzed chimeras in systems where one parameter influences an oscillator's behavior, drawn randomly from a uniform distribution, for oscillators in two-dimensional spaces. Our research builds on previous studies, such as Laing's 2019 findings on identical oscillators, to investigate the emergence and stability of these chimeras in diverse oscillator networks with a large number of elements. Interestingly, as heterogeneity in the oscillator network increases, it leads to the disappearance of stable chimeras through a saddle-node bifurcation. However, determining the algebra of quantized extended BMS charges has proven challenging. Recent advancements in celestial holography indicate a closed symmetry algebra without a central extension or anomaly, whereas other research suggests that quantizing these charges results in a deformation when combined. This paper reexamines this problem considering updated understanding of superrotation charges and finds that quantization of eBMS charges within a new phase space, which includes a spin memory mode, leads to an algebra without a deformation. The degenerate vacua are characterized by the soft news and a Schwarzian mode corresponding to deformations of the celestial metric by superrotations, potentially reconciling two manifestly non-conformal phases of the BMS theory. Furthermore, our finding aligns with a novel relation between eBMS charges and the quantum gravity NLO double soft gluon theorem. The generalization to general dimensions is also discussed. The Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller is a widely employed control strategy due to its straightforwardness and the readily accessible parameters that can be adapted through tuning. Nevertheless, conventional PID controllers are susceptible to saturation, which may lead to erratic controller behavior. To address this limitation, this research introduces a modified PID controller, referred to as PIDA (PID plus Integral Adjustment), designed for aerodynamic surfaces such as rudder and elevator control. The proposed controller combines the efficacy of the PID approach with a method for preventing saturation, utilizing a Stochastic Dual Simplex Algorithm (SDSA) to rapidly adjust the PID parameters at a high rate of 1000 times per second. Moreover, genetic filtering is incorporated into the PID controller to enhance its robustness and offer superior performance in the presence of significant disturbances. To evaluate the efficacy of the PIDA controller, it was successfully applied to the aircraft model "Plane" and achieved remarkable outcomes. Specifically, subsequent to controller implementation, plane's flight performance exhibited significant improvement, with enhanced maximum climb rates and diving speeds observed. Notably, the maximum elapidation rates were maximized at 4.8 m/s, and the maximum diving speeds were maximized at 16.7 m/s. In addition, by implementing the genetic filter, the PIDA controller demonstrated the ability to maintain a consistent and stable state even under a 40 N disturbance. As a direct result, the possibility of aircraft crash due to control saturation was effectively eliminated. Consequently, the proposed PIDA controller is expected to deliver impressive performance in terms of stability and robustness, and it may be suitably applied to various aerodynamic surface control scenarios. The presented research is also a pioneering study in using stochastic dual simplex algorithm for tuning PID parameters. The genetic filter is another innovation introduced in this paper and it has a lot of potential in making the controller robust against disturbances. A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with the intention of offering a fundamental and educational overview relevant for
honor's students and introductory graduate students in the field. We commence with a
brief review of the liquid-drop model, then explicitly demonstrate that low-energy
pion-nucleon scattering involves the exchange of two mesons between the pion and
the nucleon. Recognizing that hadrons are not purely wave-like objects but exist as
particles at low energies is a crucial insight. It is also observed that the principal
consequences of this interaction are the formation of a nucleon and a delta particle,
and a decay width that describes the probability of these particles. An alternative
method for calculating the pion-nucleon cross-section is given, along with a
discussion of the significance of the pion-nucleon system to the study of chiral
symmetry. Finally, an overview is offered of the current status of agreement between
theoretical predictions and experimental data, and the limitations of these
agreements. An analysis of the energy scales relevant in the pion-nucleon system
reveal that it is not appropriate to use quantum field theory to describe this
system, and instead that classical statistics and a two-meson exchange potential
may be the most suitable approaches. It is anticipated that this essay will be
useful for individuals seeking to understand the low-energy pion-nucleon system. 
Furthermore, this essay can serve as an educational resource to not only provide
an introduction to the subject, but also to present novel perspectives on the
energy scales relevant in the system and its historical development. Historical
developments in physics are an essential component of the scientific process and
the various approaches to understanding nature. However, at the same time, existing
assumptions and limitations within physics must also be acknowledged in order to
make meaningful progress in solving the complex and often difficult problems in
physics.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the heart of the CMS tracking system, providing vital information for trajectory calculation and helping to identify tracks originating from decay processes. Due to a damaged pixel pilot blade during the CMS shutdown in September 2016, a reduced system was operated for the 2017-2018 data collection period. Researchers utilized this opportunity to assess the effectiveness of the CMS pixel detector's reconstruction capabilities with partially injured information. As a result, highly efficient reconstruction performance was demonstrated with pilot blade hit efficiencies ranging from 98% to 99% and a five-sigma significance for identifying the origin of decay products for tracks with at least six associated hits. Furthermore, the influence of missing pilot blade hit information on track fit residuals and longitudinal impact parameter uncertainties was calculated. No substantial bias was detected. Also, the impact of reduced pixel information on the detection of J/ψ and B0 hadron decay products was assessed, revealing minimal negative effects. Studies demonstrated that the CMS pixel detector's reconstruction capabilities remain strong even with partially damaged components. Therefore, it is anticipated to perform similarly during the CMS shutdown in September 2019 with the CMS pixel detector fully operational. As part of the CMS upgrades, the silicon pixel detector will be replaced with a silicon strip sensor-based equivalent. However, the detector will still provide at least 10 times more hit information compared to a system with a single pixel layer. Further upgrades are also being considered to allow for more precise tracking and detection of J/ψ and B0 hadron decay products even with partially injured pixel detector information. Such research can contribute to a deeper understanding of particle physics at the LHC's future stages. As part of this effort, the CMS collaboration will participate in the development of up to four forward silicon pixel detector concepts that could enhance the detector's capabilities and provide deeper insights into quark-gluon plasma properties. Similarly, the CMS and ALICE collaborations will work together to integrate their systems into a single detector, providing even more precise understanding of particle interactions. Furthermore, the CMS and LHCb collaborations will join forces to develop a unified, heavy flavor expert system that will allow for a more in-depth analysis of B0 (B+) hadron decay products. Finally, the CMS and the FCC-ee collaboration will work together to create a new level of understanding in particle physics

We are exploring the potential benefits of utilizing complex numbers in complex-valued deep learning. Unlike its real-valued counterpart, a complex-valued network offers more expressive power due to its more extensive function space. However, this increased flexibility comes with a cost, as it can make training more challenging. To address these challenges, we have devised novel domain-independent loss functions that enable our method to outperform existing complex-valued approaches. Furthermore, we have shown that employing complex numbers can result in superior performance even when the dataset is solely used within its real domain, a scenario we have termed 'co-domain symmetry'. This concept revolves around a simple yet efficient technique where a complex-valued function is first evaluated on real data to produce a strong real-valued baseline. This technique enables the creation of novel supervised real-valued solvers that outperform existing alternatives. Our proposed method demonstrates promising results across a range of tasks, including regression, image processing, and vision classification, ultimately leading to a new class of real-valued solvers. Notably, we discuss how the choice of output affects the scalability of quantum models when utilizing gradient-based optimization. Experimentally, we assess the impact of varying qubit numbers in a quantum circuit and the number of training epochs in the classical circuit. We find that the folding strategy for output representation significantly influences performance and can be optimized depending on the specific problem at hand. Like classical algorithms, the performance of these hybrid algorithms appears to benefit from data augmentation. Our key finding is that no non-trivial warped product pointwise semi-slant submanifolds exist in S^2x S^2, except for the case where the spheres are concentric. We investigate numerically charge-neutral collective excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems, focusing on two specific Jain states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 near quarter filling, and the 1/4 Fermi-liquid state, contrasting them with the behavior observed at 1/3 states and those near half filling. Unlike states at 1/3 filling, which exhibit chiral magneto-rotons once magnetorotation is initiated, multiple magnetorons are found at 1/4 and certain combinations of 2/7 and 2/9 fillings. A broader range of magneto-rotational eigenmodes is predicted to appear when the energy of magnetorotation exceeds 0.4 times the energy cost of magnetic excitation. Our calculations also demonstrate that the energy density of magnetorons near quarter fillings is significantly lower compared to those at 1/3 states, but the rate of increase in magnetoron density with respect to charge density is higher, posing a challenge to identifying collective excitations based solely on their density of states. Finally, we show that the collective excitations near quarter fillings obey two distinct chiral sum rules, one of which is associated with chirality. The $O(N)$-Gravities framework proposes that local gravitons possess a specific structure involving $O(N)$-valued variables, which form the foundation of a certain principal bundle. This formulation provides a brief overview of topological t-duality for twistor spaces with elements of $O(N)$ that change smoothly within a space with a specific Stokes theorem. It also introduces t-dual transformations within the context of twistor spaces for both 2D and 3D tori, illustrating t-duality with examples for the 2D torus and utilizing it to demonstrate a non-trivial topological t-duality for the 3D torus. Furthermore, this formulation suggests the existence of topological t-duality for the twisted torus. Finally, this framework is extended to a specific type of pp-wave space, allowing for the description of topological t-duality for both 2D and 3D twisted tori. This analysis is supported by a specific instance of topological t-duality for the 3D twisted torus. The study shows that topological t-duality for both 2D and 3D twisted tori adheres to the principles of the Stokes theorem. Nonetheless, the scenario in which topological t-duality for the 3D twisted torus fails to satisfy these principles has also been identified. This break in symmetry holds significance in that it led to the discovery of topological t-duality for the 3D twisted torus. This breakthrough is significant in that it supports the idea that the set of symmetries in physics can be expanded. Such expansion could potentially lead to novel, previously unexplored areas of physics. Moreover, this analysis is significant in that it has facilitated a deeper, more significant reduction of 3D gravity to 2D chromo- Maxwell theory. This transformation was previously proposed by Polyakov, and this study demonstrates that the framework of $O(N)$-Gravities extends beyond that initial proposal by applying to all non-compact manifolds. Inspired by this, we modified the Random Lifts algorithm to embed any minor-free graph into a specific, weakly-dyadic tree structure with a certain narrow width, except for a few special graphs. Additionally, we created a new approach that allows a linear number of leaf nodes in the embedded tree. Finally, we demonstrated that any minor-free graph of a specific category cannot be embedded into a weakly-dyadic tree with a certain narrow width, except for a very specific type of graph, and that a similar property exists for planar graphs with a specific type of structure. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that this stability is a consequence of a novel trait: these orbits possess distinct cycles in their first-order approximations, thereby extending earlier work focused on monotone planar systems. Building upon this framework, the study is then adapted to investigate the global asymptotic stability of periodic orbits within certain classes of conservative systems. The theoretical findings are nonetheless shown to be encompassed by the recently established principles of elementary stability analysis. The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers for simulating molecular systems seems promising but faces challenges in the near term due to quantum error mitigation limitations.  Variational quantum algorithms may offer a possible solution by exploiting noisy intermediates for optimization, thereby minimizing the impact of errors. Our approach proposes an adaptive version of the variational quantum eigensolver that utilizes qubit one-body excitations to improve performance through two main adjustments. Firstly, the adaptation of the imaginary-time evolution operator via the Krylov subspace, Secondly, the application of qubit-excitation-based ansatz with Krylov adaptation (QAEA-KA) via a unitary transformation combining molecular Hamiltonian and excitation operators with subsequent truncation. Our results indicate that the UQAEDA-KA variant of the variational quantum eigensolver for imaginary time (VQE-ICT) yields lower ground state energies than other protocols for hydrogen, lithium hydride, and methane simulations. Moreover, the approach appears capable of generating accurate molecular orbitals for these systems. By leveraging qubit one-body excitation without second quantization, our method reduces memory consumption and keeps the problem within the scope of fermionic systems, thus allowing it to be scaled up for larger molecular systems. Overall, the accuracy and efficiency of UQAEDA-KA have the potential to make it a viable solution for quantum chemistry in the quantum computing domain. A key feature of deep generative models is their ability to sample synthetic data and find a low-dimensional representation of given data. We propose the concept of 'decoder fitting,' which involves determining the parameters of the generative model that yield exact reproduction of the data when given a specific representation. In this context, the 'deep generative decoder' refers to a part of a generative model that can be considered as encoding the data. Our analysis focuses on whether this 'decoder' can be identified and if so, whether it is unique. We demonstrate through our work that under the assumption of independence between data samples, the 'decoder' can be identified and is likely to be distinct under certain conditions. Our results are based on three types of deep generative models: autoencoders, variational autoencoders, and deep Gaussian processes. Further, we explore the application of 'decoder fitting' as an interpretation method for deep generative models, illustrating its use in interpreting representations learned by VAEs. We also use 'decoder fitting' as a training objective that can be utilized in the training of deep generative models that are score-based, relying solely on MAP estimates of data representations. We evaluated the effectiveness of 'decoder fitting' through numerical experiments involving synthetic and real-world data. Our findings demonstrate that 'decoder fitting' can generate accurate synthetic prior data and improve reconstruction quality. We also observed that 'decoder fitting' can provide valuable insights into the structure of the data. Our score-based generative model that uses 'decoder fitting' was able to generate high-quality synthetic images of functions. In summary, our work illustrates that 'decoder fitting' can be applied both as an interpretation method and a training objective for deep generative models. Our analysis relies on mathematical reasoning and numerical experiments that demonstrate the value of identifying the low-dimensional representation learned by these models. We expect that 'decoder fitting' may be of use in the future as a training objective in other contexts. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the majority of synthesized speech errors result from inaccuracies in the automatic speech recognition component, and not the speech synthesis method itself. This unsupervised speech synthesis technique does not require the computational power typical of neural-based models, and thus makes neural-based speech synthesis more accessible to those with limited resources. Our open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/hendrikrk/UnsupervisedSpeechSynthesis.
