We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties mirror those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid. Consequently, we establish a direct correspondence between a classical connected Lie groupoid's path sources and its traditional translation maps. Additionally, we define and prove the full, explicit statements of the fundamental principles: path integration, uniform path integration, the path integration atlas, and the existence of a maximal integral curve for internal paths. These principles form the basis of a comprehensive theory of integrated paths, which will serve as a foundation for developing and presenting the structure of Lie groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Moreover, our work will facilitate the internalization of Lie integration, providing a novel perspective on classical results, such as Lie's two theorems. Ultimately, our findings will contribute to a pioneering understanding of the geometry of Lie groupoids within synthetic differential geometry. To make our work accessible to a broader audience, we have included a comprehensive review of the essential principles underlying internal groupoids, with a particular focus on key theorems that are central to the study of integration. Additionally, we have included a detailed overview of path integration in Banach spaces, with a focus on the core principles of differential geometry that are relevant to the development of integration theories. Both of these appendices are designed to serve as introductory resources for readers who may not be fully familiar with the topics covered. However, for readers who are already fluent in these areas, the presentation can be viewed as a concise summary. The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding holistic workflows in cyberinfrastructures, allowing for deployment on virtual machines via cloud services such as JetStream. This cloud platform facilitates user-friendly access to dynamic computing and data analysis tools on demand. Dynaswap's security architecture incorporates role management, hierarchical relationships, and adaptable access control mechanisms. By integrating cutting-edge frameworks like Authentication-Authorization-Accounting and Blockchain technology, as well as advanced security features, Dynaswap provides a comprehensive protection system. Currently, the Dynaswap architecture is being validated in life-science research and educational settings within the Health Informatics field. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of the shared computing approach in reducing joint research costs and demonstrate the feasibility of supporting dynamic workflow security in cloud environments. This research is a contribution to understanding the requirements for securing cloud-based virtual machine environments and provides a practical implementation to facilitate secure collaborative research and education. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-third of product reviews are written in English, however English reviews often suffer from the limited scope of vocabulary, making the ABSA challenge even more pronounced. Many current approaches attempt to address this challenge through various representation learning techniques. However, these methods are inherently tied to explicit sentiment labels within the training dataset and rely on large amounts of annotated data. This inherent constraint hampers the effectiveness of these methods when dealing with rare words and negative reviews. In an attempt to overcome this constraint, we have developed a new approach, specifically the Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (SCP) method, to learn the explicit sentiment of words within review texts through the comparison of enhanced representations. The core idea behind our approach involves creating pairs of reviews with similar aspects but contrasting sentiment orientations. By fine-tuning the model using triplicate aspects per review, we have noticed a notable enhancement in the model's ability to accurately identify the precise sentiment of a particular aspect within a review. Our approach outperforms existing methods and establishes a new benchmark in the field. The complete code and model is available for download at https://github.com/DesmondJiang/SCP_ABMRC.git. We begin by defining a task for few-shot learning and establish that this type of problem is equivalent to improving an agent's execution of a predetermined policy following a review of the task's details. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this task is also comparable to a relabeling task where the agent has access to a variety of examples and each example provides relevant information to the outcome. Building upon this, we create a framework that enables the agent to utilize multiple examples to better comprehend the task, which in turn enables the agent to sample from its understanding of the task to improve its performance. As a result, we develop a method that both improves the agent's understanding of the task and eliminates any unnecessary information from the examples, which in turn enables the agent to relabel its understanding of the task to better approximate the actual outcome. We provide theoretical evidence that this method is effective and can be used repeatedly to continually improve the agent's performance. We test the method by applying it to language model samplers that either use to understand the task based on specific words or by having the agent use its understanding of the task to respond to a variety of questions. We show through a series of experiments that our method is effective and can be used to continually improve the agent's performance. The method is available at https://github.com/sb2019/comarv. To calculate energy flux, we combined wind speed, density, and kinetic energy per particle. A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a neural network to generate an approximate solution. Importantly, the traditional finite volume scheme limitations, such as spatial numerical diffusion, are mitigated. We derive analytical expressions for the neural network weights that obviate the need for empirical calculations. Furthermore, we analyze the method's convergence rate for a class of equations both with and without sources. We also address the challenge of implementing a high-convergence rate neural network for equations featuring stiff source terms. Through comprehensive numerical experiments, the efficacy of the method is demonstrated. Specifically, for the 1-dimensional Burgers equation, the method achieves convergence rates consistent with theoretical predictions. Moreover, the method successfully handles complex scenario, such as a Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model ground state calculation, and is adaptable to higher-dimensional applications. However, implementing the method for equations possessing non-local source terms is a topic for further research in the future. The code for this method can be accessed at one-sided neural network GitHub. The related work can be accessed at finite volume neural network GitHub. We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2069 early-type galaxies, identified within a specific redshift range (0.05-0.20), exhibited distinct tidal features. It is hypothesized that these distortions result from galaxy interactions that lead to the formation of new satellite galaxies. Based on observed data, we estimated the merger rates for massive (log(M*) > 11.0 in units of solar masses) early-type galaxies within a specific redshift range (0.05-0.20) to be approximately 0.024 to 0.037 times the merger-redshift parameter λ. This merger rate is higher than previously estimated values for overall early-type galaxies of similar massive proportions. However, our results provide evidence that a substantial portion (around 71 percent) of massive early-type galaxies, exhibiting distinct tidal features, have low mass ratios (<1:100) in galaxy interactions. These low-mass ratio interactions can lead to the addition of new satellite galaxies, which was not accounted for in previous studies on merger rates for massive early-type galaxies. Our analysis further indicates that a substantial portion (around 29 percent) of massive early-type galaxies, exhibiting distinct tidal features, have high mass ratios (>1:100) in galaxy interactions. This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a sequence of constrained optimization problems that can be iteratively refined. Our method, AskewSGD, is an annealed version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm that enforces training within predefined intervals. AskewSGD consistently selects suitable boundary points for optimization, ensuring diversity in its parameter exploration. Unlike existing approaches, AskewSGD avoids complex and computationally intensive optimization for the quantized codebook. Instead, it iteratively refines the current configuration's performance through localized exploration. Our experiments using AskewSGD on convolutional neural networks for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 demonstrate its effectiveness, achieving a significant 0.3% improvement in accuracy compared to standard quantized neural network approaches without increasing training epochs or batch size. To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used, which involves selecting prior samples that meet a minimum likelihood requirement. The algorithms for selecting these samples come in various forms, such as the original uniform prior sampler, a method that stratifies the sampling process, and a more sophisticated approach based on differential evolution. Here, the performance and simplicity of these methods are evaluated in the context of typical Bayesian modeling, with a focus on stress-testing the algorithms by introducing faults in their implementation. The outcome of this analysis suggests that the original uniform sampler offers sufficient precision for general Bayesian analysis despite its straightforward nature. On the other hand, the more complex differential evolution method does not consistently outperform this basic approach, which indicates that additional development is required to make it a superior sampling technique. The remaining straightforward method, however, can serve as a versatile solver for various nested sampling difficulties. The study further explores the feasibility of using uniform priors in multi-dimensional scenarios by examining different dimensionalities in the context of a radial distribution function model. The outcome reveals that this basic approach performs well even in scenarios with hundreds of dimensions but eventually starts to encounter difficulties in scenarios with thousands of dimensions. To ensure that medical imaging models produce accurate predictions, it is crucial
to implement out-of-distribution detection capabilities. There is an increasing
concern within the Vision and Machine Learning communities that needs to be addressed.
The traditional approach to out-of-distribution detection has been heavily centered on
one-class classification issues. However, in the context of medical imaging, data
is often scarce, which poses significant challenges for training effective OOD
detectors. The main issue lies in the inherent bias of prior-based and anomaly-score
approaches that rely on the assumption of a particular distribution. A recent
research study demonstrated that a specific model is always superior to others on
the OpenImages dataset and all its variants, which raises questions about the
objectivity of benchmarking methods in medical imaging contexts as well. In this
study, we propose an innovative two-layer approach based on Distributional
Gaussian Process that can effectively address the issue of learning accurate
out-of-distribution detectors with limited data, without requiring prior knowledge of
a specific data distribution. The model can be adapted to various data scenarios and
is applicable across different modalities, including X-ray images. Our model
exhibits performance superiority over all existing methods on an in-house dataset. 
Moreover, our model achieves a balanced detection performance and false positive
rate and showcases satisfactory robustness to data scarcity. Ultimately, our model
demonstrates real-time applicability in medical settings. The proposed model's code
has been made publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/dgp. The model's
weight files can be downloaded at https://github.com/asharakeh/dgp-weight-baselines.

Quantum systems driven periodically experience heat build-up due to resonant excitations and tend to concentrate population in a limited set of states.
Building on this phenomenon, researchers are exploring new methods for cooling systems rather than just driving them.
In our study, we introduce a more sophisticated approach where the population is directed towards a specific state, and we investigate it using a chain of quantum dots driven by a laser.
By using Floquet band structure and calculating the system's effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, we identify an isolated, self-sustaining state in which the system becomes self-trapped and ultimately develops a Bose-Einstein condensate.
We also show that this self-sustaining state shares similarities with so-called "scar states" commonly seen in quantum systems driven periodically.
We also determine that it's feasible to create and maintain the self-sustaining state and the Bose-Einstein condensate even in the Markov limit using a single laser pulse.
Through numerical simulations, we examine the impact of different laser pulses, such as the Gaussian and the Lorentzian, on creating the condensate and determine that the best results are typically achieved using the Gaussian pulse.
Ultimately, our approach provides a promising new pathway to create and maintain a Bose-Einstein condensate using a driven quantum system, and it has the added benefit of being relatively straightforward to create the condensate and control it using appropriate pulse design. Moreover, it's worth noting that this approach to creating the condensate is distinct from other approaches based on autoresonant excitation and can therefore be considered a supplemental method for achieving a Bose-Einstein condensate. Furthermore, it's also possible to create the condensate even in cases of weak damping by adopting a technique called compact modeling. Lastly, our approach to creating the condensate showcases the utility of both the Floquet band structure and the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in analyzing quantum systems that are driven periodically. Historically, developing these events has been a significant challenge, but recent breakthroughs have made it feasible to create optical clocks that can operate accurately and independently. These optical clocks, which are driven by lasers, can sometimes fail to behave predictably and may not recur at all. Since their inaccuracy increases over time, it's crucial to develop a framework for characterizing such optical clocks based on their individual behavior over short periods. We propose a statistical approach, which measures the accuracy of these clocks by analyzing the variations between consecutive measurements. By applying this method to theoretical and real-world clocks that are not predictable, we demonstrate its effectiveness in providing a reliable measure of accuracy. Our findings can also be used to identify the point at which these optical clocks become unreliable due to their decreasing accuracy. This study lays the groundwork for a standardized method of analyzing non-repeating optical clocks that are capable of providing ultra-precise time measurements. By enabling a straightforward comparison of their performance, researchers can create a direct link between the statistical analysis and experimentally relevant time-measuring tools, which could significantly contribute to a future revolution in time measurement. Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse set of loss functions, we've isolated specific aspects that dictate how pairs of images are mapped in relation to each other. By breaking down these essential components, we show that most of the diversity in pair-wise losses can be attributed to only two distinct elements. Our findings provide a unified framework for understanding the impact of these loss functions and offer a method to create new loss formulas that build upon this deciphered structure. When applied to face recognition tasks, our analysis leads to the development of five tailored loss functions, each reflecting the influence of the two isolated components, and consequently, the five distinct types of pair-wise loss functions that have been proposed in the past. To further analyze the effectiveness of these loss functions, we've designed an experiment that demonstrates the impact of the two isolated components on the accuracy of models by evaluating them in an environment where the identity of images is made known to the model. When applied to face recognition tasks, our designed experiment, dubbed 'gradient surgery,' reveals that most of the diversity in pair-wise loss functions can be attributed to two elements - enhancing uniformity and balancing the distribution of the margins between images in distinct classes. While uniformity involves maintaining consistent distances between images in distinct classes, a balanced distribution involves ensuring that the distances between images in distinct classes are spread out uniformly. To analyze the impact of these elements, we've developed a procedure where we modify the pre-trained models to either enhance uniformity or balance the distribution of the margins, and observed the effects of these transformations using the gradient surgery technique. When we applied this technique to the models to enhance uniformity, we saw a notable improvement of 18.2% in accuracy for the MS1MV2 loss function, a 10.9% increase in accuracy for the Triplet loss function, and a 5.9% increase in accuracy for the Cosine loss function. A small number of sources with only two or three filaments in the sample exhibit separation statistics that do not conform to a uniform pattern. While delayed settings with time-dependent delays have been thoroughly explored, their arm-dependent counterparts are largely understudied. In the experts scenario with complete knowledge, we demonstrate the existence of optimal (O) algorithms, building upon a previously defined class of adaptive (A) algorithms. However, for the bandits scenario with arm-dependent delays and incomplete knowledge, we show the impossibility of optimal algorithms and propose several efficient approaches. Notably, we present a single (O) algorithm that matches the performance of the best adaptive (A) algorithm in each setting, and an alternative approach that offers a nearly optimal regret bound when the delay parameters are known. Furthermore, we explore a situation where only the mean values of delay parameters are known, resulting in a non-trivial competition between accurate bound estimation and efficient online learning. In this setting, we suggest a practical method for bound estimation and demonstrate its effectiveness by providing a near-optimal (O) algorithm. The methods proposed here are also applicable to the experts scenario, offering a degree of flexibility. Additionally, we provide optimal regret bounds for both experts and bandits scenarios with delayed observations in a semi-realistic setting. Our methods for bandits have also been shown to generalize to the setting of linear bandits with delayed observations. Ultimately, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the fundamental issue: identifying the optimal (O) algorithm for the task of learning from delayed observations. Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed. Specifically, optimizing task success using reinforcement learning alone often leads to low lexical diversity in task-oriented settings. The proposed reason is a lack of fundamental understanding of text-generation objectives and how they impact the learning process during model pretraining. To address this, we suggest a novel pretraining task that focuses on generating human-like text. The task does not require natural language but can be executed by a rule-based system, making it suitable for various domains. We implemented this task using two popular neural language models and observed significant improvements in task success and lexical diversity. Notably, model outputs became more readable and less prone to errors. We evaluated these models on the Goal-Oriented Machine Translation and Goal-based Reasoning datasets and discovered that they perform admirably without goal-oriented annotations. Moreover, we discovered that goal-based word embeddings are not essential for success in task-oriented settings. This word embedding can be replaced by a simple rule that eliminates unnecessary dialogue history. We contend that separating data-driven model pretraining and fine-tuning phases can facilitate a deeper comprehension of the underlying objectives. To support this hypothesis, we investigated several alternative pretraining tasks and discovered that only one can effectively transfer to a goal-based classification task. The proposed framework was then applied to a multi-turn goal-based classification task without requiring multiple domains of parallel training data. Instead, we utilized a simple strategy to combine knowledge from distinct training domains into a single model. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our proposed framework leads to accurate goal-based classification in the presence of limited resource constraints and further highlight the need for fundamental improvements in text-generation objectives to yield transferable representations. Furthermore, we found that neural language models can provide human-like task success when goal descriptions are unavailable and no training data for its acquisition exists. This is demonstrated through evaluating our models on a multi-domain goal-based classification dataset and further highlights the advantages of identifying commonalities across distinct domains, rather than training separate models for each one in order to improve efficiency. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to contribute to crisis communication. By combining data collection and automatic analysis with human validation, this study demonstrates the feasibility of utilizing social media for operational insights in crisis situations. The developed methodology can be applied in other emergency scenarios. Its primary application lies in helping communicators and managers make informed decisions by providing a structured framework for analyzing public sentiment and opinions during crises. The methodology can be freely used and modified from the provided GitHub repository. The study further examines real-time sentiment changes and user engagement in relation to the earthquake. The precision of automated sentiment analysis and user classification ranges from 79% to 87%. The study also reveals a five-fold increase in automated engagement analysis compared to the provided training data, albeit with engagement precision limited to 51%. The study's findings highlight that individuals under 20 expressed more emotional support during the Izmir earthquake, whereas those above 40 displayed higher concern. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we calculate the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree for Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and their nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$. Our study shows that $\Gamma_n$ possess the $R_\infty$ property, and the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of $\Gamma_{n,c}$ varies based on the value of c. When c is less than or equal to 2, $\Gamma_{n,c}$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. For c equal to 3 or above and n is even, $\Gamma_{n,c}$ does not possess the $R_\infty$ property. Conversely, when n is odd, $\Gamma_{n,c}$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property for 2 < c < n. Our study also examines the isomorphism between the generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups and the nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups. Specifically, we prove the isomorphism between $\Gamma_{n,c}$ and a subgroup of a generalized solvable group of the form $BS_m \times C_{n-1}$. Lastly, we explore the isomorphism between the generalized solvable group of the form $AS_{n-1}^m$ and a generalized solvable group of the form $BS_{n-1}^m \times C_2$. Our study provides a definition of property $R_{\infty,c}$ and shows that a group G exhibits property $R_{\infty,c}$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce at least c twisted conjugacy classes. This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from
instrumented vehicle data collected in downtown Indianapolis over the course
of 68 driving sessions with various drivers. Each session lasted approximately
20 to 40 minutes. Our primary aim in creating this dataset is to supply the
research community with realistic driving scenarios encompassing diverse
trajectories and driving behaviors. SceNDD features a comprehensive set of
annotations, including scenario descriptions and outcome forecasts. This
dataset has the potential to boost the development of predictive models. For
instance, it has already been utilized in the Naturalistic Driving Data
Championship. Additionally, we present basic analyses of driver habits based
on this dataset as well as an examination of the most perilous driving
practices. Our findings demonstrate that drivers exhibit a considerable
amount of aggressive driving, with mean speeds reaching up to 16 mph above the
official speed limit. We contend that such behavior is rooted in the driving
environment. Our analysis of the most hazardous actions suggests that
incorporating lane markings that facilitate straight-line driving appears to be
a priority for local drivers. You can obtain the SceNDD dataset at
https://github.com/csper2107/SceNDD. The corresponding video dataset is
available at https://youtu.be/0s8j3Q2f8Gw. A comprehensive presentation of our
findings is delivered at the 2022 IPID Conference. Furthermore, we discuss
additional outcomes at the 2022 NeurIPS workshop "Naturalistic and Synthetic
Driving Data". 

\subsection{Related Work}
There are numerous benchmark driving datasets that have contributed significantly
to advanced driver-assistance systems and self-driving vehicles, such as
USDD, DDI+, and UCDD. However, most existing datasets focus on individual
events rather than comprehensive driving scenarios. This study seeks to bridge
this gap by developing a novel dataset that not only encompasses underlying
scenarios but also forecasts their eventual outcomes. 

\subsection{Dataset Collection}
The SceNDD dataset was gathered from instrumented vehicles in downtown
Indianapolis through 68 unique driving sessions with various drivers. Each
session lasted between 20 to 40 minutes. 

\subsection{Scenario Labeling}
The SceNDD dataset has been annotated by experts to identify scenarios and
predictive outcomes. There are 1,091 distinct scenario types, each associated
with possible predictions.

A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions. Our methods allow the computation of the deformation space for certain four-dimensional, four-dimensional homogeneous nearly G2-manifolds and a five-dimensional homogeneous nearly G2-manifold. We further show that the deformation space of the canonical connection on a four-dimensional, homogeneous nearly G2-manifold is one-dimensional, and derive conditions for a non-trivial deformation of the instanton to exist on corresponding three-dimensional, homogeneous nearly G2-manifolds. Using these conditions, we identify which abelian instantons can be deformed and determine the possibility of deforming the self-dual Yang-Mills equation on a three-dimensional, homogeneous nearly G2-manifold. The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and socio-economic disruption, with the rapid proliferation of the virus having far-reaching effects worldwide. As part of the effort to combat this crisis, contact tracing technology, known for its success in other outbreaks, has been suggested as an important tool for controlling the spread of the virus.  However, this tool raises concerns about user privacy, leading to hesitation in adopting it. To address these concerns, this paper proposes an innovative approach that maintains user confidentiality while facilitating the effective management of the COVID-19 outbreak. This method is centered on a decentralized, anonymous technology that utilizes blockchain and secret sharing mechanisms to protect user data. To evaluate its effectiveness, we implemented this technology as part of a mobile app called Coronav\'irus-SUS, which was developed for both iOS and Android operating systems. Our experimental results show that the proposed approach is able to identify 90% of COVID-19 cases while maintaining user confidentiality at a level of breakdown by country. This solution has been made available to the public through a GitHub repository. Following extensive user testing, we found that the app received positive feedback from our test subjects, with our results demonstrating that the use of advanced mechanisms such as Coronav\'irus-SUS does not affect the overall performance of the device. Our study concludes that the use of this technology as part of a mobile app has the potential to be an effective tool in the effort to control the spread of the virus while maintaining user confidentiality. Furthermore, following the implementation of the app, we were able to demonstrate that the use of contact tracing technology had a significant impact on the overall infection rate in Brazil, with our findings showing a significant decline following the implementation of the app. This study highlights the importance of protecting user data while maintaining the effectiveness of contact tracing technology during public health crises. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22. As a result, we further build upon the method developed in Bar22 by employing the "gluing" technique to compute T-equivariant cohomology. Specifically, when V is a two-dimensional irreducible representation, we compute the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology groups of complex projective spaces CP(V). Notably, these groups contain degree 55 components that are orthogonal to their T^2-equivariant counterparts. Consequently, this discovery implies that the T-equivariant cohomology of CP(V) contains degree 55 components that are orthogonal to its T^2-equivariant counterparts, which can be computed via a different method. This study investigates how grammatical gender influences the representation of nouns in languages that indicate gender. Using word embeddings from 19 languages, we have observed that nearby words in a lexical network often reflect the gender of its accompanying noun. Consequently, monolingual neural machines may not adequately account for grammatical gender, a crucial factor in their translation performance. We discovered that word embeddings learning from parallel texts frequently fail to accurately represent gender, in contrast to those trained on datasets that include gender information. Furthermore, we have found that the articles and pronouns, which serve as indicators of gender in gender-marking languages, benefit from this gender knowledge, whereas nouns often do not. Notably, using pre-trained word embeddings based on grammatically informed representations of nouns can significantly improve the translation capabilities of machines. Building upon these existing noun embeddings, we have developed a novel leaner, called Reviser, which effectively revises its own gender-mapped representations to better suit its translation goals. When integrated into machines, the revised gender-based representations lead to improved translations, demonstrating higher coherence and accuracy in lexically choosing equivalent words. Notably, our findings suggest that the Reviser model can also benefit languages without grammatical gender in a parallel manner, indicating its potential for use in a wide range of languages. Ultimately, our research reveals that languages can benefit from this type of revision even in contexts unrelated to gender. Importantly, our study emphasizes that the inherent characteristics of words in individual languages should not be overlooked in translation models, which in turn can lead to more effective and accurate translations. Moreover, our analysis encourages exploration of word embeddings through the lens of linguistic morphology. Finally, our collection of word embeddings alongside corresponding parse files and gold translations is available to the public on the CCL GitHub page. By sharing this resource, we hope to facilitate further research, especially in the domain of linguistics. This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, using solely observational data and causal graphs. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its underlying parameters. By leveraging these properties, it provides a versatile framework for simulating hypothetical scenarios and making predictions based on past actions. Our experiments confirm that VACA effectively approximates various interventional and counterfactual scenarios in different SCM setups. Moreover, we apply VACA to assess counterfactual fairness in training and testing phases, as required by fair machine learning algorithms. Our results indicate that VACA not only efficiently learns interventions but also an essential concept in fair machine learning – counterfactual fairness. VACA's implementation is now publicly available at https://github.com/autospacer/VACA. State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits to terabits per second. This significant data rate complicates radio data analysis and necessitates costly computation. Although top-tier computing facilities are accessible for national and international institutions, these centers struggle to respond to the rapid goals of fast radio burst (FRB) research and transient science in a timely manner. This paper describes the development of a high-performance computing system known as REALTA at the LOFAR Irish station to enhance real-time science capabilities. REALTA covers the full spectrum of correlated data from 10 MHz to 200 MHz and is equipped with advanced data analysis functionality. This system provides the capability to perform various metrics on the fly, such as flagging bad data, implementing dynamic bandwidth modes, and identifying specific radio transients including FRBs, FRB-like pulses, and FRB-like bursts. REALTA has successfully employed a 20-node architecture featuring powerful GPUs, allowing it to process the equivalent of 50 TB/day of 1-bit data per day at 10 KB/s efficiency. This computing system has already enabled the discovery of seven FRBs during its initial operation, with an average detection rate of approximately monthly. This paper discusses the REALTA architecture and its components, the FRB detection pipeline and its analysis, and the promising science outcomes and future science prospects for REALTA. REALTA is now considered a vital component of the LOFAR real-time astronomy network, known as the Core Campaign. REALTA data are now being stored alongside other LOFAR real-time data in the LOFAR Real-time Astrophysical Survey (LoRTAS) database for further analysis. REALTA data are also now being studied as part of the LOFAR Transient Astronomy Project (LOFAR-TAP) to identify the distribution and properties of FRBs. REALTA data are also now being examined as part of the LOFAR Fast Transient Astronomy Project (LOFAR-FTA) to identify repeating FRBs. REALTA data are also now being investigated as part of the Irish LOFAR Fornax Dark Matter Survey (ILOFAR-FDMS) to determine the subhalo density profile. Cyber Physical Systems are transforming into cohesive units, allowing multiple systems to collaborate in achieving a complex objective.
This trend is marked by the emergence of CPSoCs, where individual CPSs leverage AI and data exchange to maximize objective satisfaction.
In the context of our research, we're exploring the potential benefits of transitioning traditional CPSs, specifically those focusing on optimization, to the CPSoC framework.
To facilitate this transition, we've established a metric that quantifies the benefits derived from AI integration within each individual CPS.
This metric serves as the foundation for a multi-agent optimization Scoring Function that evaluates cooperation among CPSs, including those that may not utilize AI.
Our approach aims to expand existing cooperation facilitation Scoring Functions, allowing its application and validation across a wide range of CPSs, including real-world applications. 
Ultimately, this Scoring Function is intended to support a more extensive, more robust framework for autonomous CPSoC cooperation. 
This concept is demonstrated through its implementation in two practical use cases: optimizing supply and inventory levels in a large retail environment and managing the energy demand and supply within a smart microgrid. 
The approach and associated Scoring Function presented in this dissertation offer a practical solution for enabling CPSoC cooperation and taking advantage of emerging CPSoC capabilities. 
It is open-source and can be easily integrated into CPSs to demonstrate its effectiveness in empowering collaboration among individual CPSs. 
Our simulation results show that, in cooperation, these CPSs can achieve up to 200% more objective satisfaction compared to non-cooperative approaches. 
In addition, in terms of resource consumption, the outcomes indicate that cooperation can lead to a 38% reduction. 
This suggests that the ability to identify and capitalize on complementary capabilities between CPSs is possible through the Scoring Function's support.  Moreover, in our research, we discovered that the function's performance is influenced by factors such as parameter $k$, used matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and the Scoring Function's design stage. 
Ultimately, future research should focus on expanding the current framework to encompass additional features of cooperation facilitation Scoring Function.  This could involve introducing new parameters or allowing agents to modify the function's parameters dynamically in order to further enhance CPSoC collaboration.  This concept could lead to a more robust and scalable cooperation among CPSs in the future.  An additional use case is discussing the application of CPSoC Scoring Function in the disease management.  In this use case CPSoC is applied to manage a contagious disease like measles.

Light field technology captures a dynamic pattern of light in 3D space by recording multiple images from different perspectives. However, the high data dimensionality of light field data makes it difficult to compress efficiently. This paper proposes an innovative approach that utilizes a disparity model trained on a specific dataset to predict light field data. The model is designed to prioritize quality for reference data, while sacrificing some detail for microplates. A disparity model trained on a separate set was found to effectively compress light field data without prior calibration. A comprehensive evaluation of this approach was conducted on various light field datasets, showcasing significant improvements in compression ratio and quality compared to existing methods. Moreover, the framework is adaptable to any light field compression pipeline and can be applied to any light field camera without manual calibration. Experimental results demonstrated a 20-30 times increase in compression ratio with comparable video quality. Furthermore, the framework was successfully used to capture 10-minute videos on a SD card with 30 minutes of recording time. Subjective testing placed our approach among top light field compressors, surpassing commercial products such as H-Adamant and Light Field Compression real-time tools. Additionally, our approach was found to outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of quality with minimal loss in compression ratio for display applications. A significant 10 times increase in compression ratio was observed in comparison to existing methods. A hardware implementation of the framework was also performed using a VLIW processor, yielding a 10 million instructions per second processing rate for forward rendering and a 5 million instructions per second processing rate for encoding. interactive and non-interactive, prevail with synchronous and asynchronous 
query-document embeddings, respectively. Weighed against retrieval accuracy and 
computational efficiency, each approach excels and falls short. This study combines 
the benefits of these two frameworks through the development of a semi-interactive 
mechanism that constructs a non-interactive framework but unites document embedding 
with multiple associated queries in parallel to produce interactive embeddings. By 
merging these two approaches, a cross-lingual model is introduced that achieves a 
competitive 64.2% Rprec on a German-English dataset while using fewer than half the 
processors needed by the leading Baseline. Additionally, this model outperforms the 
standard English-only VectorCross model by 9.6% Rprec. We present a semantic and 
syntactic analysis of the created dataset to illustrate the importance of query-formulation 
for cross-lingual information retrieval and discuss generalizable the proposed semi-interactive 
mechanism to various tasks. The developed model, along with the German-English 
dataset, are available at https://github.com/harshgururkar/cv-cli. This research was

A key source of this data comes from household surveys, usually based on a stratified sample design that can be analyzed using advanced statistical models. 

Estimating health demographic rates, such as fertility and mortality rates for specific population groups in small areas is a key application here. A recent study aimed to address these objectives by examining two primary design-based approaches and integrating spatial covariance into two model-based methods.

To demonstrate the methods' real-world applicability, data was collected from five demographic and health studies conducted in South Africa and Democratic Republic of Congo between 2016-2017. A wide range of sub-national scenarios in both countries were investigated to evaluate the performance of the estimated models. 

Results indicated that model-based approaches, particularly those accounting for spatial correlations, provided more precise calculations. A key design-based technique called joint ratio estimation proved to be a reliable method for generating model parameters. A direct comparison of model-based and design-based techniques yielded more accurate results for the model-based approaches.

Recommendations for practitioners include: choosing appropriate spatial relationships and model specifications; being aware that our proposed methods can produce reliable results, but may not meet the strict requirements for small-area estimation as per the National Center for Health Statistics' standards; being able to integrate multiple sources of data, including geographic information systems; and considering additional data sources to enhance model performance. Further adjustments to some model-based approaches' weights and the use of more advanced spatial covariance models are suggested for improved results. This paper employs a refined hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns in multi-period time series data, which exhibit dynamics governed by various time-sensitive factors. Traditional stacked RNN and DBN models lack the capability to incorporate tendencies spanning multiple periods and often overlook redundant input variables, which contribute nothing or negatively affect predictive power. By integrating the hierarchical latent variable model with multiple transition periods and a Bayesian neural network equipped with Horseshoe priors as the input layer, our proposed method effectively filters out irrelevant variables, enables enhanced interpretation of time series characteristics, and improves the detection of changes within continuous sequences. Moreover, the incorporation of the Horseshoe prior yields a compact structural support of the input matrix, which facilitates the estimation of the measurement module's parameters by efficiently updating the variational distribution and allowing post-analysis of significant input variables through a variable selection mechanism. Simulation-based evaluations demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses alternative models in terms of variable selection, predictive accuracy, and robustness, which is further demonstrated through an application using real-world macroeconomic data. The analysis also reveals that datasets with fewer examples demand greater care in terms of making precise, fair, and confidential predictions. We have developed a new control method using learning algorithms to instruct a simulated robotic arm to perform different tasks with limited data. This approach leverages the principles of dynamical system control, incorporating various forms of information: observed trajectories, theoretical models, and physical constraints. As a result, it is possible to accomplish complex tasks such as reaching, flying, swimming, and walking with high success rates exceeding 90%, all within one trial. Importantly, our method is particularly efficient when supplemented with information about the system's dynamics. When applied to a challenging deep reinforcement learning problem in autonomous underwater vehicle navigation, we found that our method achieves a 10% to 20% improvement in success rate and reduces the required number of trials by a factor of two to four. Furthermore, it is capable of handling scenarios where failures to reach the target are penalized, a characteristic present in many real-world control problems. When such penalties exist, we discovered that our method is more robust to inaccuracies in the system model, making it resilient to physical biases in the dynamic model. This result suggests that incorporating virtual rewards into consideration can facilitate learning despite discrepancies between the assumed and true system models. Moreover, we found that our method is adept at applying back-up plans in time-critical situations to prevent accidents. It is capable of estimating the reachability of system states, identifying infeasible goals through error analysis, and accommodating changes in the system dynamics. When faced with unscheduled changes to the system dynamics during learning, we discovered that our method is able to adapt promptly in the course of one trial. Crucially, it is able to recognize the presence of such modifications by evaluating discrepancies between observed and simulated system behavior. Ultimately, our method is designed to facilitate the efficient use of scarce resources for developing autonomous robots and other controlled dynamic systems by minimizing the need for extensive testing, inaccurate virtual rewards, or costly experimentation. Prior solutions attempted to address this issue by incorporating multiple discriminators. Our proposed relation GANs utilize a different approach by integrating discriminators into a relational framework, which considers the inherent connections between multiple sampled images during training. Uniquely, our relation GANs incorporate triplet loss to further enhance discriminator training and improve generalization, ultimately leading to superior performance in generating high-resolution images. Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this limitation by training on a set of base categories, enabling their model to detect both the base categories and novel object types. However, their practical application is limited by the requirement for extensive pseudo-labeling of training data, which is costly in terms of both time and computational resources. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach using image-level novel class labels without bounding-box annotations. We introduce a base-class-aided open-vocabulary object detection framework that utilizes a two-stage learning process. First, it uses image-level novel class labels to learn base-class bounding-box representations. Then, it incorporates these representations to detect novel object categories. To reduce data-driven pseudo-label errors, particularly in situations where novel classes and base classes have different spatial features, we introduce a method to automatically select high-quality pseudo-labels. We test our framework's performance on the OpenImages dataset and achieve notable open-vocabulary detection results. Furthermore, we compare its performance with state-of-the-art object detection models on the standard COCO detection task, demonstrating competitive results. The code supporting our method is publicly available at https://github.com/AllanLin123/base-caid_OVOD.  The code has been subsequently improved and is now at https://github.com/AllanLin123/base-caid_OVOD_v2. The improved framework has also been adapted at https://github.com/AllanLin123/ovoid_duetc5fairness. The code supporting this adaptation is also publicly available.

The models assume factor loadings remain static over time despite the significant influence of contemporary events, such as global pandemics, economic downturns, and social policy changes. To improve forecasting accuracy, we developed a factor model with time-varying factor loadings. However, model parameter identification issues arise when forecasting periods are shorter than the models' span, leading to an infinite-number of possible models. We mitigated this challenge by utilizing early forecasting data to establish a system of linear equations. We then employed a non-negative least squares approach to solve for factor loadings. Specifically, our approach was shown to reduce mean absolute error by 19.6% and 17.9% for respective periods of 5 and 15 years into the future. Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing weights among different child models is a common strategy. However, we discovered that the interference caused by sharing weights across models with varying architecture can have adverse effects on child model performance. To explore this issue, we developed a simple theoretical model that examines the influence of weight perturbations on the loss of a linear classifier, which can be extended to convolutional classifiers. Furthermore, we studied the impact of weight sharing in NAS using both theoretical models and empirical tests, and investigated potential ways to mitigate its negative effects. By combining the findings from our theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we were able to identify a simple and efficient approach to weight initialization that can significantly reduce the difference in performance between standalone models and shared weights. The results of our experiments on multiple datasets and architecture search spaces confirm the effectiveness of this initialization strategy in improving the overall quality of child models. Specifically, using weight initialization alone can lead to a child model performance gain of 0.7%, 1.0%, and 1.3% for the AmoebaNet, FairDNN, and Snorkel datasets, respectively. Furthermore, when paired with other optimization methods such as gradient norm clipping, the approach enabled the non-accelerated model to match the performance of its accelerated counterpart on the ImageNet dataset. Therefore, we consider this an efficient and practical solution to address the issue of weight interference in NAS. When evaluated on other NAS benchmarks, a non-accelerated model with weight initialization achieved a top-one accuracy of 67.4% for AmoebaNet, 70.4% for FairDNN, and 54.3% for Snorkel. Moreover, a model with weight initialization and gradient norm clipping reached an accuracy of 67.9% for AmoebaNet, 70.9% for FairDNN, and 54.9% for Snorkel. Notably, the non-accelerated model with weight initialization surpassed the accelerated model with gradient norm clipping in terms of accuracy when tested on the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets. Specifically, we observed a significant improvement of at least 1% in performance when compared to other baseline models with weight sharing. Therefore, it appears that the approaches evaluated in this study to mitigate weight interference were successful. This tool can be employed by translators to pinpoint unreliable translations and, consequently, improve the overall quality of the translation. In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase a target's energy absorption. This study applies a mathematical framework to analyze the eigenchannels and identify two wide-ranging formulas that connect the scattering properties, geometric characteristics, and energy patterns within any defined area of the system. Our in-depth calculations in a simple model reveal the complex interplay between geometry and transport, and highlight novel insights such as the connection between energy patterns and the available pathways for energy entry. Additionally, the summative nature of this relationship provides a new understanding of previously established transport and energy limits. Finally, the mathematical structure of this framework offers a fresh perspective on the optimization of energy absorption and other physical interactions. We've found that using pruning methods on artificial neural networks significantly
reduces their size while maintaining their performance, and can even reveal smaller
sub-networks with higher accuracy than their full counterparts. By applying these
methods in a controlled manner, we're able to analyze the inherent structure of the
learning algorithm and identify the most critical components of the neural network.
Our findings show that when properly structured, even simple neural networks can
achieve remarkable results, and that their ability to generalize is deeply connected
to their architecture. We're exploring this relationship further, focusing on the
impact of data distribution and its differences between training and testing phases on a
network's ability to accurately reproduce its training outcomes. Ultimately, our
research has significant implications for the development of more efficient and
robust artificial intelligence algorithms. The code used in our analysis is publicly
available on GitHub, specifically within the pruned_nets repository. 

In terms of the main question we're addressing, our study suggests that when we
properly structure even basic neural networks, they are capable of achieving
satisfactory generalization; however, it's also evident that convolutional networks
possess an inherent advantage over their fully-connected counterparts. This
advantage becomes particularly apparent when the sample size used to train these
networks is limited, and more extensive research is required to fully grasp the
relationship between architecture and performance at larger data volumes. 

The code used in our analysis is publicly available on GitHub, specifically within the pruned_nets repository. 

This study was initially published as a chapter within the "Advances in Intelligent Systems" edited volume, which is part of the Advances in Intelligent Systems & Computing series, and it's also available on arXiv at the link arXiv:2109.10494. 

Related research was also presented at the 2021 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN), and the related paper can be found at the link arXiv:2102.12580. 

The work reported in this document was made possible due to a research grant from the French Fondation des Sciences Cognitives. 

The primary author of this analysis is Dr. Yassine Lghour, and the corresponding mail address is yassine.lghour@univ-lille.fr. 

The structural properties of the neural network used in our analysis were visualized using Gepspy, networks architecture were created using Keras, and the pruning algorithm itself was developed by the authors.

The VisDA 2022 Challenge seeks to demonstrate visual domain adaptation in a scenario where images are corrupted by noise. A substantial, noise-perturbed dataset was created for the challenge by applying noise to the DTD dataset. With a predefined framework, participants were required to improve image classification using a policy that utilizes feature embeddings from different domain images. The challenge operates in two phases: the first phase involves submitting scores in a semi-synthetic environment before seeing the corrupted training dataset, and the second phase entails submitting scores on held-out test data after seeing the corrupted training dataset. The semi-synthetic nature of the challenge poses a significant difficulty due to the shift in the noise distribution between the pseudo-labeled test data and the corrupted training set. As a result, we propose an innovative two-stage solution that outperforms other methods. Firstly, we use a variation of the InfoMax principle to learn a unified representation that is resilient to noise by applying self-supervision consistently across the corrupted domain adaptation scenario. Secondly, we leverage the structural connection between the pseudo-labeled test data and the corrupted training data through a generative model that samples pseudo-labels from the test data. The combination of these two stages yields the solution. Notably, we attained first place in both stage 1 and stage 2 with our solution, and this paper details the solution by broken it down into novel techniques that are supported by comprehensive experimental results. The proposed method has also been successfully applied to other domain adaptation scenarios, and it yields superior results when compared to other strong baselines. t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by data such as points on the surface of a sphere, which adhere more closely to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, this study develops a novel vMF-SNE algorithm tailored for embedding spherical data efficiently. Utilizing an iterative procedure, it achieves more effective embeddings than the conventional t-SNE method when working with such data types, as shown through its simulation on sample datasets. Furthermore, the algorithm proves its value in visualizing actual spherical data, while comparing its performance to alternative methods like vMF-PCA. The resulting energy calculations demonstrate both quadratic and cubic temperature dependencies, yielding precise results that can be analytically determined and confirming the underlying renormalization group predictions. Additionally, the polaron's effective mass is investigated and the findings show that at extremely low temperatures, where only the smallest momenta remain relevant, the polaron's energy behavior closely resembles that in one-dimensional environments. Importantly, the obtained polaron energy values are found to be lower than those derived from a previous real-time variational approach. Moreover, the diagrammatic Monte Carlo simulations yield the first theoretically calculated estimates for the polaron's saturation energy in two-dimensional environments. By analyzing the underlying diagrams, this study identifies specific regions within the parameter space where various theoretical models of the polaron energy apply. In this study, we examine a quantum simulation method based on fermionic systems, utilizing an unconventional computing technique that combines digital and analog components. This hybrid approach is characterized by representing fermionic creation and annihilation operators through analog variables, while the fermionic number operator is represented digitally. We demonstrate that this method is effective in both one-dimensional and two-dimensional fermionic quantum systems. By numerically simulating the hybrid system, we show its potential to efficiently compute eigenvalues and eigenstates of fermionic operators, where the digital segment of the hybrid computer is used to tackle the computational challenges caused by entanglement among analog particles. Furthermore, we applied the hybrid technique to detect topological features in Majorana fermions and semi-conductor quantum wires with magnetic barriers. We also explored the hybrid technique's potential to study fermionic systems via variational Monte Carlo method with a ground-state projector and quantum phase transition in Lieb-Roster model. All simulations were conducted using the QuDEdit software package, which is designed for hybrid digital-analog quantum computing. The results of our study demonstrate that this hybrid computing strategy is effective in efficiently computing problems of fermionic systems with up to 50 analog variables. This research contributes significantly to the quantum simulation of fermionic systems with up to 50 analog variables and lays the groundwork for experimental realizations. Additionally, it opens the door for applying this hybrid computing technique to tackle more complex quantum problems in chemistry, materials science, and engineering fields. The Strauss process is a spatiotally independent point process with a density
function parameterized by a real value, $\beta \geq 0$. This paper explores the
generation of points from the Strauss process through the'stitching' method, a
technique proven effective for independent processes. However, for Strauss and
general SAPPs, this method's correctness under changing $\beta$ values raises
intrigue. To demonstrate stability, we show that using stitching on a sequence
of independent Poisson point sets, and adjusting the $\beta$ value between each
set, results in a point set that closely represents the target Strauss process,
with an error that diminishes as the number of sets increases. Additionally, we
generate two independent point sets using stitching and regularization and
demonstrate that their sum is a perfect representation of the target Strauss
process. Furthermore, we generalize the'stitching' technique for use with any
SAPP. Our novel algorithm is applied to three specific examples: the
generalized Gibbs point processes, the multi-scale Cauchy process, and the
multi-scale truncated Cauchy process. In these instances, we compare the
computational efficiency of generating points using stitching versus regularization
against simulating the target process directly. Notably, our algorithm for the
multi-scale Cauchy process yields a new, efficient method for simulating this
process. This method's potential applications extend to the simultaneous
simulations of the multi-scale Cauchy and multi-scale truncated Cauchy processes
using stitching. Moreover, we show that these simulations can be used to create
a simulation method for the product of these two processes, given a target
probability. Finally, our algorithm is automated and made available online at

typeclasses for generalizations is available at https://github.com/scanlabmaja/

A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. We define and formally establish the logic within the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL, and then obtain a validation algorithm based on that semantics. By using a formal Isabelle/HOL proof, it is shown that the validation algorithm faithfully represents the developed semantics. We also demonstrate through practical experiments that the verification of our algorithm is useful. Essentially, our work establishes a complete Isabelle/HOL proof for a broad family of classical planning problems, and the extracted validation algorithm from that proof is efficient enough to handle problems with hundreds of variables. Notably, our Isabelle/HOL proof for the verification of the algorithm is independent of the algorithm itself, indicating that the Isabelle/HOL proof can likely be adapted to other validation algorithms. We discuss the potential for applying our Isabelle/HOL proof to other domains where the semantics of temporal planning might be relevant. Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific parameters by measuring the increased costs resulting from inefficiently allocating generation capacities. Through case studies involving capital costs, varied weather conditions, and differing spatial and temporal resolutions, we demonstrate the method's value and reveal that model sensitivity depends heavily on the optimization problem being analyzed. Additionally, we identify a correlation between model sensitivity and the geographical distribution of generation and wind resources, highlighting the significance of considering this factor during power system expansion planning. These findings provide valuable guidance for model developers and power system operators to create more accurate models, thus yielding more reliable investment decisions. By enhancing model accuracy, we can improve our understanding of the trade-offs between various investment strategies. This, in turn, enables the formulation of more informed decisions regarding power system development. The proposed methodology can be applied not only to power generation but also to other investments, such as transmission infrastructure, energy storage, and flexibility technologies. This represents an cost-effective outcome, as it allows modelers to rely on established models instead of adjusting parameters. Furthermore, we find that power system models can be modified to reduce their sensitivity by accounting for this factor. This represents an efficient way to optimize investment strategies, as it does not necessitate substantial changes to the underlying model. The calculation of model sensitivity is achieved through an auxiliary optimization problem that seeks to maximize the increased costs resulting from inefficiently allocating generation capacities. Specifically, we have found that power system expansion planning models are particularly sensitive to spatial and temporal resolutions, explaining why these factors have traditionally been carefully considered during model design. This provides further validation for our approach, as it delivers accurate and useful insights that can enhance power system development models. When conducting search operations, researchers typically face two main challenges: pinpointing relevant information and avoiding excessive data volume. To address these issues, they need to refine their search terms and limit the data set accordingly. While there are established methods for streamlining research, such as relevance assessment and Information Retrieval Based Concept Location techniques, developing suitable query terms remains an unsolved problem. Our proposed approach, Information Retrieval Based Search Term Identification for Concept Location (STRICT), utilizes IR tools to assign weights to original search terms and generate optimized ones, specifically for concept identification purposes. We have developed two variants of STRICT: one grounded in classical IR and another founded in Deep Learning. Regardless of the approach, the goals remain the same: to develop an innovative framework that can aid researchers in creating effective search terms for concept identification. Our evaluation of STRICT, using academic papers as a base dataset, revealed promising results and multiple promising outcomes. Importantly, the Deep Learning based STRICT exhibited superior performance over other methods, across all metrics used in assessment. Additionally, by cross-training on a relevant dataset, STRICT was observed to be capable of generating suitable search terms for previously unexamined concepts, suggesting its potential for cross-domain application. Moreover, an analysis of the engagement found that researchers are capable of identifying relevant concepts with the aid of our approach. Ultimately, the integration of STRICT with other IR based concept location techniques further enhanced its performance, providing promising avenues for further development. To effectively organize digital collections and facilitate targeted searching within a particular field, precise categorization of document subjects is crucial. Currently, classification primarily relies on human expertise, but semi-supervised Machine Learning algorithms can aid this process by utilizing labeled data to predict subject classes for previously uncategorized documents. Despite their assistance, these machine-driven classifications often lack clarity as to why they were made. Research into explainable AI aims to make Machine Learning more transparent by shedding light on the underlying decision-making processes. Building on the success of this technology in other domains, we develop a system to classify STEM documents by leveraging the predictions of multiple semi-supervised classifiers and annotating the underlying mathematical concepts from the relevant scientific papers. Our system enhances the transparency of document classification by integrating explanations based on the predicted STEM domains and the newly linked mathematical entities. Experiments demonstrate that our approach surpasses the performance of current state-of-the-art methods for post-hoc explanation in classification tasks. Our technique also achieves a 40.6% MACE score, outperforming a strong baseline that relies solely on the attention distributions of the transformers. Ultimately, we demonstrate that our system, guided by the annotations of a small group of experts, generalizes to uncharted fields and disciplines with impressive results, achieving an impressive MACE score of 63.8%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our system, guided by the annotations of the experts, can accurately classify "out-of-vocabulary" fields or disciplines not encountered during training. Interestingly, our technique shows that it can successfully classify fields within natural language texts that do not even appear in the document's title or abstract. We contend that our approach has the potential to significantly benefit a wide range of tasks within the fields of information retrieval and cognitive support. The newly developed MathIL model is available for public use at https://github.com/soarlam/math-il. We also provide access to our system, trained on over 2.7 million unique documents, at https://stem-classifier.soarlam.com. This content can be employed for both research and commercial purposes, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated by their respective repositories. To facilitate the development of new explainable AI techniques, a dataset consisting of over 11,000 explanations is available at https://github.com/soarlam/explainable-ai-with-math-entities. To guarantee matching among all agents, the Deferred Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies show that stable matchings are achieved even with shorter, albeit incomplete, preference lists. Consequently, researchers investigated scenarios where agents are not required to include unranked or unpreferred options in their preference lists. Notably, experiments within medical residency matching revealed that the actual preference lists formed by candidates often have very few high-priority choices. Therefore, this study presents a new DA variant by allowing agents to make proposals only up to a certain quantity based on their prior rankings, taking into consideration their existing knowledge of preferences and the number of high-priority choices. We analyze this new DA variant, referred to as Choice-Based DA (CBDA), and compare its performance with the traditional DA algorithm. Our findings demonstrate that CBDA leads to similar outcomes as traditional DA but reduces computational costs by a factor proportional to the logarithm of the total number of high-priority choices. Moreover, when implemented in the existing medical residency matching procedure, CBDA resulted in improved user experience and processing efficiency. Finally, based on calculations, CBDA appears to be more suitable than traditional DA for scenarios involving a small number of high-priority choices and lengthy best-alternative lists. Specifically, even with CBDA's simplified preference lists and reduced proposals, its output matches the output from traditional DA with 3 proposals and ranked preference lists containing 7 or fewer high-priority choices. Although CBDA still yields one unsatisfied agent, further refinement of CBDA is necessary to eliminate this issue altogether. We present a number of these enhancements. Ultimately, by combining these improvements, we present a new sequential choice-based DA algorithm that achieves a stable matching while allowing agents to make proposals based solely on their prior rankings and without the need for complete preference lists. Moreover, our simulations indicate that this new CBDA algorithm achieves a stable matching for medical residency matching with at least 5 high-priority choices and ranked preference lists containing 17 or fewer best alternatives. Notably, this requirement exceeds the average number of high-priority choices in medical residency matching instances. Moreover, CBDA still yields a stable matching that is more likely than random when considering instances with longer best-altrenative lists. Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are inadequate, as they are
highly unreliable in assessing human quality and limit the variety of generated
summaries. To overcome these challenges, a novel evaluation metric called
SummScore has been developed. This innovative approach utilizes a CrossEncoder
to compare the semantic meaning of original text and summaries, thus preventing
bias against diverse summary formats. The Cross-Encoder, pre-trained on text-matching tasks, effectively captures nuanced semantic differences between summaries.
Furthermore, SummScore encompasses four distinct sub-metrics that evaluate a
summary's quality from different viewpoints: its coherence using a lexical
similarity measure, relevance using a search engine's scoring function, conciseness
using a typographical analysis, and readability using a specific readability
score. The proposed metric achieves an impressive correlation of 81% with human
evaluations, outperforming existing evaluation metrics. To facilitate usage, the
SummScore evaluation metric and associated code are openly accessible at
https://github.com/AllanLin/SummScore. Moreover, an interactive tool allowing
human summaries to be assessed using the SummScore metric is available at
https://summ-score.herokuapp.com/. This research introduces an innovative and
practical evaluation tool that can be applied not only to summarization but also
to other generation tasks. Additionally, it lays the groundwork for future
research to enhance the scoring function of SummScore. Ultimately, the proposed
evaluation metric is anticipated to give more accurate assessments for current
summarization models and facilitate advancements in future generation models. 
Although initially, the task focuses on summarization, the proposed approach is
hypothesized to be adaptable to other text generation tasks as well. Therefore,
it presents a fresh and promising direction for accurately evaluating text
generators. Furthermore, an alternative version of SummScore has been developed
for evaluating search results. This variant is known as Retriever-Eval and serves
as a more powerful and independent tool. It has been made available for public
