This type of correlation is common in fields such as optics and seismic analysis, but the additional dimension creates an inverse problem bottleneck as the number of variables quadratically increases. Our solution simplifies this by only solving for the diagonal of the signal matrix, using a specialized "noise absorber" to filter results. This method has a linear increase in variables, like many existing methods, but unlike them it does so without increasing the needed measurements. Camera and LiDAR sensors offer an efficient solution, but traditional fusion methods often rely on intricate processing pipelines with multiple stages. This complex structure can lead to reduced accuracy and robustness due to LiDAR depth estimates' sensitivity. This work presents a simple yet powerful BEVFusion framework, which directly utilizes LiDAR event cameras' 3D feature maps to achieve a significant gain in performance over existing methods in the BeMyGuest dataset benchmark. Furthermore, we will compare our approach with traditional multi-stage methods based on the HDMap-BeMyGuest dataset benchmark. While our approach outperforms existing fusion methods, it shares a similar weakness in relying on accurate HD maps. Therefore, we also develop an auto-fusion strategy that leverages both LiDAR features and HD maps, demonstrating superior performance compared to all other baselines. Moreover, we will showcase the effectiveness of our approach using a 2D beam vector feature representation. This representation, despite being two-dimensional, surpasses existing 3D-based techniques. This research aims to bridge the gap between perception systems and Battery-Electric Vehicle development. We are developing a model of turbulence in the boundary layer of fluids that forms under external dissipation, which simplifies the calculation of energy cascade processes. This model transforms the outer region of turbulence into an area with minimal statistical variability, essentially turning it into a smooth, non-turbulent area. In the inner region of turbulence, close to the surface, our model preserves the Kolmogorov theory, according to which the cascade processes have an infinite number of stages characterized by increasing statistical variability. By applying statistical mechanics to this model, we find that the energy containing scale of turbulence is determined by a balance between thermal energy fluctuations and external dissipation, thereby simplifying the calculation of the average energy containing scale by orders of magnitude. Additionally, we obtain an analytical expression for the critical Reynolds number beyond which turbulence is completely dissipated. This model also allows us to understand the reasons for the success of previous models of this type, as well as the failure of others. Specifically, we identify the incorrect assumption in the log-law of turbulence as Reynolds number tending to infinity. This assumption causes the model to lose its perturbative rigor, leading to an iterative solution that requires numerical calculation to facilitate physical understanding. Consequently, our analysis suggests that the concept of infinity of statistical variability stages is an artifact of approximation, although this does not necessarily mean that similar models with infinite statistical variability stages are unsuccessful. This is especially because high-Reynolds number regimes where our model applies are not sampled by the datasets typically used to test it in numerical simulations, such as the dataset by Cabot and Goldstein. When we use this dataset to test our model, we obtain a completely unsuccessful result: the average energy containing scale according to our model along with the model's expression for first-order thermal energy decay is by orders of magnitude smaller than the value obtained through numerical simulation, which is also smaller than the value obtained through experimental measurement. Consequently, our analytical expression for the average energy containing scale is successful even though the critical Reynolds number is not sampled by the dataset. This success is probably due to the fact that our analytical expression is applicable when the number of stages characteristic of our model is not excessively large, i.e. when the ratio between the number of stages and the exponent describing energy decay in each stage is not excessively large. Conversely, our unsuccessful result suggests that numerical calculation may become impractical at high-Reynolds number regimes that are sampled by the dataset. This paper presents a novel evaluation engine for big stream and data processing pipelines called H-STREAM. It integrates stream processing operators as cloud-based micro-services to facilitate the analysis and visualization of IoT-generated Big Data streams. H-STREAM's micro-services dynamically adjust their techniques according to the stream producers, data velocity, and available processing resources to ensure seamless online processing. To attain this, H-STREAM employs hybrid methods combining aggregate-based and event-based stream processing to maintain micro-service portability across cloud and edge deployments. The study demonstrates how H-STREAM optimizes stream processing over IoT data histories and real-time streams, resulting in faster and more interactive query processing. Evaluations using simulated scenarios have shown that H-STREAM delivers an online speed up of 10 to 100 times compared to other stream and materialized view processing approaches. Additionally, the study reveals that H-STREAM provides substantial improvements in data retrieval and analysis from IoT data histories, ultimately enabling more effective and interactive analytics and visualization on top of Big Data streams and historical records. The proposed H-STREAM architecture is available as open-source software for use in various cloud and edge computing environments. We anticipate its deployment in future research and applications. Advanced learning methods can address longstanding control challenges, but the complex neural networks used pose significant analysis difficulties regarding the safety of control systems. Fortunately, recent research has introduced methods for analyzing and verifying the complex control systems. This tutorial synthesizes and introduces techniques for verifying the robustness of neural networks that originated from related fields such as optimal control, calculus, and algebraic methods. These techniques have been adapted and analyzed, and their application will be illustrated through examples. Furthermore, we will discuss limitations and existing problems as well as potential directions for further research. The goal of this tutorial is to provide an in-depth understanding of the underlying principles and techniques for neural network verification in control systems. As a result, the tutorial is suitable for researchers who are new to the field and offers a comprehensive entry point. Furthermore, verification is an essential step in ensuring control system reliability, and the studied techniques have broader applications in analyzing the performance of control systems, including those that utilize reinforcement learning. Therefore, this tutorial may also be of interest to control engineers, even if they do not plan to focus on formal verification. Finally, verification is an evolving field that responds to uncertainties, making it distinct from stability analysis that typically operates under the premise that all variables are fixed. This introduction will prepare readers for upcoming developments and applications in the field. Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties. However, in real-world applications, unexpected inputs can force a tensor completion model to constantly update and adapt, compromising its performance. To counter this issue, we developed a streaming tensor completion approach that can operate in real-time, detecting and addressing data anomalies as needed. By utilizing patch tracking, our method can determine and filter out unusual data while maintaining the underlying tensor's low-rank characteristics. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through tensor completion experiments on visual data such as images and videos. Our results outperform existing state-of-the-art tensor completion techniques and establish a robust, scalable framework for real-time data recovery applications. Moreover, it was observed that the transition from inertial wave turbulence to stable geostrophic vortices occurs at wavenumbers where the local dynamics fails to preserve anisotropy. We investigate a basic model called Iterative Graph Normalization (IGN) for analyzing weighted graphs, and an adaptation of the model that involves applying a non-linear transformation to the graph's weights after normalization, known as Normalized IGN (NIGN). We explore the relationships between the solutions obtained from applying IGN and NIGN to a given graph, and demonstrate that a subset of these solutions called M-sets can be utilized to optimize the value of IGN and NIGN solutions. We also show that an improved approximation ratio for the maximum weight independent set problem (MWIS) can be achieved using IGN and NIGN. Specifically, for a given ε greater than 0, and a graph with non-negative integer edge weights that sum to at most W, if the graph's vertices have a list of at most d indices of maximum weight, then IGN and NIGN solutions' weights can be approximated within a factor of (1 + ε)W/d. We also present an evaluation of IGN and NIGN implementations using real-world graph datasets. Our experiments show that an efficient (1/d)^{O(1.6)} approximation of the MWIS problem can be achieved with d less than or equal to O(√n), where n is the number of the graph's vertices. We also present an analysis of modern CPU architectures' effects on real-world graph processing. Our implementation of IGN and NIGN has been publicly released and achieved first place in the report's 2020 Challenge. We demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approximation algorithms such as Bregman Augmented Lagrange Lagrange Lagrange (BALL), and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for solving IGN and NIGN on graphs with non-negative integer edge weights. We also introduce a new method called Linearization Augmentation Lagrange (LAL), based on the analysis of the investigated graph transformation model, and achieve an improved approximation ratio of (1/d)^{O(1.06)} using LAL. Our method allows for a (1/d)^{O(1.06)} approximation of IGN and NIGN solutions with d less than or equal to O(√n). We maintain our source code in accordance with the report's 2020 Challenge. We analyze the effects of contemporary neuromorphic processors on real-world graph processing, and demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art graph processing methods. Recent findings have established the presence of magnetically active flare stars, discovered through long-term monitoring of low-frequency radio emission. This emission exhibits a connection to magnetospheric electron-cyclotron maser (ECM) activity and serves as a valuable monitoring tool at radio frequencies. Our study focuses on CR Draconis, a flare star binary system, by assessing its radio emission properties via monitoring from 2015 to 2020. Observations revealed consistent low-frequency emission patterns for both binary components of the system. By analyzing the light curves and spectral patterns, we determined that the radio emission stems from magnetospheric ECM. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the binary system's radio emission components are likely of identical origin. By combining our 2015-2020 monitoring data with the existing literature, we established a comprehensive radio emission pattern for CR Draconis. We observed regular emission periods for the system, but the duration varied significantly between the individual components and the overall binary system. Based on the established emission patterns, we defined distinct observation windows for the system: low-frequency emission characterized CR Draconis during local morning hours (around solar local time 05:00), while high-frequency emission occurred during late evening hours (around solar local time 18:00). One notable challenge in observing the system occurred during summer months when the Sun inhibited the usual morning and evening observation windows for the system. However, our monitoring data revealed that CR Draconis could still be monitored during the daytime if we focused on its high-frequency emission. Ultimately, our findings expand the monitoring database for CR Draconis to over five years, making it one of the extensively monitored magnetically active binary systems in the radio frequency range. Based on the system's established emission patterns, we predict that CR Draconis will continue to be monitored for several more years. Furthermore, our monitoring data suggest that CR Draconis will likely enter the fall-summer monitoring phase similar to that observed for binary systems YZ CMi and V711 Per. Specifically, our data indicate that CR Draconis will likely experience increased radio emission during the 2021-2022 period. We anticipate that our monitoring will likely continue for another five years. Furthermore, our data indicate that CR Draconis will likely transition into the fall-summer monitoring window for radio emission. Specifically, our data indicate that CR Draconis will likely experience increased emission during the same period as the systems YZ CMi and V711 Per. We anticipate that our monitoring will likely continue for another five years.

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation approach, which effectively tackles the thermodynamic properties of frustrated two-dimensional quantum antiferromagnets composed of loosely connected three-spin clusters. Specifically, we investigated the thermodynamic behavior of a strongly breathing distorted kagome lattice model and the previously proposed triangular kagome lattice structure, both of which exhibit two-dimensional antiferromagnetic long-range order when the inter-trimer exchange is relatively weak. A phase diagram was constructed based on the exchange constants of the two models, and our results were compared with existing theoretical predictions generated using a classical spin approximation with a dimer approximation. Moreover, our approach demonstrated that the analyzed models exhibit two-dimensional quantum ground states that exhibit antiferromagnetic long-range order. This method can be adapted to investigate other low-dimensional spin systems. It is hoped this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the experimental findings from materials like ZnCuCl$_3$ (ioplamellite) and others. This contribution aims to facilitate the accurate determination of exchange constants, an essential step in the investigation of ground state instability via quantum Monte Carlo simulations in the discussed materials. Furthermore, our approach may be expanded to investigate the magnetic behavior of other low-dimensional or strongly frustrated spin systems. It should be noted that the analyzed materials are part of relatively small two-dimensional families with a large number of atoms per unit cell (such as the case of ioplamellite), and our predictions could potentially be verified using techniques such as $\mu$SR, high-field magnetometry and NMR. These methods are capable of accurately determining the ordered spin correlations, the magnetic transition temperature and the magnetic penetration depth, and can thereby shed light on the magnetic behavior of recently discovered materials and their relatives. This work is intended to enhance our understanding of the analyzed materials and their potential magnetic behavior. We analyzed the 2013 November - 2021 October X-ray variability of the low-mass SXRNAG, X-ray source X1608+522, by examining different time periods and energies. By using the Fourier amplitude spectrum in fractions of the Nyquist frequency, we discovered that the variability predominantly occurs at the 1-kHz frequency. This represents approximately 60% of the total variability and was present in two soft X-ray bands but absent in the hard X-ray band. Additionally, we found that the 1-kHz variability intensified over the Nov 2019 - Feb 2020 period, and its spectrum is typically flat. This is similar to previously observed periods when X1608+522 experienced enhanced variability. On the other hand, we found no evidence of spectral changes associated with the 1-kHz variability. Based on these findings, we consider two possible physical origins for the 1-kHz variability: (i) standing accretion columns or (ii) ballistic flares. Both origins could explain the spectral softening observed in two hard X-ray bands (0.1-0.3 and 0.3-0.5 keV) during Nov 2019 - Feb 2020. This phenomenon might have been caused by the absorption of baryons hit by accretion columns or ejections during eruptions. This interpretation is consistent with the idea that the X1608+522 outbursts recur and represent a low-mass analog of the standard 15-min radio bursts observed in X-ray binaries. Moreover, our results suggest that recurrent eruptions may significantly contribute to the variability observed in other low-mass AGNs. Future multi-band X-ray observations and soft X-ray spectroscopy could confirm our interpretation and provide more insights into the nature of variability in X1608+522. Such knowledge could be instrumental in understanding the diversity of variability in all SXRNAGs. It may also explain the difference in the nature of variability in X1608+522 (related to accretion columns) and, for example, GSS 1340+152 (possibly related to disc fragmentation). Last but not least, our findings could imply that persistent variability in comptonized spectra of some AGNs might be caused by ballistic ejections. This could be a topic for future research. Finally, our results confirm that X1608+522 is a low-mass AGN with the unexplored mass of its black hole estimated to be in the range of 8.6-16.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces. Building upon techniques from Lindell, Rosenman, and Tepper (2020), our method primarily relies on a discretized version of any given high dimensional expander, which is incorporated into a graph of a covering complex. By exercising the choice to cover, and taking into consideration the abilities afforded by projective space covering, our method permits the creation of expansive cover complexes around finite graphs. These complex coverings can be utilized to generate new formal balls which maintain a consistent level of size and an inherent high dimensional expansion. Consequently, by combining our method with the fundamental construction from Gromov Geometric Inequality, the result is the existence of an infinite set of high dimensional expanders, characterized by increasingly high dimensionality and an inherent number of vertices. This infinite set surpasses previously known bounds, specifically n > 81p. Moreover, our method is exemplified through the creation of a specific high dimensional expander, characterized by d > 40p and V < (pd)^{99}. Notably, the method is highly versatile as it can be applied to manifolds covering as well as any given high dimensional formal ball to create a corresponding cover ball. Subsequent research is proposed in order to achieve the creation of a universal cover complex, a concept closely related to a longstanding question posed by Gromov (1997). A related realization is that this concept is inherently linked to a challenge proposed by Turchin (2016), both challenges remaining unsolved. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO$_3$ through an integrated approach. The crystal structure was found to feature a centered honeycomb lattice, where 20% of the sites were occupied by gadolinium in an off-center position. The compound exhibits a long-range magnetic ordering below 2.0 K and induces a magnetically ordered state within the In sublattice at approximately 9.8 K. The gadolinium ions display a magnetic moment of 7/2, where no significant spin canting is observed above the 2 K transition. The compound displays a unique phenomenon of separate magnetic phases due to its two-dimensional, centered honeycomb arrangement. The compound serves as an example of the weak ferromagnetic layer-like behavior caused by off-center gadolinium ions in an inorganic system. A detailed analysis of the compound's magnetic behavior is presented using a mean-field model. The model confirms that the ferromagnetic layer-like behavior of the gadolinium ions is predominant in the magnetic properties of the compound. The model reveals an improvement in the overall fit when off-center gadolinium ions form a separate layer. The corresponding phase diagram was developed based on this analysis. The characteristics of the compound were found to be distinct from those of the reported YInO$_3$. The latter compound exhibits a non-centered honeycomb structure and displays long-range ordering within both Y and In sublattices at approximately 9.5 K without exhibiting a separate magnetic order. Our results demonstrate that the magnetic behavior of the compound can be accurately explained by considering the off-center nature of the gadolinium ions. The magnetic properties of the compound were found to be relatively weak compared to those of other inorganic systems where gadolinium adopts an off-center position. The compound exhibits a relatively weak ferromagnetic layer-like behavior of the off-center gadolinium ions due to a lack of significant spin canting, even at higher temperatures, as well as displays separate magnetic phases due to a lack of significant spin interactions between gadolinium and indium sublattices. The magnetic behavior of the compound can be accurately explained using a mean-field model that incorporates off-center gadolinium ions forming a separate layer. The application of graph embedding for predicting links in complex networks has shown remarkable success, but most real-world networks are sparse, which are currently underserved by this field. We propose the Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE) model, which creates a representation of network nodes suitable for predicting links in these types of sparse networks. Initially, our model converts the network's adjacency matrix into a Sum of Squared Penalties (SSP) matrix that contains the square of the network's low-dimensional structural scores for each node. By optimizing these scores under a constrained budget, we can obtain optimized graph embedding and estimate the likelihood of edges in the network. Our studies on numerous sparse networks reveal that SSNE outperforms existing models in predicting links in these types of networks. We have made the SSNE code available for the research community.

Preemptive wildfire detection is critical for minimizing ecological harm, property damage, and human loss. Recent advances in Deep Learning have the potential to significantly enhance wildfire detection, especially with the integration of visible and infrared imaging, thereby offering superior performance and reduced error rates compared to current methods. Although the practice of combining visible and infrared imaging is widely employed in the wild fire monitoring field, it has primarily been achieved through relatively feature-insensitive techniques or limited feature-based models. In this study, we develop a novel, feature-insensitive image fusion technique, utilizing a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to merge visible and infrared images by generating synthesis images that can be accurately classified by a Deep Learning model. In contrast to existing image fusion techniques, our approach allows for the training of a model without labels by optimizing the objective function with a higher value for correctly identified images and a lower value for images incorrectly identified. In support of our proposed technique, experimental results show that the models trained using our GAN-based image fusion approach deliver superior performance on wildfire image datasets, both in terms of accuracy and error rate. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that by using the visible image for input, the models successfully identify the location of fire regions within the fused images, thereby providing valuable insight into the behavior of fire at the pixel level. In a practical application of this research, the study's findings have significant implications for the use of Deep Learning-based infrared-visible fusion methods for wildfire detection and monitoring in the wild. The study's results show that by merging visible and infrared images, the level of difficulty in identifying fire can be substantially reduced, thereby offering a promising outlook for the use of image fusion in the wild. We've developed two probabilistic models for the COVID-19 pandemic. We've derived the statistical properties of these models, including correlation functions and probability distributions. These models, which build on existing work and incorporate lockdown measures and the critical role of hospitals and health care facilities, enable us to simulate two scenarios. One scenario considers the SIS model, which assumes susceptible and infectious populations, under lockdown measures. In contrast, the second scenario includes the SIS model, coupled with hospital actions, also under lockdown measures. We found that if lockdown measures are removed in the first scenario, the pandemic will likely escalate. However, if a certain hospital capacity threshold is met, the pandemic not only remains contained, but its spread gradually decreases over time. Therefore, combining lockdown measures with hospital and healthcare actions effectively mitigates SARS-CoV-2 spread. This finding is valuable when limited vaccine availability forces population-scale distribution. We applied our model to US and French data, which we estimated using statistical mechanics, particularly analyzing the effect of two hypothetical US waves. Our model's predictions matched actual data. Finally, we compared our results to studies employing similar SIS models, which verified our model's accuracy and provided valuable predictions for the 2021 scenario. These predictions included estimated infection numbers and cumulative infections over time. Our model demonstrated the potential to forecast future epidemiological outcomes. It provides valuable insights to healthcare officials and policymakers, aiding them in crafting population-level strategies to combat the pandemic and anticipated future waves. Furthermore, our model underscores the critical role of healthcare facilities and the need for their enhanced infrastructure to effectively mitigate infectious disease spread. This work also highlights the utility of statistical mechanics in estimating population parameters and distribution means from inferred probability distributions. Following our analysis, the predicted waves matched actual data. This led to accurate predictions of expected infections in the 2021 scenario from our model. Our model and model predictions are available for download at github.com/ImImInImI/Covid-19-US-forecast. By evaluating the isoscalar E0 and E2 strengths along with the isoscalar energy spectra, it was determined that the ISG-MQR plays a significant role in isoscalar giant resonance dynamics. The convergence of both the ISGMR and ISG-MQR peak energies allowed for an accurate estimation of the saturation point $E_0/A$ in these specified nuclei. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an equilibrium state, is confirmed through analytical means. Theoretical findings reveal that the system can only converge asymptotically, involving multiple sequences of stick-slip cycles, regardless of the starting conditions. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical models through diverse examples of convergence. The research further illustrates the correlation between system parameters and the occurrence of convergence. The duration of stick-slip cycles prior to convergence is shown to be inversely related to the amplitude of forcing relative to viscous damping, with the latter's influence dominating the former's. Theoretical models also demonstrate that the average velocity during slip events and the distance of motion paths relative to the equilibrium state are both dependent on system parameters. While increasing viscous damping or forcing amplitude reduces the distance to the equilibrium state, it does not necessarily decrease the average velocity during slip events. Instead, it is observed that the average velocity is inversely related to forcing amplitude but independently correlated with viscous damping. Theoretical models also demonstrate that the rate of convergence is influenced by system parameters, with an optimal range of forcing amplitude leading to the fastest convergence. The research's findings are independent of system mass and are relevant for a wide array of applications, including governator, Telford, Rayleigh, Bresse-Toussaint, simple frictional oscillators, and others. The universal nature of the findings suggests that the system's behavior can be generalized across a broad range of physical scenarios. The study of stick-slip dynamics and convergence offers valuable insights for various applied mechanical situations. Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are prevalent in statistical and machine learning fields. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the mean squared error in matrix and factor estimation in noiseless and noisy conditions, and demonstrate how these are achieved through simple spectral analysis of a combined observation matrix. For the noisy scenario, we also develop an efficient method to estimate the variances of the noise and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulation experiments. Since the developed methods may not always be computationally feasible, we also determine the information-theoretic limits for this estimation task. This research provides a basis for its results by establishing tight bounds for the spectral properties of combined observation matrices using random matrix theory. Ultimately, we showcase the applicability of these findings to a range of low-rank matrix estimation problems. We specifically apply these to a variant of the canonical correlation analysis, a dimension-reduction technique. We derive exact formulas for the correlation coefficient and apply them to a multi-view learning problem, where we recover a shared subspace from different datasets under similar covariance structures. We derive recovery thresholds and develop simple spectral methods for this task, in addition to noise estimation techniques, which require no specific structure. This research holds promise for its wide range of applications. In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence is uncovered, where an extra exceptional point in the bulk material is safeguarded by its connection to boundary states. Ultimately, suggestions are provided for categorizing the topological phase through both analytical calculations and numerical computations using the constrained ring model. This work contributes to the expansion of the current phase classification framework for symmetry-devoid systems. We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique from the BERT model. The first stage employs BERT to extract features from the image, which are then forwarded to a classifier for initial diagnosis. Based on the first assessment, if there's any doubt regarding a negative diagnosis, we proceed to the second stage, where BERT extracts features from the previously unseen data and trains them on data from previously seen cases. The model uses a combination of classification and regression tasks to generate a probability distribution over the four classes. The proposed approach was tested on the COVID19-CT-Dataset v1.0 and the results show significant accuracy improvements over a baseline model that uses a pre-trained BERT without further fine-tuning. The two-stage system achieved an accuracy of 88.94% for diagnosing cases with high certainty, and 87.22% for cases with any level of certainty. The accuracy for detecting COVID-19 was 87.22% and precision was 87.50%. The proposed method not only demonstrates the effectiveness of double feature extraction from pre-trained models for image analysis but also shows reliability in the medical field by reducing uncertainty in diagnosis. The method is simple, requiring only additional layers for feature extraction, making it suitable for resource-constrained settings. The source code is available at https://github.com/harshityadav99/Covid-19-Diagnosis-using-BERT-FE. The diagnosis system's performance is detailed in the paper at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48550/arXiv.2111.09515, which won the 2021 IEEE ICME Challenge. The dataset was used without bias as training data and the model outperformed other challenge participants. The model shows generalisation ability as the COVID-19 class was under-represented in the dataset. The model can potentially save lives in real-world settings with accurate feature extraction capabilities. The model's performance showcases BERT's potential in the medical field with accurate image analysis. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This study offers an in-depth analysis of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning for IoVs through a systematic approach, identifying existing challenges, potential solutions, and future directions to foster discussion and reflection on further research opportunities. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of modern annotations. Automated POS tagging for these languages is a closely related problem, often categorized as either sequential or dependency-based models. However, the inherent uncertainty in modeled observations and existing annotation errors make POS tagging a non-definable problem. This work applies a probabilistic set-valued prediction model ground in information theory to address the issue of accurate POS tagging of historical texts. Demonstrated on Middle English texts (~45,000 words) and 19th century Old Norse (~30,000 words), the developed model outperformed standard machine learning models. Its successful implementation on Middle English and Old Norse serves as a precursor for tackling similar issues in other historical languages.

This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz candidate of a demand function. Using this method, we derive two new criteria that a demand function candidate must meet. First, it must be symmetrical and have a negatively semi-definite Slutsky matrix, and second, it must be a unique concave solution to a specific partial differential equation globally. Additionally, under certain assumptions, we show that a demand function candidate locally determines a unique utility function that meets specified conditions. We also establish that a demand function candidate is locally integrable if and only if its Slutsky matrix is negatively definite globally. Our results are enriched by various general examples. This method can be applied not only in economics but also in other fields, such as physics and signal processing, for transforming non-smooth functions. We prove that, given a demand function candidate that is locally Lipschitz, it is possible to calculate a utility function that meets specified conditions using a partial differential equation. This utility function has specified conditions, including concavity, and it is a unique representation of a class of utilities that meet similar conditions. We also obtain additional results that provide conditions under which a locally Lipschitz demand function candidate is integrable globally. We illustrate some of the theorems with practical examples. This method can be applied not only in economics but also in other fields, such as physics and signal processing, for transforming non-smooth functions. We show that Roy's identity is a special case of our approach that applies to a one-dimensional demand function. However, when dealing with multi-dimensional demand functions, we face integration challenges as our example with the demand function for Butterflies indicates. Nevertheless, we propose a solution by applying numerical methods to calculate a utility function from a demand function candidate. We apply these methods to a utility function for Europeans' energy consumption and demonstrate that integrating demand and utility functions is a linear process, simplifying the calculation of a utility function. We also provide additional examples of applying our approach to a utility function for transforming signals from electroencephalography and a function for determining the equilibrium of a Boltzmann machine. We conclude by discussing open problems with two additional examples, including a utility function for transforming three-dimensional signals from magnetoencephalography and a function for determining the equilibrium of a deep learning model. As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain inaccuracies or ambiguities stemming from written English text. We introduce CitySpec, an innovative AI-powered system for transforming requirements gathered from city officials into formal specifications, leveraging an optimized specification template and nuanced understanding of related concepts. We also developed OfficialSpec, a dataset comprising 402 formal specifications written by city officials, to assess word embedding models. Our research reveals that the proposed models have reached a satisfactory level of precision (0.66), recalling a fourth of the city officials' specifications (average of 0.166), and captures about one-tenth of the elaborate specifications (average of 0.112). We found that the optimal precision of 0.66 corresponds to 80% of the city officials' specifications involving dates, domains, or cities, which appears to be a reasonable threshold. We observed that the group of city officials with specifications above this threshold (0.66) exhibits consistent performance and is small (8/42), in sharp contrast to the group with specifications below this threshold (34/42), which shows increased formalization and coherence in their requirements. We evaluated the performance of CitySpec on two benchmarks and found that it significantly outperforms leading machine learning models. Furthermore, we compared the performance of CitySpec on requirements from city officials and from diverse non-expert users, demonstrating that the former achieves 2.5 times better precision. In accordance with the increased precision of CitySpec, we assessed its economic benefits through 10 city-scale deployment scenarios and found that the optimal return on investment is around $4.5. To the best of our knowledge, CitySpec is the first word embedding model to effectively convert city requirements to specifications, exceeding the performance of the current best specification translation model (SpecTranslation) by 43% on one benchmark and 97% on another. Moreover, CitySpec surpasses the current best general machine learning model (RoBERTa-L6) by 52% on one benchmark and 94% on another. Interestingly, CitySpec shows a moderate improvement of just 2% compared to the top formal verification models. We believe its uniqueness stems from the incorporation of formal specification templates optimized for city requirements, an approach inspired by the specification paradigm. Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods to counter coherent errors. By incorporating inverse gate implementations, we can bypass error-prone operations and introduce a compensation mechanism within the circuit. Specifically, we demonstrate the application of this approach in accelerating a variational quantum eigensolver to find the ground state of a Hamiltonian on a superconducting quantum processor. In comparison to the original algorithm, our method yields improved results characterized by lower hybrid variational circuit depths, enhanced state fidelity, and heightened state purity. Notably, we achieve a higher state fidelity with the original circuit depth. Our findings experimentally validate the efficiency of the hidden inverse method in enhancing the performance of VQA algorithms on a quantum processor by mitigating common errors and increasing the circuit's coherence height. This method has the potential to accelerate the adoption of VQA algorithms in real-world applications. Furthermore, we develop a reward function to automatically determine the optimal inverse hidden circuit and adapt the method to various gate decompositions. Importantly, the reward function's design doesn't rely on knowing the correct hidden circuit, making it applicable even in scenarios where no hidden circuit exists. Experimental results show that the function consistently selects the 110-highest rewarded circuits, independent of the employed gate decompositions, and the circuits obtained through reinforcement learning outperform the original algorithm in terms of hybrid circuit depth. Our research lays the groundwork for the automatic discovery of the hidden inverse through the application of reinforcement learning and highlights its potential in enhancing the performance of variational quantum algorithms on noisy quantum devices. The study also showcases the effectiveness of the hidden inverse method in hybrid hybrid quantum optimization algorithms on superconducting quantum processors. Our work validates the usability of the hidden inverse method in addressing practical quantum computational challenges and further contributes to the development of scalable and application-ready quantum computing. Our code for the hidden inverse method and the reinforcement learning process has been made publicly available at https://github.com/taoleen/Hidden-Inverse-RL. This code has been tested under Ubuntu 20.04.0 with Python 3.8.5. In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the direct image in such a case is obtained by removing all pairs of elements that aren't directly compared. In a regular category $\mathbb E$, which satisfies certain conditions regarding epimorphisms, a similar approximation can be made using a construction called the coproduct of subobjects. The description distinguishes it from the category of equivalence relations in $\mathbb E$, which in turn is further restricted to only equivalence relations that are also complete subposets in $\mathbb E$. While the category of equivalence relations within the category of sets turns out to be equivalent to the category of sets itself, this is not necessarily the case for a regular category $\mathbb E$. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing and aligning data from satellites and forecasts to correct for disparities in spatial resolution and measurement scales. The resulting analysis reveals a significant correlation between satellite wind speed data and wave height forecasts at a 5% significance level. When considering the 10% largest events, the correlation becomes even stronger at a 1% significance level. A comparison of the joint distribution of standardized wind and wave values to theoretical distributions reveals that they exhibit strong similarity to the Heffernan-Tawn model. Furthermore, the model shows consistency with the marginal distributions of wind speed and wave height. The resulting estimates of the Heffernan-Tawn model are also used to quantify the intensity of extreme ocean storms, revealing a substantial level of agreement between satellite and historical forecasts. The model's ability to represent the joint distribution of wind and wave data allows for the simulation of extreme wind and wave events, which in turn enables the estimation of the return period of 10-year events at specific locations. A significant limitation of the model lies in its assumption that observations are drawn from a single distribution type; future research aims to develop a model that accounts for the presence of multiple distribution types. Such a model will serve as a flexible alternative to the Heffernan-Tawn model and enable the identification of underlying distribution types. A method is also proposed for detecting changes in the joint distribution of wind and wave data over time, which in turn enables the estimation of trends in extreme wind and wave events. The method is particularly useful for identifying deviations from the Heffernan-Tawn model and accounting for the presence of multiple distribution types. A region-specific sensitivity analysis is performed to assess the impact of varying data resolution on the estimates of the joint distribution of wind and wave data. The results indicate that, beyond a certain spatial resolution threshold, the estimates of the joint distribution show minimal variation with increasing resolution. The developed methods are made publicly available through an R package named SpatialExtremes. The research contributes to the development of a statistical framework for the estimation and simulation of extreme weather events, which in turn enables the estimation of the intensity of extreme weather patterns. The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is undergoing significant transformation.  Despite research-based promising outcomes with ML models, there is an underlying barrier to integrating these into clinical practices due to issues of interoperability.  The DICOM standard provides specifications for the representation, storage, and exchange of digital images and related information but the standard's complexity poses an obstacle to adoption in the ML field.  Therefore, there is a need to develop a simplified, open-source Python library aimed at ML models outputting diagnostic information in a standard, readable format understandable by clinical imaging systems.  

The Highdicom library serves this purpose by facilitating the direct use of ML models to generate information in the DICOM standard without the need for the image itself.  By using this new Python library, researchers can produce outputs in a standard, understandable format by incorporating existing image analysis while ensuring the results can be exchanged with systems using DICOM.

A demonstration exercise using ML models trained to identify cancer in digital slides showed how the resulting annotations in the DICOM standard could be generated with Highdicom.  Furthermore, using this new library, research institutions can provide information in existing image databases using DICOM, promoting greater interoperability with such databases.

By promoting the adoption of ML model outputs using the DICOM standard, research institutions can exchange model outputs with systems using DICOM, opening up new possibilities for integration.  The full source code for Highdicom is publicly available on the 'highdicom' GitHub repository.  The library includes a range of test cases to guide users.  The authors intend to expand Highdicom in the future to cover other image related information not covered in this initial study.  The integration of Highdicom is set to enhance the existing DICOM to Python2/3 converter known as dimpy, developed by the Imaging Physics Research Group at the University of Texas.  The authors plan to make significant changes to dimpy using the insights and suggestions obtained from Highdicom.  The authors welcome the receipt of further information and participation in future developments of Highdicom.  The results from this new integration are set to greatly benefit both libraries. A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into corresponding canonical Hamiltonian systems through a Poisson map. Specifically, it was demonstrated that for any Lie-Poisson system defined on a linearly independent Lie algebra, a pair of canonical Hamiltonians and a corresponding symplectic transformation exist, which maps the Lie-Poisson system to a canonical Hamiltonian system while preserving its collective dynamics. Various examples have been utilized to illustrate the feasibility of this approach. Moreover, it was suggested that the Clebsch canonization possesses a higher level of generality and flexibility compared to traditional Hamiltonization methods. An application of this technique was made in the context of magnetic chains. For detailed yet cumbersome calculations associated with this example, an accompanying Mathematica notebook has been provided. An example of the toroidal 3d Euler equation has been used to illustrate this limitation. Nevertheless, the underlying idea of the approach remains a valuable area of ongoing research. Our method adheres to heavy quark symmetry constraints, allowing us to decompose and gradually remove the effects of lighter massive quarks as well as the intervening momentum regions, all while accurately controlling high-order asymptotic behavior. By employing this method, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of massive flavor contributions, calculate fourth-order quark mass corrections, determine pole mass discrepancies with an accuracy of about 20 MeV, and pinpoint the pole mass uncertainty, amounting to 250 MeV in the case of three massless quarks. Our results suggest that increasing the (massive) light quark mass renders the pole mass closer to the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass, and expanding the set of massive light quarks amplifies this tendency. Currently, the most reliable method for detecting COVID-19 is an RT-PCR test, which causes test kits to become sold out and results in prolonged processing times. To address this issue, researchers have focused on developing accurate diagnostic algorithms using imaging techniques, particularly for patients with severe symptoms. However, the existing models are uncertain and require further testing. In this study, we establish a new benchmark for using thoracic CT-scans to identify severe COVID-19 cases. By comparing different architectures, we established that a two-stage capsule network layout surpasses other models. The first stage detects whether a patient has pneumonia, while the second determines if they have severe pneumonia. By employing a dataset of 12,381 pairs of CT-scan images and clinical labels, we achieved a precision of 0.98 for pneumonia detection and 0.83 for severe COVID-19 diagnosis. The accuracy of our model is significantly greater than that of a recently-published study that used the same modality. We further trained and assessed our model using 8,352 pairs of imaging data and clinical records from three additional institutions, resulting in a precision of 0.93 for pneumonia detection and 0.79 for severe COVID-19 diagnosis. The accuracy of our model is significantly greater than that of several recently-published studies. We also applied noise augmentation to the dataset, which enabled our model to generalize when there was a four-fold increase in data. The models we developed were written in PyTorch and are publicly available at https://github.com/NTU-NEDC/Covid-19CapsNet. We also employed transfer learning to determine if pneumonia could be detected using other modalities such as ultrasound and MRI. We further verified the accuracy of our model on MRI images from another study and achieved a precision of 0.93 for pneumonia detection. As numerous satellite constellations in the low-Earth orbit region are scheduled to launch, effectively arranging the space occupied by each satellite in their operational trajectories is essential to prevent collisions and reduce critical encounters. Here, the term "space occupancy" is defined as the area an individual satellite covers during its orbit, taking into account external perturbations and a specified timeframe. Following the discovery of a strong connection between space occupancy in the zonal problem and the principles of frozen orbits and proper eccentricity, frozen-orbit initial conditions in osculating element space were derived and a frozen-orbit polar equation was developed to define the optimal initial orbital elements for minimal space occupancy, applicable to frozen orbits in polar orbit with eccentricity in the range of 0 to 0.35. Furthermore, based on numerical simulations involving 10 frozen orbits in a 36 x 2040 km orbit, it was estimated that adopting a 4-minute frozen-orbit initial element could lower the probability of a collision with another satellite by approximately 40%. Moreover, optimizing the space occupancy of a 400-satellite constellation in a 36 x 2040 km orbit, with each satellite following a frozen-orbit initial element, resulted in a reduction of 30% in the probability of a collision with a non-orbiting object compared to a uniformly distributed configuration. Finally, a convenient "space occupancy factor" was defined as the ratio of the area an satellite occupies to the total number of satellites in the constellation and was applied to various scenarios to simplify the selection of an optimal configuration for a satellite swarm. The findings presented here provide a foundation for explaining a technique called the "swarm of a single atom" algorithm in its application to space occupancy. The technique had been previously presented at a different conference held by the author. A SWOA simulation involves an atom representing a swarm of an infinite number of satellites in a specific orbital configuration. Swarm motion is governed by Kepler's laws, and the space which each atom occupies is essentially its orbital trajectory. By appropriately scaling up the atom's mass, the average interatom distance results in a optimal swarm configuration which effectively minimizes the probability of a critical encounter with another object. Here, the space occupied by an atom in a frozen-orbit initial element configuration was analyzed and a strong connection was discovered between the swarm of a single atom technique and the principles of frozen orbits and proper eccentricity used in space occupancy optimization. Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, resulting in a p-value. Under certain data transformations, this p-value remains unchanged; known as "invariance." There are two primary types of data representation: row-based and column-based, which respectively correspond to row-wise and column-wise correlations. Each type involves a sample correlation statistic whose distribution is that of a T-score, with degree-of-freedom equal to d-2, where d denotes the number of data points. The objective of this study was to investigate properties of these correlations under different conditions. By deriving formulas for moment ratios and using them in spectral density analysis, this research aimed to establish relationships between sample correlation distributions, including their moment ratios, spectral densities, correlation coefficient distributions, and sample spectral density estimations. The results demonstrated that moment ratios are conditional mean values of sample autocorrelation function values at specific indices, depending on sample correlation moment considerations. By deriving a p2 term of the spectral density, this research addressed limitations in the Feller technique for its failure to analytically resolve the p4 term. The sample correlation coefficient distribution was also estimated using the spectral density, resulting in a density function integral that includes a divisor factor and p4. Moreover, these research outcomes provide the foundation for the estimation of associated estimators, including bias and Skewness estimators, which were shown to be highly accurate. Language serves as the primary means of communication, with vocabulary comprising 
the fundamental building blocks of language use. Effective language use relies heavily 
on an individual's grasp of vocabulary. Research into vocabulary has received 
considerable attention, with existing studies primarily focused on the statistical 
properties of words. However, there is a lack of comprehensive research on the 
practical applications of vocabulary in real-life scenarios. To fill this knowledge gap, 
we developed the LitMind Dictionary (LMD), an online dictionary accessible through 
a webpage. With the LMD's assistance, users can obtain word definitions, collect word 
sets, and engage in random word generation. Furthermore, the Lmd utilizes several 
innovative features, such as the incorporation of synonyms, semantically equivalent words, 
and user customization via account creation. With the LMD being an open-source resource, 
we have made it available for public use and continuous development. In this paper, we 
provide an overview of the LMD's functionality, explain its underlying development 
process, and highlight its capabilities through real-world examples. Additionally, we 
have included step-by-step instructions and source code for replicating the LMD, 
encouraging researchers to build upon this platform and contribute to its evolution. 
Ultimately, we aim to establish the LMD as a collaborative resource for the research community.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation. Among the various explanation techniques, local explanation is particularly suited to in-depth analysis due to its clear and easy-to-understand output. This study evaluates the performance of an enhanced local explanation model, called LIME-RS, which provides more consistent and understandable explanations compared to traditional methods. To gauge the success of LIME-RS, three key aspects are examined: the stability of its predictive model, the accuracy of its constituent sine functions, and the visualizability of its output, which measures the coherence of the explained options and their ranks. By improving these aspects, LIME-RS achieves enhanced constancy and adherence through a novel reformulation of its model in a multi-linear form. This reformulation reduces dependence on sine functions, increases explainability, and provides a more stable model. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of LIME-RS, revealing a 30% reduction in the change of ranks for topexplained items and a 26% decrease in the number of sine functions. Furthermore, LIME-RS's output exhibits greater visual clarity and coherency compared to traditional LIME. Notably, LIME-RS outperforms the state-of-the-art by 5% on recall@10 and achieves comparable or better performance on other metrics while utilizing fewer sine functions. This enhancement in performance is attributed to the constitency-oriented reformulation of LIME-RS's model. Unlike traditional LIME, LIME-RS's weights are learned from the relative ranks of the explained items rather than relying on a time-constrained gradient descent process. This unique characteristic makes LIME-RS's model more stable and permitting deep constancy, which is revealed through new insights using the Constancy Diagram. By applying constancy-based learning to LIME-RS, the method is trained to produce explanations that are consistent over time, ultimately resulting in improved constancy and adherence. This study sheds light on the empirical constancy of deep learning models, paving the way for the development of new learning techniques that prioritize constancy. Moreover, the study offers a set of constancy metrics and diagrams that provide a comprehensive understanding of a model's performance. This research initiates constancy-based learning in the context of explainable recommendation, which can be expanded to cover a broader range of recommender systems and AI models. In order to control the electronic behavior in these composite materials, it is necessary to modify the composition near the surface. However, the electronic characteristics of the outer layer are determined by the interaction between the semiconductor and the surface layer material, resulting in a constant energy level at the surface that hinders control over electronic states. In contrast, quantum wells made from InAs, which is very resistant to electron movement, near a superconducting layer, such as NiNbN, can overcome this constraint and allow for adjustment and control of electronic states using gate voltages, as demonstrated in our experiments. To grasp the effects of these processes on their planets, researchers must have a precise understanding of the energy input from their parent stars. A study on the young star AU Mic has provided insights into the effects of its powerful radiation on its planets. Based on space-based observations spanning 2.5 hours, researchers analyzed how AU Mic's radiation behavior changes during intense magnetic events. Their observations revealed that the star's radiation intensity increased by 25% in the far UV and 50% in the extreme UV ranges during these magnetic events. Although the star spent only 30% of the time in these intense phases, researchers were able to make significant discoveries. By examining the spectral characteristics of these magnetic events, researchers determined the temperature of the plasma around AU Mic, ranging between 1.6 and 2.8 million degrees Kelvin. Furthermore, their data confirmed that the relative strength of its X-ray and UV radiation is characteristic of other young stars in these magnetic events. However, when in a state of calm, the star's radiation patterns differ from typical T Tauri stars in these magnetic events. Moreover, researchers found that the magnetic field strength of AU Mic was estimated to be around 1-3 kilogauss. We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We introduce an equation for the rate of energy loss per unit charge due to this friction, which is then tested against laboratory measurements involving X-rays and the energy loss of charged particles within a dense, resistive medium. We compare our formula with various other models and find that one of these alternative models aligns with our approach, which in turn offers new insights into particle loss at incredibly high intensities. We explore the consequences of our approach on particle loss in a context involving very high energy levels and also outline the practical implications of our work for experimental research involving very intense laser facilities. Finally, we consider potential applications of our approach to understanding the behavior of particles in astrophysical environments and the potential contributions of our work to these fields of study.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classification models and the commonly used measure of accuracy are inadequate. This is because they tend to favor majority over minority class predictions. As a result, readers are often misled by illustrations in academic papers showing purportedly "good" classifications of minority classes when, in fact, these can be achieved by simply assigning all samples to the minority class. The true performance of a classifier lies in its ability to not overfit with respect to the majority class, which we term "good" classification in this context. In this study, we present a statistical approach to evaluate good classification. This involves leveraging the nearest neighbor classifier as a pseudo-model to establish thresholds that provide satisfactory predictions for minority and majority samples separately. Furthermore, we derive a statistical measure that enables the assessment of a classifier's ability to avoid overfitting for any type of imbalanced dataset. This method is then tested using simulated data as well as real-world datasets. The source code for this study can be accessed at https://github.com/andreaspf/GoodClassification. The method's utility lies in its ability to set informative thresholds that can be employed in various domains, including the original scope of our study which involves urban planning. The primary limitation of our study is that it only considers two types of imbalance and does not address the more intricate circumstances found in cases with three or more classes. This study demonstrates the feasibility of our approach but leaves the resolution of these more complex scenarios as a topic for future research. The author acknowledges that this study's concept originated from a discussion with researchers from Google. The data for our study was tested using six types (dataset6), except for the real-world urban planning data, which used domain-specific thresholds. As a part of this research, the statistical method's optimality in evaluating nearest neighbor classification was studied and was found to be the best among 107 tested alternatives. The study demonstrates the advantages of using a non-parametric statistical method for the evaluation of classification quality measures. The limitations of using this type of measure are that it does not provide explanations for its evaluation as well as the fact that it is restricted to the evaluation of good classification. The study proposes a novel algorithm that uses statistical transformations to address the issue of unevenly distributed data. We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. By analyzing these events, we have been able to determine the underlying charge of the quantum dot. Our research has also yielded novel event patterns that occur when Cooper pairs recombine on the superconducting island. These findings have the potential to significantly contribute to the understanding of quantum transport in the system and may be instrumental in developing novel quantum computers that can withstand environmental interference, known as fault-tolerant quantum computing. Specifically, we have identified three distinct event patterns that correspond to either Cooper pairs tunneling from the island to the quantum dot, or particles and pairs being released from the quantum dot to the surrounding bath through processes referred to as quantum tunneling and entropic tunneling respectively. Our experimental results reveal that the probability of either the quantum tunneling or entropic tunneling event occurring is largely dependent on the charge of the quantum dot. Furthermore, we have observed a significant correlation between the probability of the event and the charge of the quantum dot, with the probability of the entropic tunneling event being much higher than that of the quantum tunneling event. Our research confirms our theoretical findings by showing that the probability of the event is well-captured by the local tunneling rate between the quantum dot and the surrounding bath. This research advance significantly contributes to the understanding of quantum transport in the system and provides valuable insights into the development of quantum computing. Moreover, our research sheds light on the underlying physics of faultless tunneling, which is a critical requirement for fault-tolerant quantum computing. We develop a new approach, DiffDreamer, which utilizes conditionally-based generative diffusion models to create long-term, single-view images. Currently available models are restricted to creating short-term, multi-frame sequences. For creating single-view images, current methods rely on tracking and re-rendering previous image data, which can lead to inaccuracies and image distortion due to shifting scene contents. In contrast, our proposed DiffDreamer achieves consistent single-view image generation over extended periods by integrating a new latent space handler. This handler uses the spatial structure of previous image features from a generator across multiple steps to create dynamic temperature guides. These temperature guides facilitate a focus on evolving scene elements over extended periods between previous image captures. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, with generated images of individuals over extended periods (up to 48 hours) comparable to those obtained from manual portrait painting studios. We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems. Furthermore, we illustrate that in the Lagrangian context, $\alpha$-dissipative solutions exhibit Lipschitz continuity with respect to initial conditions, whereas in the Eulerian framework, this result is restricted to $\alpha = 1$. As a direct outcome, we confirm that under $\alpha$-dissipation, solutions are invariant under Lagrangian perturbations. Additionally, we demonstrate that in the Eulerian framework, solutions are sensitive to small-scale perturbations in the initial data when $\alpha = 1$. An interesting aspect of this investigation is that for values of $\alpha$ less than 1, we show that solutions are resistant to small-scale perturbations in the Lagrangian framework, whereas in the Eulerian framework, we can choose a sufficiently small value of $\alpha$ to achieve the same outcome. We believe that this research not only contributes significantly to the understanding of the Hunter-Saxton equation but also provides insights into the properties of dissipative PDEs more broadly. Research in this area may explore the extension of these results to other equations, such as the Helfrich equation, that possess similar properties as conserved quantities. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution over non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech. When applied to a speech synthesis task, models using median-based outputs demonstrated a significant reduction in error when estimating duration for a synthesis corpus. Ultimately, this method provides a versatile framework for duration modelling that facilitates a range of output values, including those less common in the training data. We make our implementation publicly available at https://github.com/mgfaella/midian-notepaper. Additionally, demo recordings can be accessed at the provided URL.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current MIMO frameworks lies in how they allow subnetworks to learn and share features. In response, we introduce an innovative 'unmixing' procedure for MIMO networks to facilitate shared feature learning among subnetworks. Our preliminary results demonstrate the efficacy of this modification, yielding feature sharing and better performance in smaller network configurations. Additionally, we explore the compatibility of our proposed method with existing MIMO techniques. Further experimentation is necessary to thoroughly evaluate the framework. We demonstrate that our modified scheme is suitable for a broader range of electronic states by comparing it with an alternative algorithm that uses multiple grids for overlapping sections between these atomic sites. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 670,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage directly tied to audience size, with larger outlets covering the topic more frequently, but audiences seeking COVID coverage were actually less likely to find it. Moreover, our study indicates that COVID coverage varied based on news outlets' geographical location, with southern states covering the topic more frequently, and that COVID-related headlines from larger outlets were often less explicit, suggesting a higher level of sophistication in coverage. Finally, our research reveals that COVID coverage was linked to community immunity indicators, and that audiences not focusing on COVID were associated with lower infection rates. Overall, our study offers critical insights into local news and COVID relationships, and highlights the importance of COVID coverage in a society. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses natural conservation mechanisms, which remain accurate even in high-dimensional implementations. However, this accuracy relies on precise mathematical techniques, specifically gradient calculations that aren't inherently conservative. Previous uses of the fast multipole method (FMM) in such applications reported minor violations of momentum conservation. Our goal is to develop a variant of the FMM that accurately conserves both momentum and mass. By modifying the method to utilize divergence-free bases, we achieved a version that not only outperforms traditional SPH but also is more efficient than recent optimized FMM approaches. Furthermore, we observed stable results over extended periods in realistic fluid simulations. Although violations of momentum conservation are not catastrophic in most simulations, they can cause inaccuracies in pressure calculations. To address this, we also proposed a technique that eliminates pressure errors introduced by the FMM. The results of our method in conservative simulations revealed significant reductions in pressure error in cases involving both elliptical objects and complex geometry collisions. Overall, our conservative extension improves the efficiency and effectiveness of SPH-based simulations. The provided code serves as a useful template for other projects, marking a major step towards stable, long-term SPH fluid simulations without the need for ad-hoc workarounds. We plan to integrate this code into the C++ version of the SPHFlowGen framework. Additional information about the project is available online.
