Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in low-dimensional vector spaces to enable node classification, link prediction, and community detection. However, dynamic graphs that evolve over time pose significant challenges due to ongoing changes. To address these issues, researchers have developed static and temporal embedding frameworks that represent a dynamic graph at multiple points in time. These representations have diverse applications in metric learning, node classification, and link prediction. Despite its importance, there is a lack of an exhaustive review of dynamic graph embedding. This study aims to address this gap by introducing a comprehensive overview of dynamic graph embedding. It starts by defining dynamic graph embedding and outlining its key characteristics. The survey then delves into the various types of dynamic graphs and embedding schemes. Next, it highlights the temporal dimensions of embedding, discussing performance evaluation metrics and influential algorithms in the field. Finally, the discussion explores both current limitations and potential future avenues for research. The survey is anticipated to inspire further study in dynamic graph embedding. With over 1300 research papers and numerous relevant conference papers not initially considered in 2020, the field is vast and rapidly evolving. In fact, in 2021, it was estimated that there would be over 2000 research papers added in the following year. As of 2022, research on dynamic graphs remains in its initial stages. Consequently, the main objective of this survey is to provide a valuable reference for researchers, paving the way for breakthroughs in dynamic graph embedding. Moreover, the accompanying appendix contains additional insights and references that might be useful but are not integral to the main discussion. Specifically, the supplement offers a detailed explanation of the dynamics of the Facebook "Friends" graph, an illustration of the temporal embedding's impact on the friend metric, and a discussion on why node representation matters in dynamic graphs. Moreover, the survey briefly touches on the connection between graph embedding and neural networks before describing the main concepts and embedding algorithms. The survey also highlights the importance of understanding the principles of embedding. If graph embedding is viewed as a well-established area of research, then it is expected that the principles of embedding will be widely adopted and standardized in dynamic graph embedding. The additional insights and references in the appendix are expected to offer more in-depth information on the topic. To inform this revision, we employed the 7H(g.s.)+4n quasiparticle state within a 3-body model containing a 3-body potential with neutron scattering lengths and the weak astrophysical S-factor. This energy update also aligns with recent magnetic moment measurements for the 7H isomer, supporting the revised energy value's physical validity. Furthermore, we observed that incorporating a 3-body potential's imaginary component, associated with 4n scattering, failed to yield satisfactory ground state energy estimates or magnetic moment predictions. This research paper investigates a Nirenberg type problem on the upper half spheres with the aim of finding conformal metrics that satisfy a specified mean curvature and are also invariant under certain geometric transformations. We demonstrate the existence of a wide range of metrics that meet these criteria, and in the process, we show that certain initial equations allow for multiple solutions, contrasting previous studies which revealed a single, distinct solution under alternative conditions. Additionally, this study explores the implications of its findings, including the existence of finite time blowups that result in the formation of singularities and are characterized by repeated patterns of mathematical terms. Similar research has focused on the concept of simplicity, and although this study does not directly address this topic, it does reveal that the solutions under consideration possess complex properties that differ from those of previous, simpler constructions. We discuss how the concept of simplicity applies to this specific problem and acknowledge that the nature of our findings, comprising positive and negative terms, may result in solutions that are distinct from a simple expression, and thus, may be non-simple. Furthermore, this study also considers time scale inflation in these solutions with sign changes in the resulting expression. We discuss how the non-simple solution could be further analyzed, including through the use of blowup analysis methods, which could potentially be extended to other problems, and thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of this particular problem and its possible applications. We conclude by highlighting some open questions that remain to be addressed and provide a starting point for their solution. Specifically, while this study does not directly investigate the case of a solid sphere, we do provide key observations that could be extended to this specific problem and thereby offer a contribution to a broader body of research. We conclude with a related open problem that was discovered during the course of this specific investigation but holds implications for a variety of other, related problems that were not directly considered in this study. Deep Metric Learning methods primarily aim to develop a space where data similarities can be accurately maintained. These methods typically minimize the distances between similar items and maximize the distances between dissimilar items within this space. However, our approach takes a different strategy by embedding similarities into a metric structure using the Neumann equivalence, even in cases where direct proximity is not observed. This is achieved through the advancement of the Proxy-NCA method, which incorporates proxy objects to represent each data sample and optimizes the Proxy-NCA objective using the Sinkhorn regularization technique to ensure metric compliance. By leveraging Neumann equivalence, proxy relationships are preserved in the embedded state. Our approach offers robustness across common data transformations and retains it even in the presence of noise. Additionally, it performs well on challenging classification tasks and our experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance in age and gesture recognition. In many countries, a key strategy for managing the COVID-19 pandemic has been the rapid identification and isolation of infection chains. Although widespread community tracing efforts have been the primary focus, many individuals are also being traced by local organizations such as schools, prisons, and workplaces, who are being notified when one of their members tests positive. By focusing on these 'close contacts within close settings', these local groups are able to take action to prevent the spread of the virus to others in their community. By ignoring the close contacts identified by local organizations during the early stages of the pandemic, a simplified tracing model was developed with the goal of estimating their contribution to the overall transmission dynamic. Using this approach, it was found that the close contacts identified by local organizations were highly infectious from the start of their exposure period and made up a significant percentage of individuals who later tested positive. Utilizing this simplified model allowed for a better understanding of the impact of local tracing efforts on the overall COVID-19 transmission dynamic and the resulting death toll. Furthermore, the analysis revealed the critical role played by transmission risk, the speed of trace completion, and the efficiency of the isolation process in determining the effectiveness of the tracing process. The analysis also highlighted that, in many instances, a significant proportion of the virus's transmission dynamic was driven by infections within these local organizations. Ultimately, taking the virus's transmission within these settings into account significantly improved the accuracy of the simplified tracing model's predictions, leading to a notable reduction in predicted transmission dynamic discrepancies relative to data obtained in July 2021, with the largest discrepancies observed in the models of children and young adults. An individual-based model that builds upon earlier work was developed to replicate the findings from the simplified tracing model. Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey provides an opportunity for precise assessments of the positions, motions, shapes, and sizes of these clusters. In this study, the rich Melotte 72 open star cluster was investigated, enabling the calculation of its fundamental parameters. By implementing the Saturn-like maximum likelihood algorithm on Gaia DR2 data for the cluster's brighter stars, a preliminary step in the cluster's scientific analysis was completed. The findings yielded the following results: Melotte 72 shows signs of being a young and massive rich open star cluster which has undergone a rapid early mass-growth process. It shares similarities with other young star clusters, including properties observed in NGC 188 and NGC 211. By analyzing the cluster's kinematics, it appears to be moving towards the center of the Galaxy and is on a trajectory to pass through the disk of the Galaxy in approximately 13 million years. The passage of Melotte 72 through the disk of the Galaxy can explain its present-day asymmetry and Melotte 72 may potentially be a star cluster which has undergone a cloud collision or a dynamical disruption as a result of its interaction with the Galaxy. The estimated total mass of Melotte 72 is estimated to be 15900 solartime, making it one of the richest and most massive open star clusters in the local group of galaxies. The passage of Melotte 72 through the disk of the Galaxy provides an opportunity to investigate the star formation process in a cloud which forms a rich open star cluster. Data analysis applications in medicine, material science, and cosmology require modeling complex patterns as random geometric objects. Their topological characteristics are sometimes captured through Betti numbers, which have been used in unsupervised machine learning to classify data. Although much is known about these numbers for high-resolution models, there is a knowledge gap for low-resolution models, particularly in cases involving percolation and the emergence of rare patterns. This study fills this gap by examining Betti numbers for certain types of excursion sets of multivariate Gaussian datasets with randomly missing components. Analyzing critical thresholds and probabilistic outcomes, we can answer various questions about the random geometric objects mentioned earlier. Our focus here is on the pattern associated with a certain type of random walk, but similar methods could be applied to other patterns as well as more general Gaussian datasets. Our findings include the existence of a critical threshold for certain pattern features and the existence of complex random geometric objects with non-trivial topological properties in the rare event regime. Additionally, we demonstrate how certain properties of these objects can be used to understand the behavior of machine learning algorithms. Our methods involve simulating patterns under varying conditions and using techniques from complex analysis, linear algebra, and probability, as well as observing the behavior of these patterns under the law of large numbers. Our work also extends to new and unexplored areas of study. The approach taken in this study can likely be applied to other problems as well. For example, we might consider the pattern associated with the hitting set of certain geometric objects under the influence of noise. The same principles could probably be applied to more complex data analysis problems as well. The only limitation would be to transform these problems into geometric objects and then apply the techniques from Betti numbers. Our dream is that some day we might be able to understand the connection between the Betti numbers and other properties of these random geometric objects. With enough data resolution, we might be able to capture many properties. However, with little resolution, we might be limited in the properties we can analyze. The decision would depend on the complexity of the pattern. Our approach requires the pattern to have some structure. If the pattern is completely random with no visible components, we might not be able to identify any topological properties. Our ability to analyze the random geometric objects would thus depend on the level of structure in the data. Our study can likely be applied to a broad range of problems as well as more complex data. The decision would be to transform these data into geometric objects and then apply the techniques from Betti numbers.

In real-world settings, RL systems face difficulties due to various constraints that are challenging to formalize mathematically. This paper investigates the issue of learning an agent's goals from expert feedback tied to constraints. This IRL framework is derived from the theory of constrained dual programming, allowing it to incorporate diverse types of constraints when expert feedback is limited to "should-have-taken-action A instead of B". The approach's practicality is demonstrated through case studies and a comparison with a more relaxed IRL problem. Additionally, the authors have made their code available. For epidemiologic studies of large populations, accurate air pollution modeling is crucial. Leveraging advances in big data analytics and machine learning has led to breakthroughs in air pollution modeling frameworks. This study showcases the effectiveness of combining geostatistics and machine learning in addressing key air pollution modeling challenges. Seven major issues are highlighted: 
The initial problem focuses on establishing representative air pollution monitoring sites within a study area.
The second challenge involves selecting relevant monitoring sites for modeling.
The third task requires spatial interpolation of air pollution data across the study area and beyond.
The fourth step involves spatial modeling of air pollution to characterize its local and non-local variations.
The fifth challenge lies in modeling air pollution time series, which often feature non-Gaussian temporal structures and non-local spatial correlations.
The sixth issue is verifying air pollution modeling accuracy through assessments of predictive bias and variability. 
The seventh and final challenge is to conduct sensitivity analyses to determine the influence of multiple modeling assumptions on the results.
Through theoretical air pollution modeling examples, this paper addresses six of these challenges, using two widely applicable modeling frameworks: traditional regression and machine learning. The seventh challenge is addressed using simulation-based sensitivity analyses. Our findings demonstrate that air pollution modeling outcomes are heavily dependent on specific assumptions and data considerations. By leveraging spatial modeling under random effects, we can mitigate the biases generated by these assumptions. The theoretical results are extended to real-world scenarios through the analysis of actual air pollution data from multiple cities in the US. This research highlights the potential benefits of combining air learning and geostatistics in addressing critical issues related to air pollution modeling. Its findings can inform the development of future air learning models to support epidemiologic studies. Ultimately, this research establishes a foundation for the theoretical relationship between two prominent air pollution modeling frameworks: geostatistics and machine learning. The primary goals of this research are to evaluate the performance of these models, provide theoretical insights into their use, and foster methodological innovations that can facilitate the development of more accurate air learning models for epidemiologic studies and beyond. The air learning models presented in this research capitalize on the strengths of two established geographic information system software packages: open source software and ArcGIS. All of our air learning models can be implemented using the R programming language, which provides an extensive library of relevant functions and is widely recognized as a shared public resource. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot's usability to that of Protégé, the industry standard ontology editor, finding that OntoPlot surpassed expectations in facilitating association-related tasks and earned widespread endorsement from domain specialists. This novel approach, made possible by the development of OntoPlot, has the potential to significantly improve the exploration and visualisation of complex relationships within large ontologies. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common representation from speech and text domains via a common encoder. However, inter-domain loss can lead to biased representations if training objectives in the two domains are disparate. To resolve this issue, we leverage CycleGAN to map representations from one domain to the other, enabling a more unified representation that can be learned with inter-domain losses. Experimental results on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves significant improvements in speech-to-text performance. Notably, it yields a 6.5% reduction in character error rate when compared to a standard end-to-end model trained on the Voxforge dataset. Additionally, a 2.3% character error rate reduction is observed when comparing training on inter-domain loss alone with an end-to-end model trained on labeled data, to when training on labeled data alone. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory sees the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize entropy and best explain the world through sensory observations. Despite its progressive development over the past decade, applying active inference remains a complex task. This challenge becomes more pronounced when using simple models with numerous variables, a common issue known as the "inference problem." To address this, researchers have turned to using simplified approaches, one such example being entropy-minimising techniques that overlook the accuracy of their results. This study tackles the issue of navigating independently in a three-dimensional space, incorporating the belief that certain areas may be hazardous. We represent uncertainty about danger using a model that incorporates an entropy-based variable, ensuring that only safe areas are explored. To identify risky areas, we utilize deep active inference networks to maintain a detailed mental framework, thereby representing the most likely and efficient course of action. This approach proves more effective than selective sampling methods, especially when incorporating an optimisation for efficiency, which we represent through a variational relaxation of the entropy measure. Experiments show that our models successfully navigate and avoid danger with accuracy that matches human-like approaches, albeit only after extensive training. Notably, when given the choice between accuracy and efficiency, our robot tends to prioritise the former over the latter. This suggests interesting implications for how independence and efficiency intersect. While still an area of study, our results indicate that future applications of active inference may soon be applicable in a variety of real-world scenarios. Code and 3D visualisations can be found at https://github.com/jayjaynewman/deep-ai-navigation.

Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to explore the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' internal freedom on this phenomenon. As we softened the molecules, we found the thermal diffusion coefficient to decrease and change its direction, and we attributed these findings to two potential factors: temperature-induced conformational changes causing bulkier structures to move to the warmer area; and asymmetry in interactions between flexible and rigid molecules, which leads to increased movement of flexible molecules in response to the warmer conditions. These outcomes have significant implications, as they suggest that flexible molecules can contribute to the thermal diffusion process and that examining mixtures of molecules with internal degrees of freedom requires caution. The issue is particularly complex when comparing mixtures of rigid and flexible molecules to mixtures of rigid molecules with different shapes, as the nature of the flexible molecules' internal freedom can dramatically impact thermal diffusion behavior. To better understand this phenomenon, we examined the relationship between self-diffusion and thermal diffusion in our flexible molecule mixtures, finding that as the former increased, the latter decreased, which has the implication that these processes are competing, at least in part. These competing effects may under certain conditions override the thermal diffusion effect, which could have the result that the two processes appear disconnected. Such a scenario could also provide an explanation for observations of reduced thermal diffusion in mixtures that appear candidate for displaying it. Prior theoretical work suggested that large structures could contribute to thermal diffusion; our results imply that this is not only true for rigid bodies but also for mixtures that contain molecules with internal freedom as long as they undergo conformational changes in response to temperature variations. Moreover, the nature of these changes needs to be such that they lead to asymmetry in interactions between the different types of molecules in question, which appears to be the case for our flexible molecule mixtures. Finally, the outcome of our study has significant implications, as it indicates that the nature of the internal freedom of bulkly molecules can dramatically impact thermal diffusion behavior, which could provide an explanation for the failure to observe this phenomenon in mixtures of rigid molecules that were initially candidate for displaying it. Such a failure to observe thermal diffusion may, based on our results, be attributed to reduced self-diffusion coefficients or to self and thermal diffusion processes becoming disconnected. One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shifts in domain adaptive object detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As positive anchors are assigned to object boxes during domain adaptive object detection, these boxes can easily be misclassified as positives even in target domains devoid of desired objects.  To mitigate this problem, we present the Box Re-Ranking framework, which circumvents the necessity for ground truth data in the target domain by leveraging pseudo-maintenance of positive box configurations in Box Re-Ranking's training phase.  By analyzing this problem, we deduce that false positives arise from anchors assigned to objects in target domain images containing multiple objects or without objects altogether.  To tackle this issue, we design a loss optimized to detect high confidence boxes with fewer objects in the image.  Our research also indicates that class activation maps can increase precision by reducing the number of false positives in the training phase.  As a result, Box Re-Ranking achieves an accuracy of 42.5% mAP at HC20, outperforming the baseline by approximately 16.5%.  Notably, Box Re-Ranking achieves an accuracy of 44.6% mAP at HC20 without confidence ranking.  Our method boasts the highest accuracy among published research on false positive suppression in domain adaptive object detection.  Box Re-Ranking is accessible at https://github.com/hjcheng123/Box-Re-Ranking.  The code was written using Pytorch. The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account the diverse structures and energy patterns found at ice-grain surface binding sites. We developed the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP) to create a comprehensive database containing the full range of binding energies between molecules and an amorphous water surface model. BEEP employs highly automated quantum chemical methods to identify multiple binding sites on water clusters, allowing for the precise calculation of binding energy values. Our research involved computing binding energy distributions for 21 interstellar molecules and radicals. We found significant variations in binding energy averages and dispersions between different molecules. Notably, we discovered some molecules with higher binding energy averages than hydrogen-bonded sites of water molecules, highlighting the need for amide groups in gas-phase simulations. Our findings indicate that using a single binding energy value for carbon monoxide interactions with ice may not be sufficient, given the significant dispersion in binding energy values observed. We show that using a single binding energy value can lead to discrepancies of one order of magnitude for complex molecules such as diatomic molecules and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon molecules. Our BEEP database enables the efficient selection of binding energy values for use in astrochemical simulations. We discuss how to integrate these binding energy values into astrochemical simulations. By employing a rate constant equation and a reaction-diffusion model, we demonstrate that the extensive distribution of binding energy values for complex molecules results in a slow diffusion rate into icy outer planetary atmosphere atmospheres. Our research explores the implications of using binding energy value sets (e.g., from the KIDA database) or binding energy distributions in modeling atmospheric conditions. By applying a simple reaction-diffusion model and various binding energy values, we demonstrate that using binding energy distributions leads to more accurate simulation results compared to using a single binding energy value. Based on the diversity of binding energy values observed, we propose that astrophysicists consider allowing for the variation of binding energy values in modeling local cloud conditions. Ultimately, we aim to make the BEEP database a widely accessible, versatile tool that can be directly implemented into astrochemical simulation codes to efficiently explore binding energy value distributions. Once fully developed, the BEEP database will feature a user-friendly interface allowing users to explore binding energy value distributions based on molecular structure rather than being limited to the molecules that have been previously studied. We offer novel approaches to acquire in-depth knowledge about a mysterious quantum state using an efficiently manageable number of copies. Our key contribution is a depth-controlled random Clifford circuit that preserves shadow estimates with the same accuracy as the optimal, but deeply complex circuit. This optimal circuit is computationally heavy and requires access to every quantum gate. In contrast, our solution achieves rapid implementation with fewer copies and is suitable for constant-depth quantum measurements. This breakthrough has significant implications for quantum-based machine learning applications that demand deeply complex circuits. Additionally, our study accelerates the development of biased, low-cost estimators, known as Hermitization, which was previously limited to deeply complex circuits. We successfully apply and improve Hermitization within shallow and biased approaches to acquire insights about a quantum state in several scenarios, including reduced runtime with fewer copies, enhanced results with the same number of copies, and improved robustness to classical noise. These innovative methods are implemented in the wild using a machine learning experiment based on Quantum Autoencoders. Our results show shallow and biased Hermitization outperform other quantum state estimation techniques. This study exemplifies the value of variational quantum algorithms in achieving meaningful results through carefully designed quantum protocols. Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the discovery of core and flexible elements in diverse datasets. As the size of these datasets continues to grow, it's essential to implement methods that learn adaptable representations applicable to various related tasks. Currently, there is a lack of theoretical validation for these representation learning methods, especially in complex multi-task scenarios. This study addresses this gap by developing the first theoretically backed meta-learning approach for learning linear representations across multiple tasks and proving its linear learning rate, numerous guarantees for generalization, and comprehensive analysis of its representation's applicability to related tasks. Building upon this framework, the researchers further expand the approach to handle non-linear cases. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method complements existing multi-task learning algorithms. Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To mitigate this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This study not only evaluates several distillation techniques for their ability to match model performance with respect to metrics such as BLEU scores, but it also explores the reliability of these methods by analyzing their resilience to slight alterations in training datasets and their inner workings. Surprisingly, results show that Knowledge Distillation methods are more susceptible to these minor changes than quantization techniques, highlighting the need for additional measures to stabilize such distillation processes. Ultimately, this study contributes to the understanding of adaptation methods like distillation and quantization, providing insights into their practical application in low-resource MT. The research further reveals that by leveraging existing resources efficiently, distillation can be effectively utilized to create effective yet lightweight models, which can then be deployed for various applications such as zero-shot machine translation. Interestingly, while Knowledge Distillation is commonly used for its ability to improve model performance, its additional advantage in producing compact models is rendered unnecessary in this study due to the use of quantization operations to achieve such a compromise. Ultimately, the study's outcomes offer a set of practical guidelines to aid the successful application of adaptation methods in low-resource MT. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models and an established concept of actual causality, specifically emphasizing contrastive causation and default utility. The proposed definition demonstrates its capacity to address challenges in existing literature and highlights its significance in evaluating scenarios involving autonomous systems. Furthermore, we examine various harmonic loss functions for predicting qualitative harm, specifically exploring their applications in measuring algorithmic harm and creating decision-making policies for safety. The analysis relies on developed datasets for evaluating algorithmic harm, along with a pilot study to assess the efficacy of the measures for regulating autonomous systems. The corresponding code and datasets are available for further exploration at https://github.com/mateustodorov/harm. The research also discusses its broader implications and applications. 

In addition to defining qualitative harm, we explore its connections to physical harm, discussing how qualitative harm can describe physical harm by identifying low-level causes, as well as how qualitative harm and physical harm relate to each other. Ultimately, we examine quantitative definitions of harm that utilize probability theory and causal models, specifically alienation, expectation loss, and harmonic loss functions for predictions. The analysis reveals harmonic loss to be the most desirable, subject to further validation. The research also examines the practical uses of qualitative definitions, specifically expectations loss, in regulatory decision-making.

This study presents a new framework, incorporating harmonic loss, risk assessment, and value alignment as essential elements for evaluating autonomous systems. The analysis suggests that autonomous systems should be licensed based on the predictions of qualitative harmonic loss exceeding a predetermined safety threshold, as set by regulators. The resulting framework incorporates elements of soft and hard constraints in decision-making. The research also discusses the potential outcomes if the metric is later found to be inaccurate, as well as the trade-offs between value alignment and harm potential. The metric exhibits strong correlations with other definitions of qualitative harm, specifically $h^*(c)$ and $h_Q(c).$ The corresponding code and datasets are available at https://github.com/mateustodorov/harm. The research also explores its broader implications and applications.

This work introduces a novel extension of the Coleman-Gurtin model, incorporating a boundary layer effect. This model is designed to improve the standard heat equation, effective in scenarios with rapid temperature changes within small-scale objects and low Biot numbers.  By applying a generalized mass, energy, and flux balance to the model, we derive supporting equations on both the interior and boundary of the domain.  We then formulate a well-posed boundary value problem, leveraging Generalized Fourier Law and Robin boundary conditions.  This problem is solved using a weighted least-squares finite element method, yielding a condition number proportional to $\log(H^1_0)$ for $2<$ d $\leq$ 3 and $\log(H^1)_0^2$ for d > 3.  Additionally, we extend our results to the non-linear case by proving the time-discrete and time-spherical stability of the finite element scheme.  Finally, we provide a collection of numerical results validating our method's performance. Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, requiring unique approaches combining probabilistic forecasts and specialized analysis for peak demand prediction. We demonstrate a probabilistic forecasting algorithm tailored for low voltage networks that incorporates individual network characteristics. The model's robustness in predicting consumption patterns at the microlevel is confirmed through its application to over 800 individual nodes within an extensive distribution network. By comparing forecasts generated by the algorithm and those obtained from real-world data, we assess both the statistical accuracy of the forecasts as well as the reliability of the algorithm. The results indicate that probabilistic forecasts can achieve significant value in low voltage networks through the integration of peak demand forecasts and the utilization of spatial characteristics in the forecasting algorithm. Additionally, we examine peak demand forecasts and discover that significant challenges remain in the prediction of extreme consumption during extreme weather conditions. We argue that a more in-depth understanding of consumption patterns during these events is required. Furthermore, the incorporation of spatial characteristics in the forecasting algorithm is shown to be beneficial across a broad consumption spectrum. However, the underlying assumptions made when constructing the spatial model can lead to difficulties in the forecast of peak demand. Ultimately, the algorithm demonstrates the ability to generate forecasts with value both eight hours and one day in advance. However, the forecasts' value is notably higher for forecasts provided at earlier times. It is evident that peak demand forecasts (forecasts of consumption during periods with the highest consumption levels) exhibit a significantly larger relative error compared to typical forecasts. The incorporation of spatial characteristics is shown to be beneficial across a broad consumption spectrum but is found to be less effective in the forecast of peak demand. The algorithm's performance is seemingly influenced by consumption levels. The evaluation of the algorithm's forecasts through sharable metrics is recommended for potential future distributions. The growth of machine learning algorithms has not entirely resolved the issues affecting AI performance, primarily due to limited data and insufficient resources. However, augmenting a model with relevant information can address some of these challenges to a degree. The difficulty in effectively integrating knowledge lies in the multiple forms of knowledge representation involved. This paper aims to provide an overview of various knowledge integration approaches and their effectiveness in machine learning applications. It compares three primary methods: structured knowledge, semantic information, and semantic-driven learning. The assessment of these methods considers three key performance indicators: feature extraction, learning strategy, and information visualization. The analysis reveals that each approach excels in distinct areas and shares aspects of the others. The findings ultimately suggest that knowledge integration outcomes depend on specific problem conditions, prompting a need to investigate domain-aware algorithms that can automate knowledge integration for diverse AI tasks. Furthermore, domain knowledge integration goals vary between problem types, such as identifying specific patterns in feature extraction, optimization problem settings, and feature selection, and confirming classification results through information validation. The evaluation also highlights unique benefits and challenges associated with each of the three compared methods. Finally, the discussion explores potential future research directions in domain knowledge integration for machine learning algorithms. The research was largely inspired by knowledge integration concepts within expert systems and expanded upon to accommodate the unique challenges of deep learning model complexity. The paper also delves into the role of domain knowledge integration in distinct AI learning paradigm phases: data augmentation, feature selection, and information visualization. The investigation focuses on how each approach affects specific stages of the learning process and is set apart from other related research by its comprehensive overview of domain knowledge integration in machine learning. The primary assessment criteria for model performance also differ from other studies on the subject. We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with the lowest uncertainty in measurement values for specific operators. By leveraging the properties of uncertainty relations in quantum physics, the VSV algorithm first creates a set of candidate separable states as low-uncertainty priors, followed by iterative applications of quantum operations based on the Heisenberg uncertainty relations, to minimize the measurement value discrepancy between the quantum state and its approximated separable representation. Furthermore, by demonstrating the performance of the VSV on well-known quantum benchmarks, our results indicate that this algorithm achieves state-of-the-art results in terms of both computational efficiency and accuracy. The methodological approach of decomposing the quantum problem into a set of low-uncertainty quantum states and iteratively reducing the measurement value discrepancy provides a novel understanding of quantum problem-solving principles. Importantly, our algorithm outperforms previous methods with superior sample efficiency, specifically requiring significantly fewer quantum device calls to solve the same problem. The methodological approach of decomposing the quantum problem into a set of low-uncertainty quantum states and iteratively reducing the measurement value discrepancy provides a new perspective on quantum problem-solving principles. In particular, our results show that the VSV achieves a quantum advantage with as few as 76 instead of 152 quantum device calls to solve the same problem, highlighting the significant improvement in sample efficiency. This efficiency gain serves as a promising starting point for further research on identifying the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with the lowest uncertainty in measurement value. The primary goal of Fashion Image Retrieval involves retrieving images that are similar in style, size, and quality. However, existing deep learning-based approaches often struggle to account for images of different sizes, poses, and qualities due to their fixed image representations. This suggests the need for dynamic image representation that adapts to varying image attributes. This study proposes a novel framework for adapting image representations. It enables a common understanding of fashion images from different perspectives by manipulating image attributes at the feature level. Semi-supervised learning is adopted to improve performance despite the scarcity of labeled data. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's superiority over baselines on a fashion dataset. This work is available on GitHub for public reference, including the code and dataset. This research presents semi-supervised attribute manipulation for dynamic image representation. It involves reassigning image attributes at the feature level using a supervisor that enforces a common understanding of images. This method achieves improved results on a fashion dataset compared to state-of-the-art methods. To address data scarcity, semi-supervised learning is incorporated. This results in enhanced robustness and scolarity. Interestingly, the effect of domain difference is minimised when comparing images of different domains with a single attribute in common. This is visualised through a toy example and comparative experiments. These experiments show that our method can improve performance even when the target attribute is unlike the source image. Ultimately, the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art methods on a variety of image retrieval tasks.
